### What happened

`AV128Store` is the only store opcode absent from `unaryDst` in `src/cmd/internal/obj/wasm/wasmobj.go`. Every other store is listed: `AI32Store`, `AI64Store`, `AF32Store`, `AF64Store`, `AI32Store8`, `AI32Store16`, `AI64Store8`, `AI64Store16`, `AI64Store32`.

`appendp` routes a single argument based on that membership:

```go
case 1:
	if unaryDst[as] {
		p.From = obj.Addr{}
		p.To = args[0]
	} else {
		p.From = args[0]
		p.To = obj.Addr{}
	}
```

So `appendp(p, AV128Store, constAddr(offset))` stores the offset in `p.From` and zeroes `p.To`. But `assemble` reads the offset for that whole group from `p.To`:

```go
case AI32Store, AI64Store, AF32Store, AF64Store, AI32Store8, AI32Store16, AI64Store8, AI64Store16, AI64Store32, AV128Store:
	if p.To.Offset < 0 {
		panic("negative offset")
	}
	if p.To.Offset > math.MaxUint32 {
		ctxt.Diag("bad offset in %v", p)
	}
	writeUleb128(w, align(p.As))
	writeUleb128(w, uint64(p.To.Offset))
```

The result is that the memory offset encoded for every `v128.store` is 0, whatever offset the caller passed.

### Where it is reachable

Both wrapper generators use the one-argument form:

  - `wasmobj.go:880`, the `//go:wasmimport` wrapper
  - `wasmobj.go:946`, the `//go:wasmexport` wrapper

In both, the `AF64Store` line immediately above is correct, because `AF64Store` is in `unaryDst`.

`obj.WasmV128` is produced by `ssagen/abi.go:435` and `:480` when `t.IsSIMD()`, so this is reached by a `//go:wasmimport` or `//go:wasmexport` function with a SIMD-typed field. That requires `GOEXPERIMENT=SIMD`, so no default build is affected today, which is presumably why it has gone unnoticed.

Verified on master at dfc6f7db9b.

### Fix

Adding `AV128Store` to `unaryDst` makes it consistent with every other store and routes the offset to `p.To`, which is where `assemble` reads it.

This is the same class of bug as [CL 767782](https://go.dev/cl/767782) (#78799), "cmd/internal/obj/wasm: use p.To instead of p.From", which corrected a `p.From`/`p.To` mix-up in the same function.

I am happy to send a CL if this looks right. I wanted to check first in case the SIMD wasm path is still in flux and this is already known.

cc @cherrymui @khr, who reviewed [CL 767782](https://go.dev/cl/767782).

### govulncheck version

```
Go: go1.26.9
Scanner: govulncheck@v1.9.0
DB: https://vuln.go.dev
DB updated: 2026-10-08 22:31:09 +0000 UTC
```

### Does this issue reproduce at the latest version of golang.org/x/vuln?

Yes, with govulncheck v1.9.0.

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
CGO_ENABLED='1'
GO111MODULE=''
GOARCH='arm64'
GOARM64='v8.0'
GOFLAGS=''
GOOS='darwin'
GOPROXY='https://proxy.golang.org,direct'
GOSUMDB='sum.golang.org'
GOTOOLCHAIN='auto'
GOVERSION='go1.26.9'
```

### What did you do?

Hi! I'm one of the Traefik maintainers. I scanned a small module that depends on our current v2 LTS release, `github.com/traefik/traefik/v2@v2.11.59`, with `govulncheck -scan module` and with the default `govulncheck ./...`. The program only imports `github.com/traefik/traefik/v2/pkg/version` and prints `version.Version`.

### What did you see happen?

govulncheck reports 12 vulnerabilities in `github.com/traefik/traefik/v2@v2.11.59`, all with "Fixed in: N/A". The default symbol scan (`govulncheck ./...`) reports the same 12 ("Your code is affected by 12 vulnerabilities from 1 module"), even though the test program only prints `version.Version`, since these reports list no affected symbols. Most of them only exist in v3: their reports list all three Traefik modules (`github.com/traefik/traefik`, `/v2` and `/v3`), and the v1 and v2 entries have no version range, so every v1 and v2 release is flagged with no fix available.

Our advisories don't seem to be the cause. GHSA-6p8f-p8j2-rqmv only declares `github.com/traefik/traefik/v3`, and the GitHub Advisory Database entry only lists v3, yet GO-2026-6205 still marks v1 and v2 as affected. The same happens for GHSA-v67p-phpq-fc8x (GO-2026-6467), whose description even says that v2 isn't affected.

Scanners relying on the Go database show these to every v2 user, with a v3 release as the "fix". We opened golang/vulndb#6177 to fix the current ones.

### What did you expect to see?

Only the vulnerabilities that actually affect v2.

To avoid this for future reports, would it be possible, for Traefik, to build the module list from the reviewed GitHub advisory rather than adding every major version? Going forward, our advisories will list each affected module explicitly, so a module that isn't listed is out of scope on purpose.

If that isn't possible, we're happy to keep sending corrections as new reports come in. Just let us know whether you'd rather get them in one PR per batch or one per report.

Thanks!

### What did you do?

Hi! I'm one of the Traefik maintainers. I scanned a small module that depends on our current v2 LTS release, `github.com/traefik/traefik/v2@v2.11.59`, with `govulncheck -scan module` and with the default `govulncheck ./...`. The program only imports `github.com/traefik/traefik/v2/pkg/version` and prints `version.Version`.

### What did you see happen?

govulncheck reports 12 vulnerabilities in `github.com/traefik/traefik/v2@v2.11.59`, all with "Fixed in: N/A". The default symbol scan (`govulncheck ./...`) reports the same 12 ("Your code is affected by 12 vulnerabilities from 1 module"), even though the test program only prints `version.Version`, since these reports list no affected symbols. Most of them only exist in v3: their reports list all three Traefik modules (`github.com/traefik/traefik`, `/v2` and `/v3`), and the v1 and v2 entries have no version range, so every v1 and v2 release is flagged with no fix available.

Our advisories don't seem to be the cause. GHSA-6p8f-p8j2-rqmv only declares `github.com/traefik/traefik/v3`, and the GitHub Advisory Database entry only lists v3, yet GO-2026-6205 still marks v1 and v2 as affected. The same happens for GHSA-v67p-phpq-fc8x (GO-2026-6467), whose description even says that v2 isn't affected.

Scanners relying on the Go database show these to every v2 user, with a v3 release as the "fix". We opened golang/vulndb#6177 to fix the current ones.

### What did you expect to see?

Only the vulnerabilities that actually affect v2.

To avoid this for future reports, would it be possible, for Traefik, to build the module list from the reviewed GitHub advisory rather than adding every major version? Going forward, our advisories will list each affected module explicitly, so a module that isn't listed is out of scope on purpose.

If that isn't possible, we're happy to keep sending corrections as new reports come in. Just let us know whether you'd rather get them in one PR per batch or one per report.

Thanks!

### Go version

go version devel (master) darwin/arm64

### What did you do?

Profiled a program that makes many cgo callbacks (an EVM whose compiled code calls back into Go) on an Apple M4.

### What did you see happen?

`cgocallbackg1` calls `sys.DisableDIT` on every return from a callback when DIT was off on entry, which is the usual case. `DisableDIT` executes `MSR DIT, #0` unconditionally, so every callback writes PSTATE.DIT without changing it (plus the speculation barrier on darwin).

On an Apple M4, a loop calling `sys.DisableDIT` with DIT already off takes 2.72 ns per call, against 0.92 ns when the flag is read first and the write skipped. `BenchmarkCGoCallback` goes from 76.7 ns to 75.2 ns (−2%).

### What did you expect to see?

No write when DIT is already in the wanted state, as CL 729800 already does for `EnableDIT`.

A fix is in CL 849972.

### What did you do?

Ran the timeformat analyzer with fixes applied (for example `go vet -fix`, gopls quick fix, or `analysistest.RunWithSuggestedFixes`) on:

```go
package p

import "time"

func f(t time.Time) {
	_ = t.Format("Date:\t2006-02-01")
	_ = t.Format("é 2006-02-01")
}
```

### What did you expect to see?

```go
	_ = t.Format("Date:\t2006-01-02")
	_ = t.Format("é 2006-01-02")
```

### What did you see instead?

```go
	_ = t.Format("Date:\2006-01-021")
	_ = t.Format("Ȁ6-01-022-01")
```

The first result still compiles (`\200` is an octal escape), so the fix silently changes the layout string.

### Root cause

`badFormatAt` returns the index of `2006-02-01` within the constant string value, and `run` adds that index to the position of the literal plus one for the opening quote. That only matches the source text when the literal has no escape sequences (and, for raw strings, no carriage returns) before the bad format. With `\t`, `é` or `\x41` before it, the edit lands on the wrong bytes.

When the bad format itself is written with an escape, such as `"2006\x2d02-01"`, there is no verbatim text to replace, so no fix should be offered at all; today the fix rewrites it to `"2006-01-02-01"`.

```go
package main

import (
        "encoding/json"
        "fmt"
        "net"
        "os"
)

func main() {
        os.Setenv("GODEBUG", "netmarshal=1")

        hw := net.HardwareAddr{0x01, 0x02, 0x03} // 3 bytes: not 6, 8, or 20
        b, err := json.Marshal(hw)
        fmt.Printf("marshal:   %q err=%v\n", b, err)

        var hw2 net.HardwareAddr
        err = json.Unmarshal(b, &hw2)
        fmt.Printf("unmarshal: %v err=%v\n", hw2, err)
}
```

Before https://go.dev/cl/659315, `net.HardwareAddr` had no custom `MarshalText`/`UnmarshalText`, so `encoding/json` would fall back to base64 encoding, which round-trips for a byte slice of any length.

`HardwareAddr.String` now used in `HardwareAddr.MarshalText` performs no length validation and it hex-formats a byte slice of any length. But `ParseMAC` used in `HardwareAddr.UnarshalText` [only accepts 6, 8, or 20 byte addresses](https://go.googlesource.com/go/+/refs/heads/master/src/net/mac.go#50). So marshaling a `HardwareAddr` of some length other than 6, 8, or 20 succeeds, but the result cannot be unmarshaled back.

This is the same issue as #81749 for `IPMask`, fixed by https://go.dev/cl/848108

### What did you see happen?

```
marshal:   "01:02:03" err=<nil>
unmarshal:  err=address 01:02:03: invalid MAC address
```

`json.Marshal` succeeds and produces `"01:02:03"`, but `json.Unmarshal` of that same value fails.

### What did you expect to see?

The same result as when not setting `GODEBUG=netmarshal=1`:

```
marshal:   "\"AQID\"" err=<nil>
unmarshal: 01:02:03 err=<nil>
```

`HardwareAddr` values of arbitrary length previously round-tripped correctly through JSON. I think that backward-compatibility guarantee should be preserved under `GODEBUG=netmarshal=1` as well. `HardwareAddr.MarshalText` should similarly fall back to base64 encoding when its length is not one `ParseMAC` can parse, instead of silently producing JSON that can't be unmarshaled.

### Go version

go version go1.27.3 linux/amd64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
linux/amd64


Not OS-specific: the subprocess spawn happens on all platforms.
```

### What did you do?


`imports.Process` is used as a library by code generators that format each
generated file one by one (for example, the gf CLI calls it for every file
produced by `gf gen dao` — about 5 files per database table). Calling it
repeatedly on a file whose imports are already complete:

```go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "time"

    "golang.org/x/tools/imports"
)

func main() {
    src, err := os.ReadFile("input.go")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    _, _ = imports.Process("input.go", src, nil) // warmup
    for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
        start := time.Now()
        if _, err := imports.Process("input.go", src, nil); err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        fmt.Printf("run %d: %v\n", i, time.Since(start))
    }
}
```

with this `input.go` (imports complete, nothing to fix):

```go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "os"
)

func main() {
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stdout, "hello")
}
```

### What did you see happen?

When the file's imports are already complete, `getFixes` should return via the
in-memory happy path without spawning any subprocess — as in v0.26.0.
Per-call cost 0.12–0.75 ms, 0 subprocesses (verified with
`strace -f -e trace=execve`).

### What did you expect to see?

## What did you see instead?

Every call to `imports.Process` spawns a `go env -json ...` subprocess before
the happy path can return:

```text
$ strace -f -e trace=execve ./bench input.go 2>&1 | grep execve
execve("/usr/local/go/bin/go", ["go", "env", "-json", "GO111MODULE", "GOFLAGS",
     "GOINSECURE", "GOMOD", "GOMODCACHE", "GONOPROXY", "GONOSUMDB", "GOPATH",
     "GOPROXY", "GOROOT", "GOSUMDB", "GOWORK"], ...) = 0
```

Measured on the same machine (file with complete imports, 3 rounds):

| x/tools | per call | subprocesses per call |
| --- | --- | --- |
| v0.26.0 | 0.12–0.75 ms | 0 |
| v0.52.0 | 3.6–4.9 ms | 1 (`go env`) |

A single `go env` invocation costs ~5 ms on a local SSD here; on network
filesystems / slow disks it can be tens of milliseconds. For a code generator
that formats hundreds of generated files this adds up quickly: 100 tables ×
5 files ≈ 500 `go env` spawns ≈ +2.5 s locally, and far worse on slow disks.

## Root cause

`getFixes` unconditionally calls `env.goEnv()` before the happy path can
return:

```go
// internal/imports/fix.go (v0.52.0)
func getFixes(ctx context.Context, fset *token.FileSet, f *ast.File,
    filename string, env *ProcessEnv) ([]*ImportFix, error) {

    source, err := NewProcessEnvSource(env, filename, f.Name.Name)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    goEnv, err := env.goEnv() // <- spawns `go env` on EVERY call
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return getFixesWithSource(ctx, fset, f, filename, goEnv["GOROOT"], env.logf, source)
}
```

The only consumer of the resulting `GOROOT` is a self-import guard in
`addStdlibCandidates`:

```go
// internal/imports/fix.go:1231
if path.Base(pkg) == pass.f.Name.Name && filepath.Join(pass.goroot, "src", pkg) == pass.srcDir {
    return
}
```

`addStdlibCandidates` only runs on the slow path (after the first two passes
fail), so for files with complete imports the `go env` result is never used at
all.

Note that `ProcessEnv.Env` documents "Specifying all of requiredGoEnvVars
avoids a call to `go env`", but users of the public `imports.Process` API
cannot take advantage of that: it constructs a fresh `ProcessEnv{Env: nil}` on
every call. gopls is unaffected (it reuses a `ProcessEnv`), but library
consumers of `imports.Process` pay one `go env` spawn per file.

## Suggested fix

Resolve `GOROOT` lazily — it is only needed by `addStdlibCandidates`, which
runs solely on the slow path. Sketch:

```go
func getFixes(ctx context.Context, fset *token.FileSet, f *ast.File,
    filename string, env *ProcessEnv) ([]*ImportFix, error) {

    source, err := NewProcessEnvSource(env, filename, f.Name.Name)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    // GOROOT is only needed by addStdlibCandidates (slow path); resolve lazily.
    var (
        once      sync.Once
        goroot    string
        gorootErr error
    )
    getGoRoot := func() (string, error) {
        once.Do(func() {
            goEnv, err := env.goEnv()
            if err != nil {
                gorootErr = err
                return
            }
            goroot = goEnv["GOROOT"]
        })
        return goroot, gorootErr
    }
    return getFixesWithSource(ctx, fset, f, filename, getGoRoot, env.logf, source)
}
```

(`getFixesWithSource` / `computeFixesWithSource` would take a
`func() (string, error)` instead of a `string`; the exported `FixImports`
signature stays unchanged, so gopls and other callers are unaffected.)

With this change, formatting a file with complete imports requires zero
subprocesses, restoring v0.26.0 behavior, while the slow path still resolves
`GOROOT` on demand.

Happy to send a CL/PR if the approach sounds good.

@tiberiupetrache requested issue #75804 to be considered for backport to the next 1.26 minor release.

> @gopherbot please backport to Go 1.26
> 
> The fix (5a957dc, CL 774140) is on master and release-branch.go1.27 (CL 804900). release-branch.go1.26 still has the old condition in `stop` in `CoordinateFuzzing`:
> 
> ```go
> if err == fuzzCtx.Err() || isInterruptError(err) {
> ```
> 
> On go1.26.9 (windows/amd64), a fuzz target that cannot fail, run 1200 times with `-fuzztime=1s -parallel=8`, failed 3 times, each with no failing input:
> 
> ```go
> func FuzzNothing(f *testing.F) {
> 	f.Add([]byte("seed"))
> 	f.Fuzz(func(t *testing.T, b []byte) { _ = len(b) })
> }
> ```
> 
> ```
> --- FAIL: FuzzNothing (1.17s)
>     context deadline exceeded
> FAIL
> ```
> 
> The same harness on go1.27.3 failed 0 times in 1200 runs. We also hit it in CI on go1.26.9 linux/amd64 with `-fuzztime=60s`.
> 
> The race can also hide a real crash. If it hits while a crasher is being minimized, the deferred `writeToCorpus` in `CoordinateFuzzing` still writes the input to testdata/fuzz, but it wraps the error in a `crashError` only when `err == nil`. Here the error stays `context.DeadlineExceeded`, so "Failing input written to ..." is never printed and the crash looks like a timeout flake. The fix closes this path too.
> 
> The fix changes one condition in `stop`. The workaround, `-fuzztime=Nx`, replaces the time budget with an execution count.

### Go version

go version go1.27.1 darwin/arm64, golang.org/x/image v0.47.0 (also master at a998c07)

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
GOARCH='arm64'
GOOS='darwin'
GOVERSION='go1.27.1'
CGO_ENABLED='1'
GOFLAGS=''
GOPROXY='https://proxy.golang.org,direct'
GOTOOLCHAIN='auto'
```

### What did you do?

Decoded truncated TIFF input with `tiff.Decode` and `tiff.DecodeConfig`:

```go
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"image"
	"image/png"
	"io"

	"golang.org/x/image/tiff"
)

func main() {
	// A TIFF header whose IFD offset is past the end of the input.
	b := []byte("II*\x00\xf0\xff\xff\x7f")
	_, err := tiff.Decode(bytes.NewReader(b))
	fmt.Printf("tiff.Decode:       %v\n", err)
	_, err = tiff.DecodeConfig(bytes.NewReader(b))
	fmt.Printf("tiff.DecodeConfig: %v\n", err)
	_, err = tiff.Decode(struct{ io.Reader }{bytes.NewReader(b)})
	fmt.Printf("tiff.Decode, not an io.ReaderAt: %v\n", err)

	// Every prefix of a valid TIFF and a valid PNG.
	img := image.NewGray(image.Rect(0, 0, 16, 16))
	var t, p bytes.Buffer
	tiff.Encode(&t, img, nil)
	png.Encode(&p, img)
	count := func(data []byte, decode func(io.Reader) (image.Image, error)) map[error]int {
		m := map[error]int{}
		for n := range len(data) {
			_, err := decode(bytes.NewReader(data[:n]))
			m[err]++
		}
		return m
	}
	fmt.Printf("tiff prefixes (%d): %v\n", t.Len(), count(t.Bytes(), tiff.Decode))
	fmt.Printf("png prefixes (%d): %v\n", p.Len(), count(p.Bytes(), png.Decode))
}
```

### What did you see happen?

```
tiff.Decode:       EOF
tiff.DecodeConfig: EOF
tiff.Decode, not an io.ReaderAt: EOF
tiff prefixes (430): map[<nil>:20 EOF:402 unexpected EOF:8]
png prefixes (72): map[unexpected EOF:59 png: invalid format: not enough pixel data:7 png: invalid format: unexpected EOF:6]
```

`tiff.Decode` returns a bare `io.EOF` for 402 of the 430 prefixes. Only the prefixes shorter than the 8-byte header get `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF`. (The 20 prefixes that decode only drop trailing bytes the decoder does not read, such as the resolution values.)

The IFD reads, the reads of IFD values stored outside the entry, and the reads of uncompressed pixel data all pass `io.EOF` through. This happens with and without an `io.ReaderAt`.

### What did you expect to see?

`io.ErrUnexpectedEOF`, as `image/png` and `image/jpeg` return for truncated input. `io.EOF` means the input ended cleanly, not that the file was cut short.

#11391 reported this in 2015. [CL 205458](https://go.dev/cl/205458) closed it by fixing only input shorter than the 8-byte header, and `TestEOF` in `tiff/reader_test.go` checks just empty input.

Converting `io.EOF` to `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF` in `Decode` and `DecodeConfig` fixes it for every read path. I have that change with a test that decodes every prefix of a file, and can send it as a CL.

The following is an LLM-generated summary. The issue described is valid, to the best of my ability to determine. This was reported to us as a potential security issue; we feel that it is a non-security bug.

----

Value.SetIterKey and Value.SetIterValue construct the temporary Value for the current map entry using the full flag word of the map (iter.m.flag) instead of only its read-only bits (iter.m.flag.ro()):

```go
elem := Value{vtype, iterelem, iter.m.flag | flag(vtype.Kind()) | flagIndir}
elem = elem.assignTo("reflect.MapIter.SetValue", v.typ(), target)
typedmemmove(v.typ(), v.ptr, elem.ptr)
```

This causes two bugs where v.SetIterKey(iter) and v.SetIterValue(iter) diverge from their documented equivalents (v.Set(iter.Key()) and v.Set(iter.Value())):

1. Missing copy when assigning to an interface (flagAddr missing):
   When iter.m is a non-addressable map Value (such as from reflect.ValueOf(m)), iter.m.flag lacks flagAddr. When assigning the entry to an interface destination (e.g., any), packEfaceData assumes a Value without flagAddr owns immutable memory and skips copying the value. As a result, the destination interface holds a live pointer directly into the map's internal storage rather than a copy, so subsequent writes to that map key mutate the stored interface value.
2. Corrupted Kind for interface-typed map entries (Kind bits not masked):
   iter.m.flag retains the Map kind bits (21 / 0b10101). Bitwise OR-ing with Interface (20 / 0b10100) produces Map (0b10101). Because assignTo and valueInterface check whether the source Kind is Interface, an interface-typed map entry is not unwrapped; instead, it is boxed with the interface type itself as the dynamic type:
      * A nil interface entry (e.g., error(nil)) assigned into an any becomes a non-nil any.
      * Assigning an interface entry to another interface type with methods panics in ifaceE2I with *runtime.TypeAssertionError.

Reproduction:

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"reflect"
)

func main() {
	// 1. Aliasing map storage when assigning to an interface
	m := map[string]string{"k": "before"}
	var dst any
	iter := reflect.ValueOf(m).MapRange()
	iter.Next()
	reflect.ValueOf(&dst).Elem().SetIterValue(iter)

	m["k"] = "after"
	fmt.Println("dst:", dst) // prints "after", expected "before"

	// 2. Interface-typed map entry corrupted Kind
	m2 := map[string]error{"k": nil}
	var dst2 any
	iter2 := reflect.ValueOf(m2).MapRange()
	iter2.Next()
	reflect.ValueOf(&dst2).Elem().SetIterValue(iter2)

	fmt.Println("dst2 == nil:", dst2 == nil) // prints "false", expected "true"
}
```

### Go version

go version go1.27.3 linux/amd64; unchanged on master (c0be467486).

### What did you do?

Read conn.hijackLocked in src/net/http/server.go (lines 324 to 344 on master) and conn.serve.

```go
c.r.abortPendingRead()

c.hijackedv = true
rwc = c.rwc
rwc.SetDeadline(time.Time{})

if c.r.hasByte {
	if _, err := c.bufr.Peek(c.bufr.Buffered() + 1); err != nil {
		return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("unexpected Peek failure reading buffered byte: %v", err)
	}
}
```

### What did you see happen?

The connection is marked hijacked, and its deadlines cleared, before the Peek that collects the background read's byte. If that Peek fails, Hijack returns an error and no connection, but c.hijackedv stays true. conn.serve then takes the hijacked path after the handler returns: it releases the connReader and returns without closing the connection, the deferred cleanup skips c.close and the StateClosed hook because c.hijacked() is true, and setState was never reached so the hook never saw StateHijacked either. The net.Conn is only released when the garbage collector finalizes its descriptor.

The Peek cannot fail with the readers the server sets up today: with hasByte set, connReader.Read returns the stored byte without touching the socket, and the bufio.Reader can never be exactly full after a request's header has been consumed, so bufio.ErrBufferFull is out of reach. The defect is in the error path, which exists for a reason and should leave the connection in a consistent state.

### What did you expect to see?

A failed hijack leaves the connection with the server, as if Hijack had not been called, so the server closes it as usual and reports its state. That only needs the hijacked mark, the deadline reset and the writer hand-over to come after the Peek. I have a change ready, with a test that builds a connection whose buffer is exactly full with the background byte pending, so that the Peek fails deterministically.

as in Go 1.27. The first should also match strings.SplitN("foobar", "", 3).

### Go version

go version go1.27.3 linux/amd64, golang.org/x/net v0.61.0; unchanged on master (4af4fce62e).

### What did you do?

```go
n, err := dnsmessage.NewName(strings.Repeat("a", 64) + ".example.")
fmt.Println(err)
b := dnsmessage.NewBuilder(nil, dnsmessage.Header{})
b.StartQuestions()
err = b.Question(dnsmessage.Question{Name: n, Type: dnsmessage.TypeA, Class: dnsmessage.ClassINET})
fmt.Println(err)
```

### What did you see happen?

```
<nil>
Name: segment length too long
```

NewName checks only that the name fits in its 255 bytes (dns/dnsmessage/message.go, NewName), so a name with a label of 64 bytes or more is accepted and only fails later, when a Builder packs it, from a function the caller may not associate with the name. MustNewName panics for a name of 256 bytes but not for one with a 64-byte label, although neither can be carried by any message; RFC 1035 limits a label to 63 octets.

### What did you expect to see?

NewName to fail for a label longer than 63 bytes, with the packer's error "segment length too long", so that a bad name is reported where it is made. Names without a trailing dot, or with an empty label, would stay accepted: the package's tests require them to round-trip through String, and a caller may hold them without ever packing them. I have a change ready.

For some reason, net/http/cookiejar contains its own copy of the IDNA Punycode algorithm, and does its own IDNA translation. Naturally, it doesn't do it in the same way as net/http, and it can make different decisions on how to map Unicode names to ASCII than net/http does.

This was reported to us as a potential vulnerability. We don't believe this is a vulnerability, but it's super weird (that's a technical term) and we should be consistent about IDNA name translation.

> **Disclosure:** a coding agent (Claude Code) did this investigation and wrote this report, and I reviewed it before filing. All output below comes from local runs.

### Go version

```
go version go1.26.9 darwin/amd64
```

The same program also reproduces on go1.22.12, go1.24.13, go1.25.12, go1.26.10 and go1.27.3 (darwin/amd64), and on go1.26.9 linux/amd64. It does not reproduce on go1.21.13.

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

```shell
CGO_ENABLED='1'
GOAMD64='v1'
GOARCH='amd64'
GODEBUG=''
GOEXPERIMENT=''
GOFLAGS=''
GOHOSTARCH='amd64'
GOHOSTOS='darwin'
GOOS='darwin'
GOVERSION='go1.26.9'
```

(Intel Core i9-9980HK, macOS / Darwin 25.6.0.)

### What did you do?

The program below has no `unsafe`, no cgo, no finalizers and no data races. `f` takes a struct larger than 128 bytes by value. A closure that is not inlined reads it, so the closure captures it by address and the argument becomes a stack object. After the closure's call, the argument is dead. `f` drops every other reference to the object the argument points at, collects (which frees that object), and then calls `runtime.Goexit`. `f`'s deferred call collects again.

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"runtime"
)

type big struct {
	p   *[4]int
	pad [32]int // keeps big above the 128 bytes a closure captures by value
}

var (
	sink  *[4]int
	value int
)

//go:noinline
func use(p *[4]int) { value = p[0] }

//go:noinline
func call(fn func()) { fn() }

//go:noinline
func f(w big) {
	defer func() {
		runtime.GC()
		runtime.GC()
	}()
	call(func() { use(w.p) }) // w is address-taken, and dead after this
	sink = nil
	runtime.GC() // frees *w.p: nothing live points to it
	runtime.GC()
	runtime.Goexit()
}

func main() {
	fmt.Println(runtime.Version(), runtime.GOOS+"/"+runtime.GOARCH)
	for i := 0; i < 200; i++ {
		done := make(chan struct{})
		go func() {
			defer close(done)
			p := new([4]int)
			p[0] = i
			sink = p
			f(big{p: p})
		}()
		<-done
	}
	fmt.Println("no crash")
}
```

`GOMAXPROCS=4 go run .` (any `GOMAXPROCS` works)

### What did you see happen?

The program crashes on every run (5/5 on each version listed above). Depending on whether the freed slot was reused, it fails as either `found pointer to free object` or `found bad pointer in Go heap`.

With `GOEXPERIMENT=nogreenteagc`:

```
runtime: marked free object in span 0x12a8920, elemsize=32 freeindex=0 (bad use of unsafe.Pointer or having race conditions? try -d=checkptr or -race)
0x28f551d4e0c0 free  marked   zombie
000028f551d4e0c0: 00000000 00000000  00000000 00000000  ................
000028f551d4e0d0: 00000000 00000000  00000000 00000000  ................
fatal error: found pointer to free object
```

With the default (Green Tea) build:

```
runtime: pointer 0x1fee91bc4020 to unallocated span span.base()=0x1fee91bc4000 span.limit=0x1fee91bc5f80 span.state=0
runtime: found in object at *(0x1fee91b99ea0+0x0)
fatal error: found bad pointer in Go heap (incorrect use of unsafe or cgo?)

runtime stack:
runtime.throw({0x107a6305?, 0x6?})
	$GOROOT/src/runtime/panic.go:1229 +0x48
runtime.badPointer(0x1354c188, 0x1fee91bc4020, 0x1fee91b99ea0, 0x0)
	$GOROOT/src/runtime/mbitmap.go:1334 +0x165
runtime.findObject(0x700003b11c70?, 0x1fee91b99e88?, 0x108391c0?)
	$GOROOT/src/runtime/mbitmap.go:1386 +0x9e
runtime.scanblock(0x1fee91b99ea0, 0x8, 0x107a6ad0, 0x1fee91b51260, 0x700003b11d18)
	$GOROOT/src/runtime/mgcmark.go:1511 +0xdd
runtime.scanstack(0x1fee91b845a0, 0x1fee91b51260)
	$GOROOT/src/runtime/mgcmark.go:1038 +0x58e
runtime.markroot.func1()
	$GOROOT/src/runtime/mgcmark.go:306 +0xb1
```

`mgcmark.go:1038` is the `scanblock` in `scanstack`'s loop over reachable stack objects.

Controls on go1.26.9, 5 runs each:

- Remove `f`'s defer: 0/5 crashes.
- Shrink `pad` to `[4]int`, so the closure captures `w` by value and there is no stack object: 0/5.
- Replace `runtime.Goexit()` with `panic(...)`, with or without a `recover()` in the deferred call: 5/5.
- Build with `-race`: still crashes.

### What did you expect to see?

`no crash`.

### Analysis

This is our reading of the runtime source; we have not confirmed it with runtime instrumentation.

While `Goexit` (or a panic) runs `f`'s deferred call, `(*_panic).nextFrame` has set `p.fp = unsafe.Pointer(u.frame.fp)` for `f`'s frame. On amd64 `frame.argp == frame.fp`, so `_panic.fp` is exactly the address of `f`'s stack-argument area, which is where the stack object `w` lives. `scanstack` calls `state.putPtr(uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(gp._panic)), false)`, scans the `_panic` record precisely as a stack object, and so queues its `fp` (and `sp`, `startSP`, `slotsPtr`, ...) as pointers into the stack. `findObject` resolves `fp` to the stack object `w`, so `w` is treated as reachable and is scanned with its type even though it is dead at `f`'s PC. `w.p` was not marked by the earlier cycle (`w` was dead and unreachable then), so it was freed; the scan now greys a pointer to a free slot. The sweeper then reports a zombie, or the marker hits an unallocated span if the span was freed.

In other words, the frame-position fields of `_panic` (which are only there so the runtime can resume unwinding) act as liveness roots for stack objects. That resurrects dead stack objects that may hold dangling heap pointers. Go 1.21 does not reproduce. The 1.22 panic/defer rewrite, which introduced these fields, looks like the likely origin, but we have not bisected.

### How we found it

A real test suite hit this (race-built, darwin/amd64): `t.Skipf` → `runtime.Goexit` while a test-body frame holding a 224-byte struct argument was running its deferred `Close` of a database. `GODEBUG=gccheckmark=1` reported `checkmark found unmarked object`, with `found obj at *(base+0x18)`. That base was the test body's frame pointer, and the scan came from `scanstack`'s stack-object loop. In practice this means any test that skips or fails (`t.Skip*`, `t.Fatal*`) out of such a frame can crash the test binary.

Not verified: arm64, where `frame.argp = frame.fp + 8`, so `fp` may not fall inside the argument the same way.

Possibly related: #80799 (under Green Tea, `reportZombies` prints every slot `unmarked`, which hid the zombie in our first crashes).

```

`mgcmark.go:1038` is the `scanblock` in `scanstack`'s loop over reachable stack objects.

Controls on go1.26.9, 5 runs each:

- Remove `f`'s defer: 0/5 crashes.
- Shrink `pad` to `[4]int`, so the closure captures `w` by value and there is no stack object: 0/5.
- Replace `runtime.Goexit()` with `panic(...)`, with or without a `recover()` in the deferred call: 5/5.
- Build with `-race`: still crashes.

### What did you expect to see?

`no crash`.

### Analysis

This is our reading of the runtime source; we have not confirmed it with runtime instrumentation.

While `Goexit` (or a panic) runs `f`'s deferred call, `(*_panic).nextFrame` has set `p.fp = unsafe.Pointer(u.frame.fp)` for `f`'s frame. On amd64 `frame.argp == frame.fp`, so `_panic.fp` is exactly the address of `f`'s stack-argument area, which is where the stack object `w` lives. `scanstack` calls `state.putPtr(uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(gp._panic)), false)`, scans the `_panic` record precisely as a stack object, and so queues its `fp` (and `sp`, `startSP`, `slotsPtr`, ...) as pointers into the stack. `findObject` resolves `fp` to the stack object `w`, so `w` is treated as reachable and is scanned with its type even though it is dead at `f`'s PC. `w.p` was not marked by the earlier cycle (`w` was dead and unreachable then), so it was freed; the scan now greys a pointer to a free slot. The sweeper then reports a zombie, or the marker hits an unallocated span if the span was freed.

In other words, the frame-position fields of `_panic` (which are only there so the runtime can resume unwinding) act as liveness roots for stack objects. That resurrects dead stack objects that may hold dangling heap pointers. Go 1.21 does not reproduce. The 1.22 panic/defer rewrite, which introduced these fields, looks like the likely origin, but we have not bisected.

### How we found it

A real test suite hit this (race-built, darwin/amd64): `t.Skipf` → `runtime.Goexit` while a test-body frame holding a 224-byte struct argument was running its deferred `Close` of a database. `GODEBUG=gccheckmark=1` reported `checkmark found unmarked object`, with `found obj at *(base+0x18)`. That base was the test body's frame pointer, and the scan came from `scanstack`'s stack-object loop. In practice this means any test that skips or fails (`t.Skip*`, `t.Fatal*`) out of such a frame can crash the test binary.

Not verified: arm64, where `frame.argp = frame.fp + 8`, so `fp` may not fall inside the argument the same way.

Possibly related: #80799 (under Green Tea, `reportZombies` prints every slot `unmarked`, which hid the zombie in our first crashes).

Build mode: c-shared.
Android NDK r29 (29.0.14206865).
Device: Redmi 13, Android 16 (API 36), arm64-v8a.
```

### What did you do?

I built a small Go shared library with `GOOS=android`, `GOARCH=arm64` and `CGO_ENABLED=1` using `-buildmode=c-shared`, then loaded it on the phone from a C program. Before loading the library with dlopen, the program called `prctl(PR_SET_DUMPABLE, 0, 0, 0, 0)`, checked whether it could open `/proc/self/auxv`, and read `getauxval(AT_HWCAP)` from Android libc. After loading the library, it called an exported Go function that reported internal/cpu.HWCap. I repeated the same steps in a fresh process using `prctl(PR_SET_DUMPABLE, 1, 0, 0, 0)`. Both runs used the same library built with unmodified Go 1.27.2.


### What did you see happen?

With `dumpable=0`, Go did not detect AES or PMULL, even though Android libc's `getauxval(AT_HWCAP)` still returned `0x119fff`, which includes both features. Opening `/proc/self/auxv` failed with `EACCES`, and Go's internal/cpu.HWCap remained 0. AES-GCM therefore used the software implementation. With the same library loaded in a fresh process with `dumpable=1`, Go detected both features correctly. I got the same results in three runs of each case.

### What did you expect to see?

I expected Go to detect AES and PMULL on this device with both `dumpable=0` and `dumpable=1`, since Android libc reports those features in both cases. Go should be able to use hardware-accelerated AES-GCM when the CPU information is available through getauxval, even if `/proc/self/auxv` cannot be opened.

### What did you do?

Compiled a generated switch whose cases make distinct calls to a
non-inlined function:

```sh
python3 - <<'PY' > switch.go
n = 4000
print('package p')
print('//go:noinline')
print('func F(x int) int { return x }')
print('func Lookup(x int) int { switch x {')
for i in range(n):
    print(f'case {i}: return F({i * 3 + 1})')
print('}; return -1 }')
PY
go tool compile -d=ssa/prove/time switch.go
```

Repeated with 1,000, 2,000, 4,000 and 8,000 cases.

### What did you see happen?

Median prove-pass times over five runs on an Intel i9-13900K:

| Cases | Prove time |
| ---: | ---: |
| 1,000 | 0.88 ms |
| 2,000 | 3.24 ms |
| 4,000 | 12.40 ms |
| 8,000 | 69.13 ms |

The jump-table case in
[`getBranch`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/d8b7594888df608969f1f0045088d02d6f95c982/src/cmd/compile/internal/ssacompile/prove.go#L1797)
scans the successors for each case visited by prove. An 8,000-case CPU
profile attributes 60 ms of 360 ms sampled compiler CPU time to this
scan through `SparseTree.IsAncestorEq`.

[CL 841945](https://go.dev/cl/841945) changes traversal order in the same pass, but leaves this scan
unchanged.

### What did you expect to see?

Branch lookup should not scan the whole jump table for each direct
successor. This produces quadratic work as the number of cases grows.

### What happened

Building any package with SVE code under `-d=maymorestack` fails in the arm64 assembler:

```
$ GOEXPERIMENT=simd GOARCH=arm64 go test -c -gcflags='all=-d=maymorestack=runtime.mayMoreStackMove' simd/archsimd/internal/simd_test
illegal combination from SVE: 00004 (.../simd_test/simd_arm64_test.go:231)	ZSTR	Z0, 16(RSP)
illegal combination from SVE: 00008 (.../simd_test/simd_arm64_test.go:231)	ZSTR	Z1, 48(RSP)
illegal combination from SVE: 00048 (.../simd_test/simd_arm64_test.go:231)	ZLDR	16(RSP), Z0
illegal combination from SVE: 00052 (.../simd_test/simd_arm64_test.go:231)	ZLDR	48(RSP), Z1
```

`runtime.mayMoreStackPreempt` fails the same way. I saw this on master at d8b7594888, with go.dev/cl/840905 and go.dev/cl/840906 applied; those only touch runtime memmove.

### Cause (I think)

The maymorestack prologue spills and reloads register arguments with plain `ZSTR`/`ZLDR` at byte offsets from RSP. Those can't be encoded. Ordinary SVE spills go through `sveStackAddr` in `cmd/internal/obj/arm64/obj7.go`, which rewrites them to `MOVD $off(RSP), R27; ZSTR Zn, (R27)`. The maymorestack spill path doesn't seem to.

It doesn't break normal builds. I found it while trying to force stack moves to reproduce #82408.

### Summary

A template literal that contains an *unnecessary* escape (for example `\a`) followed later by an *invalid* escape (for example a truncated `\uc1`) crashes the parser with an uncaught `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of either compiling (tagged template, valid per the ES2018 template literal revision) or reporting a parse error (untagged template).

The real-world trigger is the swagger-ui 5.32.11 distribution bundles (`swagger-ui-bundle.js`, `swagger-ui.js`, `swagger-ui-es-bundle.js`, `swagger-ui-es-bundle-core.js`), which contain this sample value:

```js
"application/rtf": () => String.raw`{\rtf1\adeflang1025\ansi\ansicpg1252\uc1`
```

### Reproduction

`repro.js`:

```js
function tag(s) { return s.raw[0]; }
tag`\a\uc1`;
```

Node evaluates this fine (`s.raw[0]` is `\a\uc1`, the cooked value is `undefined` as the spec requires for a tagged template with an invalid escape).

```
java -jar closure-compiler-v20261019.jar --js repro.js
```

No other flags; it behaves the same with `--compilation_level SIMPLE --language_in STABLE --language_out NO_TRANSPILE --env BROWSER --warning_level QUIET`, and the same on `v20260811`.

```
java.lang.RuntimeException: Exception parsing "repro.js"
	at com.google.javascript.jscomp.parsing.ParserRunner.parse(ParserRunner.java:158)
	at com.google.javascript.jscomp.CompilerInput$JsAst.parse(CompilerInput.java:678)
	...
Caused by: java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException: Range [4, 8) out of bounds for length 6
	at java.base/java.lang.String.substring(String.java:2823)
	at com.google.javascript.jscomp.parsing.IRFactory.normalizeString(IRFactory.java:3996)
	at com.google.javascript.jscomp.parsing.IRFactory$TransformDispatcher.processTemplateLiteralToken(IRFactory.java:2440)
	at com.google.javascript.jscomp.parsing.IRFactory$TransformDispatcher.processTemplateLiteralPortion(IRFactory.java:2811)
	at com.google.javascript.jscomp.parsing.IRFactory$TransformDispatcher.process(IRFactory.java:3534)
	at com.google.javascript.jscomp.parsing.IRFactory.transform(IRFactory.java:1045)
	at com.google.javascript.jscomp.parsing.IRFactory$TransformDispatcher.processTemplateLiteral(IRFactory.java:2802)
```

(Line numbers from the `v20261019` jar; Java 21.)

Variants, all with the same `tag` function:

| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| ``tag`\uc1` `` | OK, emitted unchanged |
| ``tag`\uc1\a` `` | OK, emitted unchanged |
| ``tag`\r\uc1` `` | OK (`\r` is a valid escape, so no warning is recorded) |
| ``tag`\a\uc1` `` | **crash**, `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` |
| ``tag`\q\uc1` `` | **crash**, `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` |
| ``tag`\a\xg` `` | **crash**, `IllegalStateException: unexpected: g` |
| ``tag`\a\u{zz}` `` | **crash**, `NumberFormatException: For input string: ""` |
| ``var s = `\uc1`; `` (untagged) | correct `JSC_PARSE_ERROR Parse error. Hex digit expected` |
| ``var s = `\a\uc1`; `` (untagged) | **crash** instead of the parse error |

So the crash needs two escapes in one literal: a warning-level one first, then an invalid one.

### Cause

- `Scanner.skipTemplateCharacters` keeps only the first `SkipTemplateCharactersResult` that carries a message, regardless of its level ([Scanner.java#L1012-L1016](https://github.com/google/closure-compiler/blob/8c263671b5/src/com/google/javascript/jscomp/parsing/parser/Scanner.java#L1012-L1016)); `SkipTemplateCharactersResult.hasError()` is `errorMessage != null` ([L1384-L1385](https://github.com/google/closure-compiler/blob/8c263671b5/src/com/google/javascript/jscomp/parsing/parser/Scanner.java#L1384-L1385)). An "Unnecessary escape" `WARNING` for `\a` therefore masks the later "Hex digit expected" `ERROR` for `\uc1`.
- `TemplateLiteralToken.hasError()` only returns true for `ErrorLevel.ERROR` ([TemplateLiteralToken.java#L60](https://github.com/google/closure-compiler/blob/8c263671b5/src/com/google/javascript/jscomp/parsing/parser/TemplateLiteralToken.java#L60)), so `IRFactory.processTemplateLiteralToken` takes the "no error" path and calls `normalizeString` on the raw text ([IRFactory.java#L2452](https://github.com/google/closure-compiler/blob/8c263671b5/src/com/google/javascript/jscomp/parsing/IRFactory.java#L2452)).
- `normalizeString` assumes every escape is well formed and reads four characters after `\u` ([IRFactory.java#L4010-L4011](https://github.com/google/closure-compiler/blob/8c263671b5/src/com/google/javascript/jscomp/parsing/IRFactory.java#L4010-L4011)), which throws when the escape is truncated; the `\x` and `\u{...}` branches fail in their own ways as shown above.

A fix on the scanner side would be to let an `ERROR`-level result replace a previously recorded `WARNING`-level one in `skipTemplateCharacters` (check the level rather than `hasError()`), so the token is flagged and the cooked value becomes `null` as it already does when the invalid escape comes first. Making `normalizeString` defensive against malformed escapes would additionally turn any remaining cases into a reported parse error rather than an uncaught exception.

body_text:
`disableWarningsInGeneratedCode` does not suppress warnings in files annotated with `jakarta.annotation.Generated`

## Description

`-XepDisableWarningsInGeneratedCode` / `disableWarningsInGeneratedCode` does not suppress errors or warnings in Java source files annotated with `jakarta.annotation.Generated`, even though it does work for `javax.annotation.processing.Generated`.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Use Hibernate ORM 6.x (or any annotation processor that emits `@Generated` using `jakarta.annotation.Generated`)
2. Enable `disableWarningsInGeneratedCode` via the error-prone Gradle plugin or `-XepDisableWarningsInGeneratedCode`
3. Build — error-prone reports violations (e.g. `UnnecessarilyFullyQualified`) on the generated metamodel classes (`Analysis_.java`, etc.)

Hibernate's metamodel processor generates files like:

```java
import jakarta.annotation.Generated;

@StaticMetamodel(Analysis.class)
@Generated("org.hibernate.processor.HibernateProcessor")
public abstract class Analysis_ { ... }
```

Despite the `@Generated` annotation being present, error-prone does not treat the file as generated code.

## Root cause

`ASTHelpers.getGeneratedBy(Symbol)` uses `symbol.getRawAttributes()` to find `@Generated` annotations. `jakarta.annotation.Generated` has `@Retention(SOURCE)`, so during compilation the annotation is present in the source AST but appears not to be surfaced by `getRawAttributes()` in the way that error-prone expects. The result is that `SuppressionInfo.isGenerated()` returns `false` for these classes.

The name matching itself (`getSimpleName().contentEquals("Generated")`) is already package-agnostic and correct — the issue is purely about retention/attribute visibility.

This is the same class of problem as #1863 (Lombok's `@Retention(CLASS)` annotation being invisible), applied to `@Retention(SOURCE)`.

## Context

- `javax.annotation.processing.Generated` (Java 9+, `@Retention(SOURCE)`) — **works correctly**
- `jakarta.annotation.Generated` (Jakarta EE, `@Retention(SOURCE)`) — **not recognized**

Both annotations have identical simple names and identical retention policies, so the discrepancy is unexpected. It may be that `getRawAttributes()` populates differently for these two annotations in the javac symbol table, or that there is a special case somewhere that handles `javax.annotation.*` but not `jakarta.annotation.*`.

## Workaround

Exclude annotationProcessor output via `excludedPaths`:

```kotlin
options.errorprone {
    disableWarningsInGeneratedCode.set(true)

## Description

`-XepDisableWarningsInGeneratedCode` / `disableWarningsInGeneratedCode` does not suppress errors or warnings in Java source files annotated with `jakarta.annotation.Generated`, even though it does work for `javax.annotation.processing.Generated`.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Use Hibernate ORM 6.x (or any annotation processor that emits `@Generated` using `jakarta.annotation.Generated`)
2. Enable `disableWarningsInGeneratedCode` via the error-prone Gradle plugin or `-XepDisableWarningsInGeneratedCode`
3. Build — error-prone reports violations (e.g. `UnnecessarilyFullyQualified`) on the generated metamodel classes (`Analysis_.java`, etc.)

Hibernate's metamodel processor generates files like:

```java
import jakarta.annotation.Generated;

@StaticMetamodel(Analysis.class)
@Generated("org.hibernate.processor.HibernateProcessor")
public abstract class Analysis_ { ... }
```

Despite the `@Generated` annotation being present, error-prone does not treat the file as generated code.

## Root cause

`ASTHelpers.getGeneratedBy(Symbol)` uses `symbol.getRawAttributes()` to find `@Generated` annotations. `jakarta.annotation.Generated` has `@Retention(SOURCE)`, so during compilation the annotation is present in the source AST but appears not to be surfaced by `getRawAttributes()` in the way that error-prone expects. The result is that `SuppressionInfo.isGenerated()` returns `false` for these classes.

The name matching itself (`getSimpleName().contentEquals("Generated")`) is already package-agnostic and correct — the issue is purely about retention/attribute visibility.

This is the same class of problem as #1863 (Lombok's `@Retention(CLASS)` annotation being invisible), applied to `@Retention(SOURCE)`.

## Context

- `javax.annotation.processing.Generated` (Java 9+, `@Retention(SOURCE)`) — **works correctly**
- `jakarta.annotation.Generated` (Jakarta EE, `@Retention(SOURCE)`) — **not recognized**

Both annotations have identical simple names and identical retention policies, so the discrepancy is unexpected. It may be that `getRawAttributes()` populates differently for these two annotations in the javac symbol table, or that there is a special case somewhere that handles `javax.annotation.*` but not `jakarta.annotation.*`.

## Workaround

Exclude annotationProcessor output via `excludedPaths`:

```kotlin
options.errorprone {
    disableWarningsInGeneratedCode.set(true)
    excludedPaths.set(".*/build/generated/sources/annotationProcessor/.*")
}
```

## Environment

- Gradle error-prone plugin: net.ltgt.errorprone 4.1.0
- Hibernate ORM: 7.0.0.Final (metamodel processor uses `jakarta.annotation.Generated`)

### What version of Error Prone are you using?

2.50.0

### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release?

Yes. 2.50.0 is the latest release at time of writing, and the crash is present in every release
back to 2.36.0 — see the version table below. It is not a regression.

### What did you do?

`BadImport` crashes with `SourcePositionException` (aborting the whole compilation) when the
bad-named nested class it wants to qualify appears as the type of a **record component that also
carries an annotation whose `@Target` includes `ElementType.TYPE_USE`**.

This reproduces with **default Error Prone settings** — `BadImport` is on by default, so no
configuration is needed to hit it.

Three files, no dependencies beyond Error Prone itself:

`repro/model/Outer.java`

```java
package repro.model;

public class Outer {
  public enum Key {
    A
  }
}
```

`repro/TypeUse.java`

```java
package repro;

import java.lang.annotation.ElementType;
import java.lang.annotation.Target;

@Target(ElementType.TYPE_USE)
public @interface TypeUse {}
```

`repro/Repro.java`

```java
package repro;

import repro.model.Outer.Key;

public record Repro(@TypeUse Key key) {}
```

  -J--add-exports=jdk.compiler/com.sun.tools.javac.file=ALL-UNNAMED \
  -J--add-exports=jdk.compiler/com.sun.tools.javac.main=ALL-UNNAMED \
  -J--add-exports=jdk.compiler/com.sun.tools.javac.model=ALL-UNNAMED \
  -J--add-exports=jdk.compiler/com.sun.tools.javac.parser=ALL-UNNAMED \
  -J--add-exports=jdk.compiler/com.sun.tools.javac.processing=ALL-UNNAMED \

commonly-used names can make code harder to read [...] Here we recommend using qualified class:
Outer.

### Narrowing

Only the combination *record component* + *TYPE_USE-targeted annotation* crashes. Every other
shape of the same declaration produces a correct suggested fix:

| declaration                                                                | result                     |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| record component + TYPE_USE-targeted annotation                            | **CRASH**                  |
| record component, no annotation                                            | finding only, fix is clean |
| record component + FIELD / PARAMETER / METHOD / RECORD_COMPONENT-only annotation | finding only, fix is clean |
| class field / method parameter / return type / local + TYPE_USE annotation | finding only, fix is clean |

Further observations:

- Severity is irrelevant: it crashes at default severity, at `:WARN`, and at `:ERROR`.
- The generic wrapper is irrelevant: `@TypeUse Key key` and `@TypeUse Map<Key, String> key`
  crash identically.
- The reported start offset (`67` above) is the offset of the `@` of `@TypeUse`, **not** of the
  `Key` identifier at offset `76`. So the replacement region is being computed over the
  `AnnotatedType` node wrapping the component's type rather than over the identifier itself, and
  that node has no end position recorded (`-1`) — presumably because the record component's type
  tree is reached through a synthesized member rather than the original source tree.

### Is this a regression?

**No — it is not a regression.** It reproduces on every Error Prone release I could run on JDK 25:
**2.36.0 through 2.50.0, 15 consecutive releases** spanning 2024-11-19 to 2026-06-10.

| Error Prone       | result                                                                |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 2.50.0 (latest)   | **CRASH** — `SourcePositionException: invalid source position: [67, -1)` |
| 2.49.0            | **CRASH** — `SourcePositionException`                                 |
| 2.48.0            | **CRASH** — `SourcePositionException`                                 |
| 2.47.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException: invalid replacement: [67, -1)` |
| 2.46.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.45.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.44.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.43.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.42.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.41.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.40.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.39.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.38.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.37.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.36.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.35.1 and older  | not testable — Error Prone does not run on JDK 25 (`NoSuchFieldError: Class com.sun.tools.javac.code.TypeTag does not have member field 'UNKNOWN'` from `ASTHelpers.<clinit>`) |

Two notes on reading that table:

- The change of exception type at 2.48.0 is cosmetic, not behavioural: both are thrown from the
  same `Replacement.create` call site with the identical offsets `[67, -1)`.
  `SourcePositionException` is a wrapper introduced around the pre-existing
  `Preconditions.checkArgument` failure.
- The floor at 2.35.1 is a **JDK 25 incompatibility in Error Prone itself**, unrelated to this bug.
  I had only JDK 25 available, so I cannot say whether the crash predates 2.36.0 — only that it has
  been present in every release since.

Consequently there is no "pin to an older version" workaround; disabling `BadImport` is the only
option.

### Impact

Because an annotation with a `TYPE_USE` target is enough, this is easy to hit in ordinary code.
`jakarta.validation.constraints.@NotNull` (and the rest of Bean Validation) lists `TYPE_USE` among
its targets, so any validated record DTO whose component type is an imported nested class named
`Builder` / `Key` / `Type` / `Id` / `Factory` / … aborts the build. In our case a single such DTO
made `BadImport` unusable repository-wide, and there is no per-site suppression that helps because
the crash happens while rendering the fix for the *import* statement.

### Version history

Not a regression — it crashes in every release I tested, back to 2.30.0. Only the failure mode
changed: 2.36.0 introduced `SourcePositionException`, before that the same bad region surfaced as
`IllegalArgumentException`, and 2.35.1 and older report it as a generic unhandled plugin exception.

| Error Prone | Result | Reported as |
| ----------- | ------ | ----------- |
| 2.50.0 - 2.48.0 | CRASH | `SourcePositionException: invalid source position: [67, -1)` |
| 2.47.0 - 2.36.0 | CRASH | `IllegalArgumentException: invalid replacement: [67, -1)` |
| 2.35.1 - 2.30.0 | CRASH | unhandled exception thrown by the Error Prone plugin |

### Suggested direction

Either skip the fix (emit the finding without a `SuggestedFix`) when the end position of the
usage's enclosing tree is unavailable, or resolve the replacement region from the identifier node
rather than from its enclosing `AnnotatedType`.

### Narrowing

Only the combination *record component* + *TYPE_USE-targeted annotation* crashes. Every other
shape of the same declaration produces a correct suggested fix:

| declaration                                                                | result                     |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| record component + TYPE_USE-targeted annotation                            | **CRASH**                  |
| record component, no annotation                                            | finding only, fix is clean |
| record component + FIELD / PARAMETER / METHOD / RECORD_COMPONENT-only annotation | finding only, fix is clean |
| class field / method parameter / return type / local + TYPE_USE annotation | finding only, fix is clean |

Further observations:

- Severity is irrelevant: it crashes at default severity, at `:WARN`, and at `:ERROR`.
- The generic wrapper is irrelevant: `@TypeUse Key key` and `@TypeUse Map<Key, String> key`
  crash identically.
- The reported start offset (`67` above) is the offset of the `@` of `@TypeUse`, **not** of the
  `Key` identifier at offset `76`. So the replacement region is being computed over the
  `AnnotatedType` node wrapping the component's type rather than over the identifier itself, and
  that node has no end position recorded (`-1`) — presumably because the record component's type
  tree is reached through a synthesized member rather than the original source tree.

### Is this a regression?

**No — it is not a regression.** It reproduces on every Error Prone release I could run on JDK 25:
**2.36.0 through 2.50.0, 15 consecutive releases** spanning 2024-11-19 to 2026-06-10.

| Error Prone       | result                                                                |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 2.50.0 (latest)   | **CRASH** — `SourcePositionException: invalid source position: [67, -1)` |
| 2.49.0            | **CRASH** — `SourcePositionException`                                 |
| 2.48.0            | **CRASH** — `SourcePositionException`                                 |
| 2.47.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException: invalid replacement: [67, -1)` |
| 2.46.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.45.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.44.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.43.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.42.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.41.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.40.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.39.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.38.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.37.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.36.0            | **CRASH** — `IllegalArgumentException`                                |
| 2.35.1 and older  | not testable — Error Prone does not run on JDK 25 (`NoSuchFieldError: Class com.sun.tools.javac.code.TypeTag does not have member field 'UNKNOWN'` from `ASTHelpers.<clinit>`) |

Two notes on reading that table:

- The change of exception type at 2.48.0 is cosmetic, not behavioural: both are thrown from the
  same `Replacement.create` call site with the identical offsets `[67, -1)`.
  `SourcePositionException` is a wrapper introduced around the pre-existing
  `Preconditions.checkArgument` failure.
- The floor at 2.35.1 is a **JDK 25 incompatibility in Error Prone itself**, unrelated to this bug.
  I had only JDK 25 available, so I cannot say whether the crash predates 2.36.0 — only that it has
  been present in every release since.

Consequently there is no "pin to an older version" workaround; disabling `BadImport` is the only
option.

### Impact

Because an annotation with a `TYPE_USE` target is enough, this is easy to hit in ordinary code.
`jakarta.validation.constraints.@NotNull` (and the rest of Bean Validation) lists `TYPE_USE` among
its targets, so any validated record DTO whose component type is an imported nested class named
`Builder` / `Key` / `Type` / `Id` / `Factory` / … aborts the build. In our case a single such DTO
made `BadImport` unusable repository-wide, and there is no per-site suppression that helps because
the crash happens while rendering the fix for the *import* statement.

### Version history

Not a regression — it crashes in every release I tested, back to 2.30.0. Only the failure mode
changed: 2.36.0 introduced `SourcePositionException`, before that the same bad region surfaced as
`IllegalArgumentException`, and 2.35.1 and older report it as a generic unhandled plugin exception.

| Error Prone | Result | Reported as |
| ----------- | ------ | ----------- |
| 2.50.0 - 2.48.0 | CRASH | `SourcePositionException: invalid source position: [67, -1)` |
| 2.47.0 - 2.36.0 | CRASH | `IllegalArgumentException: invalid replacement: [67, -1)` |
| 2.35.1 - 2.30.0 | CRASH | unhandled exception thrown by the Error Prone plugin |

### Suggested direction

Either skip the fix (emit the finding without a `SuggestedFix`) when the end position of the
usage's enclosing tree is unavailable, or resolve the replacement region from the identifier node
rather than from its enclosing `AnnotatedType`.

body_text:
When a `BugChecker` throws from its constructor, a `CompilationTestHelper` test fails under the `en_US` locale with `ErrorProne suffered an internal crash`. Under `de_DE` the same test passes: the checker never runs, and `doTest()` returns normally. `ja_JP` and `zh_CN` behave like `de_DE`.

### Reproducer

`src/test/java/repro/ThrowingCheckerTest.java`:

```java
package repro;

import com.google.errorprone.BugPattern;
import com.google.errorprone.CompilationTestHelper;
import com.google.errorprone.bugpatterns.BugChecker;
import java.util.Locale;
import org.junit.Test;

public class ThrowingCheckerTest {

  @BugPattern(summary = "Fails to initialize", severity = BugPattern.SeverityLevel.ERROR)
  public static class ThrowingChecker extends BugChecker {
    public ThrowingChecker() {
      throw new IllegalStateException("checker failed to initialize");
    }
  }

  @Test
  public void checkerThatCannotBeConstructedFailsTheTest() {
    System.out.println("Locale.getDefault() = " + Locale.getDefault());
    CompilationTestHelper.newInstance(ThrowingChecker.class, getClass())
        .addSourceLines("Test.java", "class Test {}")
        .doTest();
  }
}
```

`build.gradle` (plus a `settings.gradle` with `rootProject.name = 'ep-locale'`):

```groovy
plugins { id 'java' }
repositories { mavenCentral() }
dependencies {
  testImplementation 'com.google.errorprone:error_prone_check_api:2.50.0'
  testImplementation 'com.google.errorprone:error_prone_test_helpers:2.50.0'
  testImplementation 'junit:junit:4.13.2'
}
test {
  jvmArgs(['api', 'code', 'comp', 'file', 'main', 'model', 'parser', 'processing', 'tree', 'util']
    .collect { "--add-exports=jdk.compiler/com.sun.tools.javac.$it=ALL-UNNAMED" })
  jvmArgs "-Duser.language=${findProperty('lang')}", "-Duser.country=${findProperty('country')}"
  testLogging { events 'passed', 'failed'; showStandardStreams = true }
  outputs.upToDateWhen { false }
}
```

```bash
gradle test -Plang=en -Pcountry=US
gradle test -Plang=de -Pcountry=DE
```

Under `en_US` the test fails, as expected:

```text
ThrowingCheckerTest > checkerThatCannotBeConstructedFailsTheTest STANDARD_OUT
    Locale.getDefault() = en_US
ThrowingCheckerTest > checkerThatCannotBeConstructedFailsTheTest FAILED
    com.google.common.truth.AssertionErrorWithFacts at ThrowingCheckerTest.java:23
1 test completed, 1 failed
```

```text
com.google.common.truth.AssertionErrorWithFacts: ErrorProne suffered an internal crash: An exception has occurred in the compiler (21.0.9). Please file a bug against the Java compiler via the Java bug reporting page (https://bugreport.java.com) after checking the Bug Database (https://bugs.java.com) for duplicates. Include your program, the following diagnostic, and the parameters passed to the Java compiler in your report. Thank you.
java.lang.AssertionError: com.google.errorprone.scanner.ErrorProneInjector$ProvisionException: Failed to initialize repro.ThrowingCheckerTest.ThrowingChecker
	at com.google.errorprone.ErrorProneAnalyzer.lambda$scansPlugins$2(ErrorProneAnalyzer.java:163)
```

Under `de_DE` it passes:

```text
ThrowingCheckerTest > checkerThatCannotBeConstructedFailsTheTest STANDARD_OUT
    Locale.getDefault() = de_DE
ThrowingCheckerTest > checkerThatCannotBeConstructedFailsTheTest PASSED
BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 1s
```

`ja_JP` and `zh_CN` pass the same way. `fr_FR` fails like `en_US`.

### Which tests are affected

Under `de_DE`, the crash goes unnoticed only where nothing else checks the diagnostics or the compilation result:

- A source with no `// BUG: Diagnostic ...` markers, and no `expectNoDiagnostics()` or `expectResult(...)`, passes. This is the reproducer above.
- A test that expects `doTest()` to throw because the checker cannot initialize, written as `assertThrows(AssertionError.class, helper::doTest)` with JUnit 4.13.2, fails with `expected java.lang.AssertionError to be thrown, but nothing was thrown`.
- `expectNoDiagnostics()` still fails, because the result check catches it: `Expected compilation result to be OK, but was ERROR. No diagnostics were emitted.`
- A source with a `// BUG: Diagnostic contains: x` marker still fails, because the expected diagnostic is missing: `Did not see an error on line 3 matching x. There were no errors.`

### Expected behavior

`doTest()` throws `AssertionError` with `ErrorProne suffered an internal crash: ...` whatever the JVM default locale is, as it does under `en_US`. Commit 5abc8e596df2c05e22b348c14df565d75cfeb150 (from #4112) added that check for this case, a checker that fails in its constructor.

### Cause (my reading of the code; the report above stands without it)

A checker constructor that throws is not reported as an `error.prone.crash` diagnostic: the checker is instantiated from `ErrorProneAnalyzer.finished` (see the stack trace above), and the exception propagates into javac, which prints its `msg.bug` banner and returns a failure from `JavacTask.call()`. `doTest()` recognizes that banner by its English text ([`CompilationTestHelper.java#L342-L344`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/f9edd2e3906ff3b5ed35d1a6feb4de9d3e0f7037/test_helpers/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/CompilationTestHelper.java#L342-L344) on master):

```java
assertWithMessage("ErrorProne suffered an internal crash: %s", stringifiedOutput)
    .that(stringifiedOutput)
    .doesNotContain("An exception has occurred in the compiler");
```

javac localizes `msg.bug`, and JDK 21.0.9 prints it in German, Japanese, and Simplified Chinese. This is the first line of the compiler output for the reproducer under `de_DE`, `ja_JP`, and `zh_CN`, read from the helper's private `outputStream` field after `doTest()` returned:

```text
Im Compiler (21.0.9) ist eine Ausnahme aufgetreten. Erstellen Sie auf der Java-Seite zum Melden von Bugs (https://bugreport.java.com) einen Bugbericht, nachdem Sie die Bugdatenbank (https://bugs.java.com) auf Duplikate geprüft haben. Geben Sie in Ihrem Bericht Ihr Programm, die folgende Diagnose und die Parameter an, die Sie dem Java-Compiler übergeben haben. Vielen Dank.
コンパイラで例外が発生しました(21.0.9)。バグ・データベース(https://bugs.java.com)で重複がないかをご確認のうえ、Javaのバグ・レポート・ページ(https://bugreport.java.com)から、Javaコンパイラに対するバグの登録をお願いいたします。レポートには、該当のプログラム、次の診断内容、およびJavaコンパイラに渡されたパラメータをご入力ください。ご協力ありがとうございます。
编译器 (21.0.9) 中出现异常错误。如果在 Bug Database (https://bugs.java.com) 中没有找到有关该错误的 Java 编译器 Bug，请通过 Java Bug 报告页 (https://bugreport.java.com) 提交 Java 编译器 Bug。请在报告中附上您的程序、以下诊断信息以及传递到 Java 编译器的参数。谢谢。
```

### A possible direction

In this case `JavacTask.call()` returns `false` and the diagnostic collector holds no diagnostics. I checked that by calling `BaseErrorProneJavaCompiler.getTask(...).call()` directly under `de_DE`: `call()=false diagnostics=0`. A result of `ERROR` with no error diagnostic would be a locale-independent signal. I have not checked whether a legitimate compilation failure can also produce it.

Setting the task locale does not help: with `task.setLocale(Locale.ENGLISH)` before `call()`, the banner under `de_DE` is still German.

### Versions

- Error Prone 2.50.0 (`error_prone_check_api`, `error_prone_test_helpers`). The string check is unchanged on master at f9edd2e3906ff3b5ed35d1a6feb4de9d3e0f7037.
- JDK: Amazon Corretto 21.0.9+10-LTS
- Gradle 9.8.0, JUnit 4.13.2
- macOS 26.5.1, aarch64

I searched the issues and pull requests for `locale`, `"An exception has occurred in the compiler"`, `CompilationTestHelper`, `user.language`, and `"suffered an internal crash"` and found no report of this. The nearest is #4112, which added the check.

NullAway found this when it added a locale axis to its CI test matrix (https://github.com/uber/NullAway/pull/1781): four tests in `ErrorProneCLIFlagsConfigTest` that expect NullAway to fail initialization stopped failing under `de_DE`.

`ja_JP` and `zh_CN` pass the same way. `fr_FR` fails like `en_US`.

### Which tests are affected

Under `de_DE`, the crash goes unnoticed only where nothing else checks the diagnostics or the compilation result:

- A source with no `// BUG: Diagnostic ...` markers, and no `expectNoDiagnostics()` or `expectResult(...)`, passes. This is the reproducer above.
- A test that expects `doTest()` to throw because the checker cannot initialize, written as `assertThrows(AssertionError.class, helper::doTest)` with JUnit 4.13.2, fails with `expected java.lang.AssertionError to be thrown, but nothing was thrown`.
- `expectNoDiagnostics()` still fails, because the result check catches it: `Expected compilation result to be OK, but was ERROR. No diagnostics were emitted.`
- A source with a `// BUG: Diagnostic contains: x` marker still fails, because the expected diagnostic is missing: `Did not see an error on line 3 matching x. There were no errors.`

### Expected behavior

`doTest()` throws `AssertionError` with `ErrorProne suffered an internal crash: ...` whatever the JVM default locale is, as it does under `en_US`. Commit 5abc8e596df2c05e22b348c14df565d75cfeb150 (from #4112) added that check for this case, a checker that fails in its constructor.

### Cause (my reading of the code; the report above stands without it)

A checker constructor that throws is not reported as an `error.prone.crash` diagnostic: the checker is instantiated from `ErrorProneAnalyzer.finished` (see the stack trace above), and the exception propagates into javac, which prints its `msg.bug` banner and returns a failure from `JavacTask.call()`. `doTest()` recognizes that banner by its English text ([`CompilationTestHelper.java#L342-L344`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/f9edd2e3906ff3b5ed35d1a6feb4de9d3e0f7037/test_helpers/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/CompilationTestHelper.java#L342-L344) on master):

```java
assertWithMessage("ErrorProne suffered an internal crash: %s", stringifiedOutput)
    .that(stringifiedOutput)
    .doesNotContain("An exception has occurred in the compiler");
```

javac localizes `msg.bug`, and JDK 21.0.9 prints it in German, Japanese, and Simplified Chinese. This is the first line of the compiler output for the reproducer under `de_DE`, `ja_JP`, and `zh_CN`, read from the helper's private `outputStream` field after `doTest()` returned:

```text
Im Compiler (21.0.9) ist eine Ausnahme aufgetreten. Erstellen Sie auf der Java-Seite zum Melden von Bugs (https://bugreport.java.com) einen Bugbericht, nachdem Sie die Bugdatenbank (https://bugs.java.com) auf Duplikate geprüft haben. Geben Sie in Ihrem Bericht Ihr Programm, die folgende Diagnose und die Parameter an, die Sie dem Java-Compiler übergeben haben. Vielen Dank.
コンパイラで例外が発生しました(21.0.9)。バグ・データベース(https://bugs.java.com)で重複がないかをご確認のうえ、Javaのバグ・レポート・ページ(https://bugreport.java.com)から、Javaコンパイラに対するバグの登録をお願いいたします。レポートには、該当のプログラム、次の診断内容、およびJavaコンパイラに渡されたパラメータをご入力ください。ご協力ありがとうございます。
编译器 (21.0.9) 中出现异常错误。如果在 Bug Database (https://bugs.java.com) 中没有找到有关该错误的 Java 编译器 Bug，请通过 Java Bug 报告页 (https://bugreport.java.com) 提交 Java 编译器 Bug。请在报告中附上您的程序、以下诊断信息以及传递到 Java 编译器的参数。谢谢。
```

### A possible direction

In this case `JavacTask.call()` returns `false` and the diagnostic collector holds no diagnostics. I checked that by calling `BaseErrorProneJavaCompiler.getTask(...).call()` directly under `de_DE`: `call()=false diagnostics=0`. A result of `ERROR` with no error diagnostic would be a locale-independent signal. I have not checked whether a legitimate compilation failure can also produce it.

Setting the task locale does not help: with `task.setLocale(Locale.ENGLISH)` before `call()`, the banner under `de_DE` is still German.

### Versions

- Error Prone 2.50.0 (`error_prone_check_api`, `error_prone_test_helpers`). The string check is unchanged on master at f9edd2e3906ff3b5ed35d1a6feb4de9d3e0f7037.
- JDK: Amazon Corretto 21.0.9+10-LTS
- Gradle 9.8.0, JUnit 4.13.2
- macOS 26.5.1, aarch64

I searched the issues and pull requests for `locale`, `"An exception has occurred in the compiler"`, `CompilationTestHelper`, `user.language`, and `"suffered an internal crash"` and found no report of this. The nearest is #4112, which added the check.

NullAway found this when it added a locale axis to its CI test matrix (https://github.com/uber/NullAway/pull/1781): four tests in `ErrorProneCLIFlagsConfigTest` that expect NullAway to fail initialization stopped failing under `de_DE`.

### Error Prone version

Error Prone 2.49.0 (javac 21.0.8, `--source/--target 21`)

### Affected checks

`AssignmentExpression`

### Description

`AssignmentExpression` produces different findings when redundant parentheses are added to or removed from an inner assignment. For example, `a = b = 0` is not flagged, while `a = (b = 0)` is flagged. Similarly, `result = (bresult = new byte[len])` is flagged, while `result = bresult = new byte[len]` is not. The reproducer also includes unchanged findings and non-findings to show the result at each assignment site.

Per JLS §15.8.5, parentheses around an expression do not change its value, type, or constant-expression status. Adding or removing these parentheses should therefore not change the check's findings at the corresponding sites.

I verified the following pair on Error Prone 2.49.0:

| Check | Rewrite | BEFORE | AFTER | Effect |
|---|---|:--:|:--:|---|
| `AssignmentExpression` | `a = b = 0` ↔ `a = (b = 0)` and the related sites below | 2 | 3 | verdict drift as parentheses are added/removed |

The matcher appears to depend on `ParenthesizedTree` nodes around assignments. A possible fix is to account for redundant parentheses when inspecting the assignment expression and its enclosing context, for example by using `ASTHelpers.stripParentheses` where appropriate.

### Reproducers

#### `AssignmentExpression` — verdict is not parenthesis-invariant

The check flags an assignment used inside a larger expression, but the result depends on redundant parentheses around the inner assignment — in **both** directions: `a = b = 0` is not flagged while `a = (b = 0)` is, whereas `result = (bresult = new byte[len])` is flagged while `result = bresult = new byte[len]` is not.

```java
// BEFORE — 2 findings (on `int i = j = 0;` and `result = (bresult = ...)`)
public class Sample {
  int a, b, j, l;
  byte[] bresult;
  void m1() { a = b = 0; }                        // NOT flagged
  void m2() { if ((a = b = 0) != 1) {} }          // NOT flagged
  void m3() { int i = j = 0; }                    // flagged
  void m4(int len) {
    int k = (l += 1);                             // NOT flagged
    byte[] result;
    result = (bresult = new byte[len]);           // flagged

}
```

    result = bresult = new byte[len];             // now NOT flagged

The `BEFORE` and `AFTER` versions should produce the same findings at each corresponding assignment site. Adding or removing redundant parentheses around an inner assignment should not change whether that site is reported.

### Actual behavior

The `BEFORE` version produces 2 findings, while the `AFTER` version produces 3. The findings change at individual sites as follows:

| Site | BEFORE | AFTER |
|---|---|---|
