With Error Prone 2.50.0 on JDK 25, `RemoveUnusedImports` reports an import as unused when it is only
referenced from a Markdown doc comment (JEP 467, `///`). It happens when javac runs in-process, e.g.
Maven's `maven-compiler-plugin` with the default `<fork>false</fork>`. The same source compiled with
`<fork>true</fork>` reports nothing.

The import is needed: removing it, as the suggested fix does, breaks javadoc with `error: reference
not found`. Classic `{@link List}` references are handled correctly in both modes.

```java
package example;

import java.util.List;

/// Wraps a [List].
final class MarkdownLink {}
```

```java
package example;

import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;

/// Delegates to ([Collections#unmodifiableList(List)].
final class MemberLink {}
```

```java
package example;

import java.util.List;

/**
 * Wraps a {@link List}.
 */
final class ClassicLink {}
```

`pom.xml`:

```xml
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
    <groupId>example</groupId>
    <artifactId>ep-md-repro</artifactId>
    <version>1.0</version>
    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>
    </properties>
    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.15.0</version>
                <configuration>
                    <compilerArgs>
                        <arg>-XDcompilePolicy=simple</arg>
                        <arg>--should-stop=ifError=FLOW</arg>
                        <arg>-Xplugin:ErrorProne -XepDisableAllChecks -Xep:RemoveUnusedImports:ERROR</arg>
                    </compilerArgs>
                    <annotationProcessorPaths>
                        <path>
                            <groupId>com.google.errorprone</groupId>
                            <artifactId>error_prone_core</artifactId>
                            <version>2.50.0</version>
                        </path>
                    </annotationProcessorPaths>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
```

`.mvn/jvm.config` holds the usual `--add-exports`/`--add-opens` flags for `jdk.compiler`, from
https://errorprone.info/docs/installation#maven.

`mvn compile` (OpenJDK 25.0.2, Maven 3.9.16):

```
[ERROR] MarkdownLink.java:[3,1] [RemoveUnusedImports] Unused imports: java.util.List
[ERROR] MemberLink.java:[3,1] [RemoveUnusedImports] Unused imports: java.util.Collections, java.util.List
```

`ClassicLink` is not reported. With `<fork>true</fork>` (and the same flags passed as `-J`
arguments), none of the three is reported.

Expected: imports referenced from Markdown doc comments count as used regardless of how javac is
invoked, as they do for `{@link}`.

body_text:
A check that decides by the context of an expression (the call it is an argument of, the variable it initializes, the assignment it is the right-hand side of) reads `state.getPath().getParentPath().getLeaf()`. When the user writes the expression in redundant parentheses, that parent is a `ParenthesizedTree`, the check's `instanceof` tests all fail, and the verdict changes although JLS §15.8.5 says the parenthesized expression is the same expression. `ASTHelpers` offers `stripParentheses` for looking down into an expression, and nothing for looking up out of the parentheses around it, so every check that gets this right carries its own loop, and a check that forgets it changes its findings under redundant parentheses.

### What happens today

`AssignmentExpression` checks one level of parentheses only ([`AssignmentExpression.java:59`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/AssignmentExpression.java#L59)), and for any other parent it compares the leaf it got directly. #6218 shows the result: `a = b = 0` is not flagged and `a = (b = 0)` is, because the parent of `b = 0` becomes a `ParenthesizedTree` instead of an `AssignmentTree`.

Five places in Error Prone already walk up through the parentheses, each with its own loop:

- [`TargetType.java:101-106`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/check_api/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/util/TargetType.java#L101-L106)
- [`HashCodeInObjectsHash.java:141`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/HashCodeInObjectsHash.java#L141)
- [`RandomCast.java:64`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/RandomCast.java#L64)
- [`EqualsGetClass.java:240`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/EqualsGetClass.java#L240) and [`EqualsGetClass.java:266`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/EqualsGetClass.java#L266)

Three more check exactly one level, which misses `((x))`: [`AssignmentExpression.java:59`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/AssignmentExpression.java#L59), [`BadInstanceof.java:81`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/BadInstanceof.java#L81), and [`PatternMatchingInstanceof.java:383`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/PatternMatchingInstanceof.java#L383).

The same gap reaches third-party checkers. Metamorphic testing of NullAway (wrapping expressions in redundant parentheses) found false positives in four places that compared the parent of a lambda, or the arguments of the enclosing call, with the unparenthesized tree:

- uber/NullAway#1999: `GenericsChecks` expected the parent of a lambda passed to unmarked code to be a `MethodInvocationTree`. `m.computeIfAbsent(key, (k -> null))` reported `returning @Nullable expression from method with @NonNull return type`, which the same call without the parentheses does not.
- uber/NullAway#2002: `SynchronousCallbackHandler` looked for the lambda among the arguments of its parent call, so a parenthesized callback passed to `Iterable.forEach` lost the access paths of the enclosing method.
- uber/NullAway#2010: `FluentFutureHandler` tested `methodInvocation.getArguments().contains(enclosingLambda)`. `Futures.transform(in, (s -> { return null; }), e)` reported `returning @Nullable expression from method with @NonNull return type`.

Each fix is a copy of the same loop, `while (path.getLeaf() instanceof ParenthesizedTree) path = path.getParentPath();`, or a `stripParentheses` applied to every argument before comparing it with the leaf.

### What I am asking for

A public method that answers "what is the parent of this expression, ignoring the parentheses around it". Acceptance: the five loops above call it and keep their behavior, and its test covers `x`, `(x)`, and `((x))` as an argument of a call, all three yielding the same `MethodInvocationTree`.

One possible shape, the name and the return type being yours to choose:

```java
/**
 * Returns the path to the outermost {@code ParenthesizedTree} that encloses the leaf of
 * {@code path}, or {@code path} itself when its parent is not parenthesized. The parent of the
 * returned path is the syntactic context of the expression.
 */
public static TreePath outermostParenthesized(TreePath path)
```

Returning the path rather than the parent leaf lets a caller find the argument index too, since the returned leaf is the element of `getArguments()`, which is what the `SynchronousCallbackHandler` fix needed.

### Out of scope

- Changing what `VisitorState.getPath()`, `findEnclosing`, or `findPathToEnclosing` return.

When the user writes the expression in redundant parentheses, that parent is a `ParenthesizedTree`, the check's `instanceof` tests all fail, and the verdict changes although JLS §15.8.5 says the parenthesized expression is the same expression. `ASTHelpers` offers `stripParentheses` for looking down into an expression, and nothing for looking up out of the parentheses around it, so every check that gets this right carries its own loop, and a check that forgets it changes its findings under redundant parentheses.

### What happens today

`AssignmentExpression` checks one level of parentheses only ([`AssignmentExpression.java:59`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/AssignmentExpression.java#L59)), and for any other parent it compares the leaf it got directly. #6218 shows the result: `a = b = 0` is not flagged and `a = (b = 0)` is, because the parent of `b = 0` becomes a `ParenthesizedTree` instead of an `AssignmentTree`.

- [`HashCodeInObjectsHash.java:141`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/HashCodeInObjectsHash.java#L141)
- [`RandomCast.java:64`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/RandomCast.java#L64)
- [`EqualsGetClass.java:240`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/EqualsGetClass.java#L240) and [`EqualsGetClass.java:266`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/EqualsGetClass.java#L266)

Three more check exactly one level, which misses `((x))`: [`AssignmentExpression.java:59`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/AssignmentExpression.java#L59), [`BadInstanceof.java:81`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/BadInstanceof.java#L81), and [`PatternMatchingInstanceof.java:383`](https://github.com/google/error-prone/blob/47eb5be1fe42c30d73b62cf0af272488ffbdebe1/core/src/main/java/com/google/errorprone/bugpatterns/PatternMatchingInstanceof.java#L383).

- uber/NullAway#1999: `GenericsChecks` expected the parent of a lambda passed to unmarked code to be a `MethodInvocationTree`. `m.computeIfAbsent(key, (k -> null))` reported `returning @Nullable expression from method with @NonNull return type`, which the same call without the parentheses does not.
- uber/NullAway#2002: `SynchronousCallbackHandler` looked for the lambda among the arguments of its parent call, so a parenthesized callback passed to `Iterable.forEach` lost the access paths of the enclosing method.
- uber/NullAway#2010: `FluentFutureHandler` tested `methodInvocation.getArguments().contains(enclosingLambda)`. `Futures.transform(in, (s -> { return null; }), e)` reported `returning @Nullable expression from method with @NonNull return type`.

 * Returns the path to the outermost {@code ParenthesizedTree} that encloses the leaf of

 * returned path is the syntactic context of the expression.

```

Hi — this is a friendly report from the [GLD Serializer Benchmark](https://github.com/leo-gan/GLD.SerializerBenchmark), an independent multi-language suite that times serializers **and** checks them against the published format specs (RFC 8259, YAML 1.2, …).

We measured **gson 2.14.0** on **Java**. The suite recorded spec-profile misses for this pin. The catalog is **report-only**: a miss is not a CI failure, and some cases are older or stricter profiles (for example RFC 4627 vs RFC 8259) rather than a crash.

## Compliance results (please start here)

This link opens the live heatmap on **Java** with **gson** already selected (All standards). Click a scored cell for each FAIL and the cited spec paragraph:

https://leo-gan.github.io/GLD.SerializerBenchmark/dashboard/#compliance/java/gson

- https://leo-gan.github.io/GLD.SerializerBenchmark/compliance/
- https://leo-gan.github.io/GLD.SerializerBenchmark/compliance/reading-results/

I am not pasting the case list here so you can use the Dashboard (filters, heatmap, and spec links) rather than a static dump.

Optional: one standard family only — `#compliance/java/gson/json` (or `yaml`, `cbor`, …).

Details table (this library pre-selected):

https://leo-gan.github.io/GLD.SerializerBenchmark/dashboard/?lang=java&ser=gson&data=document@n=1&mode=bytes#detailed-analytics

That page is the live L1 snapshot, not a claim that one library is “best.”

## Ask

Please look at the Compliance view for **gson**. If a miss is a real decoder/encoder bug you want to fix, great. If it is an intentional default (accepting NaN, YAML 1.1 bools, …), a short note here is enough — we will keep the catalog as-is unless the library’s documented contract changes.

Thanks for the library.

# Gson version
`main` at 854c825 (2.14.1-SNAPSHOT), which includes #3075

# Java / Android version
OpenJDK 21.0.10

# Used tools
- [ ] Maven; version:
- [ ] Gradle; version:
- [ ] ProGuard (attach the configuration file please); version:
- [x] None, plain `javac` / `java`

# Description
#3075 made `InetAddress` deserialization reject host names, unless `gson.allowDnsInetAddress` is set, so that deserialization does not perform host-name resolution. The check is a regex pre-filter, `.*:.*|[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+){3}`, followed by `InetAddress.getByName(s)`. The code comment assumes that any string the regex lets through which is not a valid IP literal is rejected by `getByName` without a lookup.

That does not hold. `InetAddress.getByName` treats the string as a literal only if it is a valid IPv4 literal, or if it starts with a hex digit, `:` or `[`. Everything else goes to the name service. The regex lets through two such kinds of string:

- IPv4-shaped strings with out-of-range parts, such as `"300.1.1.1"` or `"999.999.999.999"`.
- Strings that contain `:` but don't start with a hex digit, `:` or `[`, such as `"zz:1"`.

## Expected behavior
These strings are rejected with `JsonSyntaxException`, without any name lookup, like `"evil.example.com"` is.

## Actual behavior
They are resolved through the system name service. With the default resolver the lookup fails with `UnknownHostException: 300.1.1.1: Name or service not known`, after a real resolver query. With a hosts file that maps them, they resolve successfully:

```
inet evil.example.com -> JsonSyntaxException: Failed parsing 'evil.example.com' as InetAddress; at path $; to allow DNS addresses, set system property gson.allowDnsInetAddress to "true"
inet 300.1.1.1 => 300.1.1.1/10.9.9.9
inet zz:1 => zz:1/10.8.8.8
```

# Reproduction steps
```java
Gson gson = new Gson();
gson.fromJson("\"300.1.1.1\"", InetAddress.class);
gson.fromJson("\"zz:1\"", InetAddress.class);
```

Run with `-Djdk.net.hosts.file=hosts`, where `hosts` contains:

```
10.9.9.9 300.1.1.1
10.8.8.8 zz:1
```

This shows that the name service is consulted.

Possible fixes:
- Tighten the IPv4 branch to octets 0–255, and require the IPv6 branch to start with a hex digit, `:` or `[`. `getByName` then parses these strings as literals, and throws `UnknownHostException("invalid IPv6 address literal")` without a lookup for invalid ones.
- On JDK 22+, use `InetAddress.ofLiteral`.

# Exception stack trace
Not applicable. No exception is thrown when resolution succeeds.

Hi folks,

(Sorry for filing an issue, I wasn't sure how else to reach out to maintainers)

My name is Andrey, I'm xoogler and am leading Flakiness.io project. We do test analytics for GitHub and GitLab.

We'd like to collaborate with the Guava project:
- We would provide a free testing dashboard, with up to 100GB of storage for artifacts. The dashboard will show test reports, per-test statistics, detects flakiness and regressions in Pull Requests, and so on. I see you have a lot of different environments to run tests, so we hope that the dashboard will be useful for you.
- In exchange, we'd appreciate feedback on our project and JUnit integration.

We already support other open-source projects, here are some public dashboards:
- WordPress: https://flakiness.io/wordpress/gutenberg
- Nuxt: https://flakiness.io/nuxt/nuxt

Let me know if you find this interesting.

The project that I work on has some defences in place against supply chain attack, this requires that any code we either deploy or use during our product release process has to be signed by a verifiable signature. See [here ](https://shibboleth.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/DEV/pages/3269918721/Supply+Chain+Defence+for+the+Shibboleth+Java+Products)for the details

I am currently refreshing our dependencies and I see that version 5.1.0 (required by maven-core version 3.9.15 - I don't know they need such an old version) is signed with GPG key [0x5E975CB00C643DBF](https://keyserver.ubuntu.com/pks/lookup?search=0x5E975CB00C643DBF&fingerprint=on&op=index) 7.0.0 is signed by key [0xBEC27E87C49F2E2B](https://keyserver.ubuntu.com/pks/lookup?search=0xBEC27E87C49F2E2B&fingerprint=on&op=index)

It is extremely helpful to developers everywhere that software can be verified as coming from you.  In our case we cannot move forward important dependencies without it.  I would therefore be grateful if you could upload all your public keys to your git repository (or any of the other places noted in the link above).

Thank you

Rod

body_text:
### Problem

HTTP and Artifactory uploads configured with `trusted_certificates` or client-certificate settings construct a fresh transport for every artifact attempt. [Request execution calls the client factory each time](https://github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser/blob/628c889d7f2a34066649833be419fdb9abe01174/internal/http/http.go#L387-L429), including [retries](https://github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser/blob/628c889d7f2a34066649833be419fdb9abe01174/internal/http/http.go#L345-L364). Those custom transports have no idle timeout or owner cleanup.

### Evidence

Independent local TLS tests exercised both real publishing pipes with three sequential artifacts. Production created three TCP connections and TLS handshakes; one retry per artifact created six. Equivalent shared-client controls used one connection in either case, with matching payloads, authentication, headers, and TLS verification. Custom idle connections remained after publication, context cancellation, and GC, until explicit server cleanup. Empty responses excluded unread response bodies as the cause. Client-certificate and trusted-certificate cases were covered. These are connection/resource observations, not a wall-time benchmark or public-service failure.

### Correction

Share one client per upload configuration, then close only its owned custom transport after all workers finish, including error paths. Do not close the borrowed default client or share credentials across configurations. Add local regressions for connection reuse, retries, retained TLS/authentication behavior, and owned-resource cleanup.

---

HTTP and Artifactory uploads configured with `trusted_certificates` or client-certificate settings construct a fresh transport for every artifact attempt. [Request execution calls the client factory each time](https://github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser/blob/628c889d7f2a34066649833be419fdb9abe01174/internal/http/http.go#L387-L429), including [retries](https://github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser/blob/628c889d7f2a34066649833be419fdb9abe01174/internal/http/http.go#L345-L364). Those custom transports have no idle timeout or owner cleanup.

### Evidence

Independent local TLS tests exercised both real publishing pipes with three sequential artifacts. Production created three TCP connections and TLS handshakes; one retry per artifact created six. Equivalent shared-client controls used one connection in either case, with matching payloads, authentication, headers, and TLS verification. Custom idle connections remained after publication, context cancellation, and GC, until explicit server cleanup. Empty responses excluded unread response bodies as the cause. Client-certificate and trusted-certificate cases were covered. These are connection/resource observations, not a wall-time benchmark or public-service failure.

### Correction

Share one client per upload configuration, then close only its owned custom transport after all workers finish, including error paths. Do not close the borrowed default client or share credentials across configurations. Add local regressions for connection reuse, retries, retained TLS/authentication behavior, and owned-resource cleanup.

body_text:
The queue works well, but it adds noticeable latency to simple requests compared with a plain HTTP call. For Gradio 7 we want queued endpoints to be about as fast as a regular request, so using the queue is an easy choice for any app.

**Scope**
- Profile where time goes for a trivial queued function (join → SSE open → process → result), both on the Python and JS client sides
- Reduce round trips and per-event overhead (e.g. faster paths for events that don't need to wait)
- Add a benchmark so we can track regressions

**Acceptance**
- A benchmark showing queued vs. non-queued latency for a no-op function, with the gap brought close to zero

body_text:
When several Gradio apps run locally at once (e.g. through Pinokio), each has its own queue. Heavy jobs in different apps can run at the same time and cause out-of-memory errors.

**Proposal**
Let local Gradio apps optionally share one queue, so jobs across apps are scheduled together and don't compete for the same GPU/RAM.

**Open design questions**
- Backing store: a file/SQLite-based queue, Redis, or a small local coordinator process?
- How apps opt in (e.g. a `launch()` parameter or environment variable)
- How concurrency limits apply across apps (per-app vs. global)
- What users see in the UI when their job is waiting on another app's job

Today a user has to wait for a generation to finish before submitting another one. Users should be able to submit several generations into the queue by default, and those jobs should be placed in the queue in a sensible way (e.g. so one user can't crowd out everyone else).

**Things to design**
- UI for several pending/in-progress jobs from the same user on the same event
- Queue placement for a user's second, third, etc. job (e.g. round-robin between users rather than FIFO)
- Per-user limits and how they interact with `concurrency_limit`
- How outputs from several jobs are shown

Before the Gradio 7 launch, do a full security audit of Gradio and confirm it is safe to run both locally and on Hugging Face Spaces.

**Scope (to refine)**
- File access and upload/download routes (allowed/blocked paths, `gr.File`, caching)

body_text:
Gradio's components are secure, responsive and accessible. Developers building `gr.Server` apps (or non-Gradio apps) should be able to reuse them easily.

**Proposal**
Make it simple to get the source of any Gradio component, as Svelte or plain HTML/JS, and drop it into your own frontend. Possible approaches:
- A CLI command that copies a component's source into your project (similar to `shadcn add`)
- Standalone builds/web components that can be used without the full Gradio frontend
- Docs showing how to wire the component to a `gr.Server` endpoint via `@gradio/client`

body_text:
OAuth is easy when using Hugging Face as the provider, but setting it up with other providers (Google, GitHub, generic OIDC, etc.) is painful right now.

**Proposal**
- Built-in support for common OAuth/OIDC providers with the same simple API as HF OAuth (e.g. `gr.LoginButton(provider=...)`)
- Works for Blocks apps and `gr.Server` apps
- Consistent with the MCP + OAuth work in #11472

Related: #8592 (custom login page), #11472 (HF OAuth with MCP)

body_text:
We want Gradio to be a lightweight alternative to FastAPI for any app, including `gr.Server` apps that don't use Gradio's built-in components.

**Proposal**
- Make the base `pip install gradio` minimal: server, queue, client, and `gr.Server`
- Move the UI components and their heavy dependencies (e.g. image/audio/video processing, pandas) to an optional extra: `pip install gradio[components]`
- Show a clear error message when a component is used without the extra installed

**Considerations**
- Migration path and messaging for existing users (this is a breaking change for Gradio 7)
- Spaces' default Gradio SDK install should probably include the extra
- Measure install size and import time before and after

body_text:
A frustrating experience on Spaces is running a prediction that just fails with a generic "Error" and no details. Consider making `show_error=True` the default so users get an informative message.

**Tasks**
- Audit the ~100 most popular Spaces to check whether showing exception messages by default would leak sensitive information
- Based on that, decide whether to change the default, or to show a sanitized message (exception type and message, no traceback)
- Update docs to explain the behavior and how to opt out

Related: #11149 (better UX around errors)

Also make sure computing ETAs adds no noticeable overhead to the queue.

# Problem

Currently, Gradio maintains session state entirely in-process memory. If the server is restarted or scaled, the user will lose the state. This will result in a frustrating experience, particularly in applications that are time-consuming or require continuity, such as audio and video processing.

The documentation suggests to enable stickiness here: https://gradio.app/guides/deploying-gradio-with-docker#enable-stickiness-for-multiple-replicas

Probably it works but it appears to be a handicap given the availability of various tools designed to maintain reliability in applications where high RPS is expected.

## Scenario

A simple demo helps you to reproduce the problem:

```python
# demo/multi_replica_counter/run.py

import gradio as gr


def turn(counter, request: gr.Request):
    counter = (counter or 0) + 1
    return counter, f"count={counter} session={request.session_hash}"


def show(request: gr.Request):
    return 0, f"session={request.session_hash} (fresh page load)"


with gr.Blocks() as demo:
    gr.Markdown("## Session counter (one per tab)")
    state = gr.State(0)
    out = gr.Textbox(label="last turn")
    btn = gr.Button("turn")
    btn.click(turn, state, [state, out], api_name="turn")
    demo.load(show, None, [state, out])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo.launch()
```

1. run this demo `python demo/multi_replica_counter/run.py`.
2. visit this url on the browser: http://127.0.0.1:7860
3. click turn button. it will count, 1, 2, 3..
4. stop the demo server, and rerun.
5. come back to browser, don't refresh the page for staying in the same session. click turn button.

### What's happening?

It starts to count from zero.

### What do we expect?

Continue to count from the last number: 4, 5, 6...

# Solution Suggestion

I noticed that the Redis solution has been discussed previously. Some users do not favor it as an alternative; however, if Kubernetes, Docker Compose, or cloud tools are used in the development environment, I see no issue with using Redis, Valkey, or Upstash. If we make this pluggable, we can leave the choice to the developer. Also, the developer can configure the redis client using Helm, environment variables by the traffic, cloud capacity, etc.

I started to work on the suggestion here: 
https://github.com/gkmngrgn/gradio/pull/2

This proposal introduces a pluggable **`SessionStore` seam** (`gradio/session_store.py`) that decouples session persistence from process memory, while keeping the default single-process developer experience completely untouched.

## Open Questions

We have to decide the scope as well, it's just a first step of making Gradio apps fully scalable and ready to peak times. Maybe we have to expand the scope writing also the file store like session store, and consider also the auth mechanism.

The first question here is, should we make these adapters (file store, session store, queue broker, etc) independent or developer should do a choice between in memory or pluggable alternatives for all adapters.

The second question is, I try to design the session store environment variables like Django database settings (`GRADIO_SESSION_STORE_URL`). But some variables are redis specific: `GRADIO_REDIS_SOCKET_CONNECT_TIMEOUT`, `GRADIO_REDIS_SOCKET_TIMEOUT`, ...

We have to decide how the name the variables if we also plan to support relational databases, cloud nosql.

# Related Issues

- https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio/issues/10487
- https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio/issues/9136

body_text:
### Describe the bug

Cancelling one job cancels every running job of the same function in the same session, and the other cancelled jobs never complete. `POST /gradio_api/cancel` carries an `event_id`, but the server cancels by `{session_hash}_{fn_index}` only. The Python client submits all of its jobs on one session hash, so with `concurrency_limit=2`, `job_one.cancel()` also kills `job_two`: its function body stops, it gets no completion message, its event id stays in the session's pending set and `job_two.result()` waits until it times out.

```python
import asyncio
import time
import os

os.environ.setdefault("GRADIO_ANALYTICS_ENABLED", "False")

import gradio as gr
from gradio_client import Client

finished = []


async def slow(x):
    await asyncio.sleep(3)
    finished.append(x)
    return x


with gr.Blocks() as demo:
    inp = gr.Textbox()
    out = gr.Textbox()
    inp.submit(slow, inp, out, api_name="slow", concurrency_limit=2)

demo.launch(server_port=7861, prevent_thread_lock=True, quiet=True)
try:
    client = Client("http://127.0.0.1:7861/", verbose=False)
    job_one = client.submit("one", api_name="/slow")
    job_two = client.submit("two", api_name="/slow")
    while sum(j is not None for j in demo._queue.active_jobs) < 2:
        time.sleep(0.05)
    print("running before cancel:", sum(j is not None for j in demo._queue.active_jobs))

    job_one.cancel()  # posts fn_index, session_hash and the event_id of job_one only
    time.sleep(0.5)
    print("running after cancel:", sum(j is not None for j in demo._queue.active_jobs))

    try:
        print("job_two result:", repr(job_two.result(timeout=8)))
    except Exception as e:
        print("job_two result: raised", type(e).__name__)
    print("functions that finished:", finished)
    print("pending event ids left for the session:",
          sum(len(v) for v in demo._queue.pending_event_ids_session.values()))
    print("expected: running after cancel 1, job_two result 'two', finished ['two'], 0 pending ids")
finally:
    client.close()
    demo.close()
```

At 526c24340, `cancel_event` in `gradio/routes.py` line 1718 calls `cancel_tasks({f"{body.session_hash}_{body.fn_index}"})`. `cancel_tasks` (`gradio/utils.py` lines 1157-1170) splits each task name on `<gradio-sep>` and compares only the `{session_hash}_{fn_index}` half, so every running task of that function in the session matches. Only `body.event_id` then receives a `ProcessCompletedMessage` (lines 1729-1735). The other tasks end with `CancelledError`, which the `except Exception` in `Queue.process_events` (`gradio/queueing.py` line 1033) does not catch, so no completion message is ever sent for them.

`set_task_name` (`gradio/utils.py` line 1175) already puts the event id after `<gradio-sep>`, so `/cancel` can match on the full `{session_hash}_{fn_index}<gradio-sep>{event_id}` name when the body has an event id. The broader `{session_hash}_{fn_index}` match would then stay only for the `cancels=` path, which sends no event id.

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**  
The guide [guides/11_other-tutorials/deploying-gradio-with-modal.md](https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio/blob/main/guides/11_other-tutorials/deploying-gradio-with-modal.md#sticky-sessions) states that Modal does not provide sticky sessions, recommending `max_containers = 1` as the workaround:

> Gradio relies on a REST API, which is itself stateless. But it does require sticky sessions, meaning that every request from a particular client must be routed to the same  container. However, Modal does not make any guarantees in this regard.
>
> A simple way to satisfy this constraint is to set `max_containers = 1` in the `@app.function` decorator...

This is outdated. Modal SDK 1.6.0 added native sticky sessions using the `@modal.sessioned()` decorator.

**Describe the solution you'd like**  
Update the "Sticky Sessions" section in the Modal deployment guide to:

1. Retain `max_containers = 1` as the simple default for single-container demos and prototypes.
2. Document Modal's native `@modal.sessioned()` decorator for multi-container deployments needing session affinity and autoscaling.
3. Link to Modal's official [Sticky Sessions guide](https://modal.com/docs/guide/sticky-sessions).

**Additional context**  

- Modal Sticky Sessions documentation: https://modal.com/docs/guide/sticky-sessions
- Target file: `guides/11_other-tutorials/deploying-gradio-with-modal.md`

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**  
Getting Started templates and curated workflow options were added in #13573 and #13511 respectively. The templates location is [hard-coded in JS](https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio/blob/c270f35d91995d3f33b77b9504567d6d1c9b7216/js/workflowcanvas/workflow/workflow-templates.ts#L11-L12) while the curated options location is [defined in Python](https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio/blob/c270f35d91995d3f33b77b9504567d6d1c9b7216/gradio/workflow.py#L60-L61) in a way that facilitates end-user customization.

**Describe the solution you'd like**  
It may be helpful to have a single way of handling these quite similar resources, probably with both being defined in Python where it will be easier for advanced users to insert custom defaults when desired.

**Additional context**  
I may have misunderstood the way these features are supposed to work in the `gr.Workflow` module as I don't normally use Spaces.

### Describe the bug

> This is a dependency-update request, not a report of a vulnerability in Gradio. The vulnerability is in Pillow, has already been disclosed and fixed upstream, and its advisory is public. The fix is now available (Pillow 13.0.0), but Gradio's version pin prevents upgrading to it.

`requirements.txt` on main declares:
```
pillow>=8.0,<13.0
```
Pillow advisory GHSA-8g5g-8vmr-9782 (CVE-2026-112403, Critical, CVSS v4 9.2, CWE-122 heap-based buffer overflow) affects Pillow <= 12.3.0. The only patched release is Pillow 13.0.0. Because of the <13.0 upper bound, no Gradio release can be installed alongside a patched Pillow.

### Have you searched existing issues?  🔎

- [x] I have searched and found no existing issues

### Reproduction

Tested with `gradio==6.30.0` using Poetry:

```bash
poetry init -n --python ">=3.10,<4.0"
poetry add "gradio==6.30.0" "pillow>=13.0.0"
```

Result:

```
Updating dependencies
Resolving dependencies...

Because gradio (6.30.0) depends on pillow (>=8.0,<13.0)
 and no versions of gradio match >6.30.0,<7.0.0, gradio (>=6.30.0,<7.0.0) requires pillow (>=8.0,<13.0).                                                                                                                
So, because repo depends on both gradio (^6.30.0) and pillow (13.0.0), version solving failed. 
```

body_text:
### Current Behavior

With **both** the configuration cache and configure-on-demand enabled, a build fails
hard with:

```
* What went wrong:
Failed to apply plugin class '...'.
> This operation is not supported while in the Stored state.
```

when a project that configure-on-demand deferred is configured **at execution time**
and registers a Dataflow/Flow action (`FlowScope.always(...)`) during its configuration.

The exception originates in `BuildFlowScope`:

```
Caused by: java.lang.IllegalStateException: This operation is not supported while in the Stored state.
    at org.gradle.internal.flow.services.BuildFlowScope$State.illegalState(BuildFlowScope.kt:60)
    at org.gradle.internal.flow.services.BuildFlowScope$State.add(BuildFlowScope.kt:51)
    at org.gradle.internal.flow.services.BuildFlowScope.always(BuildFlowScope.kt:128)
    at ...RegisterFlowActionPlugin.apply(build.gradle.kts:26)
```

The configuration cache stores the flow scope (moving it to the `Stored` state) at the
end of the configuration phase. Because configure-on-demand deferred one project, that
project is configured later, during execution — and registering a flow action then hits
the already-`Stored` flow scope, which throws instead of degrading gracefully.

### Expected Behavior

The build should not fail hard. With either feature disabled individually the same build
succeeds, so the combination should degrade gracefully (as it does when configure-on-demand
is off), rather than throwing an internal state-machine error.

### Context

Hit while enabling the configuration cache on a large multi-project build that also uses
configure-on-demand. `gradle/gradle#2868` suggests configure-on-demand is known-fragile,
but this specific interaction with Dataflow Actions does not appear to be reported.

### Steps to Reproduce

Minimal project (Gradle 9.7.1). `:a` depends on `:b:bTask`; `:c` is unrelated so
configure-on-demand defers configuring it until `:b:bTask` reaches into it at execution
time; `:c` registers a Flow action during configuration.

Full reproducer as a gist: https://gist.github.com/bryant-tran-x/05a645a31a1f0e8bd0b66907b9236f5a

**`gradle.properties`**
```
org.gradle.configuration-cache=true
org.gradle.configureondemand=true
```

**`settings.gradle.kts`**
```kotlin
rootProject.name = "cc-cod-repro"
include(":a", ":b", ":c")
```

**`a/build.gradle.kts`**
```kotlin
tasks.register("aTask") {
    dependsOn(":b:bTask")
    doLast { println("Running :a:aTask") }
}
```

**`b/build.gradle.kts`**
```kotlin
tasks.register("bTask") {
    notCompatibleWithConfigurationCache("reaches into the Project object graph at execution time")
    doLast {
        // Under configure-on-demand, :c has not been configured yet.
        // Forcing evaluation of all subprojects configures :c at EXECUTION time.
        val root = project.rootProject
        root.subprojects.forEach { sub -> sub.evaluationDependsOn(sub.path) }
    }
}
```

**`c/build.gradle.kts`**
```kotlin
import org.gradle.api.flow.FlowAction
import org.gradle.api.flow.FlowParameters
import org.gradle.api.flow.FlowProviders
import org.gradle.api.flow.FlowScope
import org.gradle.api.flow.BuildWorkResult
import javax.inject.Inject

abstract class RegisterFlowActionPlugin : Plugin<Project> {
    @get:Inject abstract val flowScope: FlowScope
    @get:Inject abstract val flowProviders: FlowProviders
    override fun apply(target: Project) {
        flowScope.always(PrintResult::class.java) {
            parameters.buildResult.set(flowProviders.buildWorkResult)
        }
    }
}

abstract class PrintResult : FlowAction<PrintResult.Parameters> {
    interface Parameters : FlowParameters {
        @get:Input val buildResult: Property<BuildWorkResult>
    }
    override fun execute(parameters: Parameters) {}
}

apply<RegisterFlowActionPlugin>()

tasks.register("cTask") { doLast { println("Running :c:cTask") } }
```

Run:
```

With **both** the configuration cache and configure-on-demand enabled, a build fails
hard with:

```
* What went wrong:
Failed to apply plugin class '...'.
> This operation is not supported while in the Stored state.
```

when a project that configure-on-demand deferred is configured **at execution time**
and registers a Dataflow/Flow action (`FlowScope.always(...)`) during its configuration.

The exception originates in `BuildFlowScope`:

```
Caused by: java.lang.IllegalStateException: This operation is not supported while in the Stored state.
    at org.gradle.internal.flow.services.BuildFlowScope$State.illegalState(BuildFlowScope.kt:60)
    at org.gradle.internal.flow.services.BuildFlowScope$State.add(BuildFlowScope.kt:51)
    at org.gradle.internal.flow.services.BuildFlowScope.always(BuildFlowScope.kt:128)
    at ...RegisterFlowActionPlugin.apply(build.gradle.kts:26)
```

The configuration cache stores the flow scope (moving it to the `Stored` state) at the
end of the configuration phase. Because configure-on-demand deferred one project, that
project is configured later, during execution — and registering a flow action then hits
the already-`Stored` flow scope, which throws instead of degrading gracefully.

### Expected Behavior

The build should not fail hard. With either feature disabled individually the same build
succeeds, so the combination should degrade gracefully (as it does when configure-on-demand
is off), rather than throwing an internal state-machine error.

### Context

Hit while enabling the configuration cache on a large multi-project build that also uses
configure-on-demand. `gradle/gradle#2868` suggests configure-on-demand is known-fragile,
but this specific interaction with Dataflow Actions does not appear to be reported.

### Steps to Reproduce

Minimal project (Gradle 9.7.1). `:a` depends on `:b:bTask`; `:c` is unrelated so
configure-on-demand defers configuring it until `:b:bTask` reaches into it at execution
time; `:c` registers a Flow action during configuration.

Full reproducer as a gist: https://gist.github.com/bryant-tran-x/05a645a31a1f0e8bd0b66907b9236f5a

**`gradle.properties`**
```
org.gradle.configuration-cache=true
org.gradle.configureondemand=true
```

**`settings.gradle.kts`**
```kotlin
rootProject.name = "cc-cod-repro"
include(":a", ":b", ":c")
```

**`a/build.gradle.kts`**
```kotlin
tasks.register("aTask") {
    dependsOn(":b:bTask")
    doLast { println("Running :a:aTask") }
}
```

**`b/build.gradle.kts`**
```kotlin
tasks.register("bTask") {
    notCompatibleWithConfigurationCache("reaches into the Project object graph at execution time")
    doLast {
        // Under configure-on-demand, :c has not been configured yet.
        // Forcing evaluation of all subprojects configures :c at EXECUTION time.
        val root = project.rootProject
        root.subprojects.forEach { sub -> sub.evaluationDependsOn(sub.path) }
    }
}
```

**`c/build.gradle.kts`**
```kotlin
import org.gradle.api.flow.FlowAction
import org.gradle.api.flow.FlowParameters
import org.gradle.api.flow.FlowProviders
import org.gradle.api.flow.FlowScope
import org.gradle.api.flow.BuildWorkResult
import javax.inject.Inject

abstract class RegisterFlowActionPlugin : Plugin<Project> {
    @get:Inject abstract val flowScope: FlowScope
    @get:Inject abstract val flowProviders: FlowProviders
    override fun apply(target: Project) {
        flowScope.always(PrintResult::class.java) {
            parameters.buildResult.set(flowProviders.buildWorkResult)
        }
    }
}

abstract class PrintResult : FlowAction<PrintResult.Parameters> {
    interface Parameters : FlowParameters {
        @get:Input val buildResult: Property<BuildWorkResult>
    }
    override fun execute(parameters: Parameters) {}
}

apply<RegisterFlowActionPlugin>()

tasks.register("cTask") { doLast { println("Running :c:cTask") } }
```

./gradlew :a:aTask

```

### Expected Behavior

- When Daemon JVM criteria are configured, keep the current behavior.
- When Daemon JVM criteria are not configured and JVM taken from` JAVA_HOME` is not supported by the Gradle Daemon (lower than Java 17), a compatible JVM should be discovered by the Gradle Client JVM. 
  - Like when Daemon VM criteria are configured, Java 8 specified in `JAVA_HOME` should be sufficient.
  - For instance, the highest compatible JVM found could be selected. For selection, https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/35148 may be appropriate.

### Current Behavior (optional)

- When Daemon JVM criteria are configured, a JVM matching the criteria is discovered by the Gradle Client JVM and set as Gradle Daemon JVM. Consequently, `JAVA_HOME` must point to Java 8 at a minimum.
- When Daemon JVM criteria are not configured, the Gradle Daemon JVM is taken from `JAVA_HOME`. Consequently, `JAVA_HOME` must point to Java 17 at a minimum.

### Context

Consider a machine with these JVMs:

- Adoptium JDK 8 (taken from `JAVA_HOME`)
- Adoptium JDK 25 (taken from IntelliJ JDKs directory)

A Gradle project has Daemon JVM criteria specified in `gradle-daemon-jvm.properties`:

```
toolchainVersion=25
toolchainVendor=ADOPTIUM
# Toolchain URLs can be omitted
```

Running 

```
./gradlew javaToolchains
```

works as expected. Gradle discovers the JDK 25 matching the criteria, runs the Daemon using this JDK and subsequently discovers the available Java toolchains JDK 8 and JDK 25.

However, if properties file is absent, the same command immediately fails: 
```
Gradle requires JVM 17 or later to run. Your build is currently configured to use JVM 8.

body_text:
### Current Behavior

A remote build-cache store added almost 16 minutes to an otherwise successful Caffeine CI build. The cache entry was only 242.4 KiB. A later run of the same test task stored a similarly sized entry in 62 ms.

| Measurement | [Slow run](https://caffeine.develocity.cloud/s/qwa6xic6bnado/performance/build-cache) | [Comparison run](https://caffeine.develocity.cloud/s/syrtdvdtgn7ko/performance/build-cache) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Total `frayTest` task duration | 28m38.936s | 12m12.789s |
| Task action execution | 12m47.738s | 12m12.574s |
| Packing | 45 ms | 45 ms |
| Remote store | **15m50.988s** | **62 ms** |
| Cache entry size | 242.4 KiB | 242.3 KiB |
| Reported average store rate | 261 B/s | 3.8 MiB/s |

The comparison is a later build with a different commit and cache key, not a controlled reproduction with identical inputs. Both use the same Fray task and runtime configuration.

In the slow run:

- The final test executor completed at approximately **06:03:40 UTC on September 6, 2026**. The task completed at **06:19:32 UTC**. The remaining interval is attributed to the remote store. See the [test executor timeline](https://caffeine.develocity.cloud/s/qwa6xic6bnado/tests/overview) and [task timeline](https://caffeine.develocity.cloud/s/qwa6xic6bnado/timeline).
- During that interval, the resource metrics show no remaining test-worker memory and near-zero CPU usage.
- The 15 remote cache hits earlier in the build took a combined 3.541 seconds for 3.7 MiB.
- The store is recorded without a reported exception or rejection. The build completed successfully.
- The slow entry's cache key was `fe1eb77c730032877dda1d5d5a469f8e`.

The reported transfer rate is size divided by elapsed time; it does not establish that bytes were continuously transferred at that rate. I do not have a thread dump, server logs, or HTTP response details establishing whether this was a blocked write, connection-pool wait, retry, or server-side delay.


### Expected Behavior

An optional cache upload should have a configurable end-to-end deadline, covering connection acquisition, connection establishment, writing, waiting for the response, and retries. For example, after a configurable 30-second budget, the client should cancel the actual network operation, log a warning, and allow the successful build to continue.

Gradle's [BuildCacheService contract](https://docs.gradle.org/current/javadoc/org/gradle/caching/BuildCacheService.html) already supports nonfatal upload failures through `BuildCacheException`. **The requested behavior is a bounded, best-effort remote store** rather than an optional cache operation substantially extending the build.


### Context (optional)

This made the test task appear to be a CI straggler even though the test workers had finished. I want to retain remote build-cache benefits without allowing a stalled upload to delay an otherwise successful build indefinitely.

Inspection of the installed 4.5.0 plugin found defaults of 5 seconds for connection establishment and 10 seconds for socket reads. I did not identify a total-call, write, or connection-pool acquisition deadline. Connection lifetime can be limited separately, but that does not bound an upload already in progress.

**Disabling build-cache results for this test task in CI was applied as a workaround.**

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

The issue is intermittent, and I do not yet have a minimal, deterministic reproducer. The affected project and execution are public:

- Project: [ben-manes/caffeine at the affected revision](https://github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/tree/96ab564ab88bfb0d8ab98880aef56bb544084767)
- [Affected GitHub Actions job](https://github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/actions/runs/34014777892/job/101436812297)
- [Workflow configuration at that revision](https://github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/blob/96ab564ab88bfb0d8ab98880aef56bb544084767/.github/workflows/build.yml)
- Task invocation: `./gradlew :caffeine:frayTest`, with remote-cache push enabled and the JDK provisioning and credentials supplied by CI.

The observed sequence was a remote-cache miss, approximately 13 minutes of test execution, then the prolonged remote store. Re-running this task does not reliably reproduce the delay, as the comparison scan demonstrates.


### Gradle version

9.7.1

### Build scan URL (optional)

[Slow run](https://caffeine.develocity.cloud/s/qwa6xic6bnado) and [Comparison run](https://caffeine.develocity.cloud/s/syrtdvdtgn7ko)

### Your Environment (optional)

- Develocity Gradle plugin 4.5.0, using `remote(develocity.buildCache)`
- GitHub Actions, `ubuntu-latest`, Linux x86-64
- Gradle daemon: Temurin 26; test runtime: Amazon Corretto 25.0.4.1+8-LTS
- Task: `:caffeine:frayTest`, using Fray 0.9.0
- Hosted server: `https://caffeine.develocity.cloud`, cache path `cache`
- Access-key authentication; remote push enabled; local build cache disabled
- Edge discovery and Expect-Continue disabled

body_text:
## Current Behavior

I write a `@ParameterizedTest` the same way I write a `@Test`, with no `name` attribute. In `build/test-results/test/*.xml` the `@Test` method keeps its name and the parameterized invocations lose theirs. Two parameterized methods in one class that take the same arguments produce identical `<testcase>` entries.

The reproducer below compiles with `-parameters`, so JUnit renders each argument as `name = value`. `TEST-example.ReportNamesTest.xml` contains:

```xml
<testcase name="[1] value = """ classname="example.ReportNamesTest" time="0.001"/>
<testcase name="[2] value = "plain"" classname="example.ReportNamesTest" time="0.001"/>
<testcase name="[3] value = "a\\b"" classname="example.ReportNamesTest" time="0.0"/>
<testcase name="plainTestMethod()" classname="example.ReportNamesTest" time="0.001"/>
<testcase name="[1] value = """ classname="example.ReportNamesTest" time="0.001"/>
<testcase name="[2] value = "plain"" classname="example.ReportNamesTest" time="0.0"/>
<testcase name="[3] value = "a\\b"" classname="example.ReportNamesTest" time="0.002"/>
```

Seven test cases, six of which do not say which method ran, and three of the six names appear twice.

A `@ParameterizedClass` loses the class arguments too. All four test cases of `ParameterizedClassNamesTest` land under two names, and the `flag = true` and `flag = false` rows are indistinguishable:

```xml
<testcase name="[1] value = "x"" classname="example.ParameterizedClassNamesTest" time="0.085"/>
<testcase name="[2] value = "y"" classname="example.ParameterizedClassNamesTest" time="0.001"/>
<testcase name="[1] value = "x"" classname="example.ParameterizedClassNamesTest" time="0.001"/>
<testcase name="[2] value = "y"" classname="example.ParameterizedClassNamesTest" time="0.001"/>
```

## Expected Behavior

## For `@ParameterizedTest`

`name` names the method that ran and the arguments it ran with, so that `classname` plus `name` is unique within a run and a reader can tell from the report alone which case failed. For example:

```xml
<testcase name="firstParameterizedMethod(String) [1] value = """  classname="example.ReportNamesTest"/>
<testcase name="secondParameterizedMethod(String) [1] value = """ classname="example.ReportNamesTest"/>
<testcase name="plainTestMethod()" classname="example.ReportNamesTest"/>
```

The exact rendering is yours to choose. What I need is the method name and the arguments. The `value = "..."` form is what JUnit already produces for a class compiled with `-parameters`, and it beats a bare `"x"`, which says nothing about which parameter took it.

## For `@ParameterizedClass`

The same, plus the arguments of the class invocation, because otherwise the four test cases of `ParameterizedClassNamesTest` carry two names between them and nothing says whether a failing row ran with `flag = true` or `flag = false`. For example:

```xml
<testcase name="[1] flag = true > methodInParameterizedClass(String) [1] value = "x"" classname="example.ParameterizedClassNamesTest"/>
<testcase name="[2] flag = false > methodInParameterizedClass(String) [1] value = "x"" classname="example.ParameterizedClassNamesTest"/>
```

The constructor parameter name comes from `-parameters` as well, so JUnit already renders the class invocation as `[1] flag = true`. It builds the same information for its own report, joining the display names of every ancestor with `>`:

```text
ParameterizedClassNamesTest > [1] flag = true > methodInParameterizedClass(String) > [1] value = "x"
```

## Values, not indices

`junit-platform-console-standalone` writes `methodInParameterizedClass(String)[2][1]`, which is unique but not diagnostic. An index does not say what ran, and it moves when a row is added to the argument source, so a report archived last week names a different case today. I would rather not have Gradle adopt that form.

Argument values are already bounded: JUnit truncates each one at 512 characters by default, configurable through `junit.jupiter.params.displayname.argument.maxlength`.

## Context

CI reads the XML. When a parameterized test fails, the report gives me `[3] "a\\b"` and I cannot tell which of the two methods it belongs to without opening the console log. Flaky-test dashboards and history tools key on `classname` plus `name`, so two different tests are tracked as one.

The name in the report is also not something I can act on. `--tests` accepts the method name and reruns all its invocations:

```text
./gradlew test --tests 'example.ReportNamesTest.firstParameterizedMethod'   # runs 3 tests
```

Neither the name from the XML nor the indexed form JUnit uses is accepted:

```text
./gradlew test --tests 'example.ReportNamesTest.[1] ""'
> No tests found for given includes: [example.ReportNamesTest.[1] ""](--tests filter)

./gradlew test --tests 'example.ReportNamesTest.firstParameterizedMethod(String)[1]'
> No tests found for given includes: [example.ReportNamesTest.firstParameterizedMethod(String)[1]](--tests filter)
```

A single invocation can be rerun through the JUnit unique id, which selects exactly one case:

```text
--select-unique-id='[engine:junit-jupiter]/[class:example.ReportNamesTest]/[test-template:firstParameterizedMethod(java.lang.String)]/[test-template-invocation:#2]'
```

Gradle's XML carries no unique id, so that string is not available from the report either. `<testcase>` has `name` and `classname` and nothing else, and `<system-out>` is empty. That leaves the name as the only thing a reader gets, which is why I would like it to carry the values.

The per-annotation workaround, `@ParameterizedTest(name = "...")`, means writing the method name into a string in every annotation and keeping those strings correct across every rename and signature change. I would rather the default report be unambiguous.

## Self-contained Reproducer Project

The whole project is below: single module, `java` plugin only. Create the three files, run `./gradlew test`, then read `build/test-results/test/*.xml`. I can attach it as an archive if that is easier.

`src/test/java/example/ReportNamesTest.java`:

```java
package example;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.ValueSource;

class ReportNamesTest {

    @Test
    void plainTestMethod() {
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @ValueSource(strings = {"", "plain", "a\\b"})
    void firstParameterizedMethod(String value) {
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @ValueSource(strings = {"", "plain", "a\\b"})
    void secondParameterizedMethod(String value) {
    }
}
```

`src/test/java/example/ParameterizedClassNamesTest.java`:

```java
package example;

import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedClass;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.ValueSource;

@ParameterizedClass
@ValueSource(booleans = {true, false})
class ParameterizedClassNamesTest {

    ParameterizedClassNamesTest(boolean flag) {
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @ValueSource(strings = {"x", "y"})
    void methodInParameterizedClass(String value) {
    }
}
```

`build.gradle.kts`:

```kotlin
plugins {
    java
}
repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}
dependencies {
    testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:6.1.3")
    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
}
tasks.test {
    useJUnitPlatform()
}
tasks.withType<JavaCompile>().configureEach {
    options.compilerArgs.add("-parameters")
}
```

`-parameters` is what lets JUnit render `value = "x"` rather than `"x"`. The defect is the same without it; the names are just less readable to begin with.

## Gradle version

9.7.1

## Your Environment

- JDK 21.0.9 (Corretto)
- `org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:6.1.3`
- macOS 15 (Darwin 25.5.0)
- Configuration cache enabled
- Compiled with `-parameters`

## Workaround

Setting the JUnit configuration parameter for the whole build restores the method name without touching any annotation:

```kotlin
tasks.test {
    systemProperty(
        "junit.jupiter.params.displayname.default",
        "{displayName} [{index}] {argumentSetNameOrArgumentsWithNames}"
    )
}
```

`name` then reads:

```xml
<testcase name="firstParameterizedMethod(String) [1] value = """ classname="example.ReportNamesTest"/>
<testcase name="secondParameterizedMethod(String) [1] value = """ classname="example.ReportNamesTest"/>
```

This does not reach the `@ParameterizedClass` case. The setting changes the display name of the class invocation as well, but Gradle does not report that container, and the leaf's pattern has no placeholder for the enclosing arguments, so the four test cases keep two names between them. I filed junit-team/junit-framework#6041 for that. Note that the Expected Behavior above does not depend on it: the class arguments are on the `TestPlan` today.

## Possible cause

I read the code to find out where the name is lost. This part is a guess and may be wrong; the sections above stand without it.

`JUnitPlatformTestExecutionListener.createDescriptorIfAbsent` passes two names, and the first one is the one JUnit intends for reports:

`platforms/jvm/testing-jvm-infrastructure/src/main/java/org/gradle/api/internal/tasks/testing/junitplatform/JUnitPlatformTestExecutionListener.java`

```java
return createTestDescriptor(node, node.getLegacyReportingName(), node.getDisplayName());
```

`TestMethodResult` keeps both, as `getName()` and `getDisplayName()`. The XML writer uses the display name:

`platforms/software/testing-base/src/main/java/org/gradle/api/internal/tasks/testing/junit/result/JUnitXmlResultWriter.java`

```java
return new TestCase(methodResult.getDisplayName(), className, methodResult.getDuration(), discreteTestCaseExecutions(classId, methodResult));
```

If that is right, `methodResult.getName()` is already in hand and would at least restore the method name. It carries indices rather than values, so on its own it does not meet the Expected Behavior above; combining the method name from `getName()` with the display name that holds the values would.

Whichever form you choose, it changes `name` for every existing parameterized test, so it may belong behind a `JUnitXmlReport` option or in a major release.

Two further notes from the same reading:

- `JUnitXmlResultWriter.groupExecutions` keys the rerun grouping on `getDisplayName()` as well. With `mergeReruns` enabled and two parameterized methods sharing a display name, executions of different tests would land in one group. I have not reproduced this and it may deserve its own issue.
- For the `@ParameterizedClass` case the listener drops the intermediate container that holds the class arguments. They are still reachable: JUnit puts the invocation index into the legacy reporting name (junit-team/junit-framework#5441, in 6.1 and 5.14.4), and the argument values are the display name of the parent, which `TestPlan.getParent` returns. JUnit's own report walks exactly that chain (junit-team/junit-framework#5524, backported to 5.14.4).

return createTestDescriptor(node, node.getLegacyReportingName(), node.getDisplayName());
```

`TestMethodResult` keeps both, as `getName()` and `getDisplayName()`. The XML writer uses the display name:

`platforms/software/testing-base/src/main/java/org/gradle/api/internal/tasks/testing/junit/result/JUnitXmlResultWriter.java`

```java
return new TestCase(methodResult.getDisplayName(), className, methodResult.getDuration(), discreteTestCaseExecutions(classId, methodResult));
```

If that is right, `methodResult.getName()` is already in hand and would at least restore the method name. It carries indices rather than values, so on its own it does not meet the Expected Behavior above; combining the method name from `getName()` with the display name that holds the values would.

Whichever form you choose, it changes `name` for every existing parameterized test, so it may belong behind a `JUnitXmlReport` option or in a major release.

Two further notes from the same reading:

- `JUnitXmlResultWriter.groupExecutions` keys the rerun grouping on `getDisplayName()` as well. With `mergeReruns` enabled and two parameterized methods sharing a display name, executions of different tests would land in one group. I have not reproduced this and it may deserve its own issue.
- For the `@ParameterizedClass` case the listener drops the intermediate container that holds the class arguments. They are still reachable: JUnit puts the invocation index into the legacy reporting name (junit-team/junit-framework#5441, in 6.1 and 5.14.4), and the argument values are the display name of the parent, which `TestPlan.getParent` returns. JUnit's own report walks exactly that chain (junit-team/junit-framework#5524, backported to 5.14.4).

File system is a shared resource that can be used and misused during a build.

For Parallel IP, if one project writes to a file during its configuration and another project happens to read from the same file, this can result in flaky build results.

For Incremental IP, when a project configuration can be skipped due to up-to-dateness, today, nothing ensures that the same file will be written. Therefore, if there was any execution time logic that relied on the file being present/written, this logic might run over a broken invariant.

To ensure reliable builds with consistent build results under IP, Gradle must either categorically forbid such situations from happening or detect the cases when this happens and let the user know. Either way, a build must not succeed if this might have happened.

---

This is somewhat related to
- https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/38708

body_text:
### Current Behavior

A custom `tasks.register("myCompile", JavaCompile)` or` project.task("myCompile", type: JavaCompile)` task does not use the JVM required in the toolchain and instead uses the daemon JVM,
In contrast, custom tasks based on `Javadoc`, `JavaExec`, and `Test` do use the toolchain JVM.

### Expected Behavior

`JavaCompile` should use the toolchain JVM just like the other task types mentioned.

### Context (optional)

### Affected
While uncommon, sometimes projects define custom compile tasks. They assume that the toolchain JVM that is responsible for the build will be the one executing this compilation, especially when this is the case for the other tasks. However, the daemon JVM will be used silently, which can produce different binaries.

Real-world example: JavaFX defines a [custom compile task](https://github.com/openjdk/jfx/blob/1a3ebac4f909d8f01390bd6222de8a615966dfb2/build.gradle#L4383) and is hit by this.

Related are:
- #37158
- #32562

### Workaround
Manually configure the toolchain:
```groovy
tasks.withType(JavaCompile).configureEach {
    javaCompiler = javaToolchains.compilerFor {
        languageVersion = java.toolchain.languageVersion
    }
}
```

### Cause
The AI claims to have found the cause, pasting verbatim:

The `javaCompiler` convention is set in two places, and they are not
equivalent.

`platforms/jvm/language-java/src/main/java/org/gradle/api/tasks/compile/JavaCompile.java`
— applies to every `JavaCompile`, and its fallback is an *empty* toolchain
spec, which resolves to the current JVM:

```java
Provider<JavaCompiler> javaCompilerConvention = ...
    .flatMap(javaToolchainService::compilerFor)
    .orElse(javaToolchainService.compilerFor(it -> {}));   // <-- empty spec
getJavaCompiler().convention(javaCompilerConvention);
```

`platforms/jvm/plugins-java-base/src/main/java/org/gradle/api/plugins/JavaBasePlugin.java`
— the convention that consults `java.toolchain`, applied **only inside the
per-source-set configuration**:

```java
javaCompile.getJavaCompiler().convention(
    getToolchainTool(project, JavaToolchainService::compilerFor, toolchainOverrideSpec));
```

So a hand-created `JavaCompile` never sees `java.toolchain` and lands on the
empty-spec fallback.

The same file wires the other three at project level, via
`tasks.withType(...).configureEach`, which is why they behave correctly however
they were created:

```java
javaExec.getJavaLauncher().convention(
    getToolchainTool(project, JavaToolchainService::launcherFor, toolchainOverrideSpec));
javadoc.getJavadocTool().convention(
    getToolchainTool(project, JavaToolchainService::javadocToolFor, toolchainOverrideSpec));
```

Moving the `JavaCompile` wiring to `tasks.withType(JavaCompile).configureEach`
would make all four consistent.


### Self-contained Reproducer Project

Two different JDKs are required - one for the daemon and one for the build/toolchain.
The build file hardcodes Java 26, but you can change it to any version that isn't the same as the daemon's.

[javacompile-toolchain-fallback.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32001998/javacompile-toolchain-fallback.zip)

When executing `:toolchainReport` locally, I get 

```
Gradle daemon on Java 25, java.toolchain requests Java 26

  compileJava         (source set) -> Java 26
  handCreatedCompile  (registered) -> Java 25   <-- daemon JVM, java.toolchain ignored
  javadoc             (source set) -> Java 26
  handCreatedJavadoc  (registered) -> Java 26
  test                (source set) -> Java 26
  handCreatedTest     (registered) -> Java 26
  handCreatedJavaExec (registered) -> Java 26
```

As can be seen, only `handCreatedCompile` is wrong.

### Gradle version

9.7.0, 9.7.1

### Build scan URL (optional)

_No response_

### Your Environment (optional)

Win 10

{"repository": "gradle/gradle", "task_candidate_id": 6711, "repository_id": 118, "issue_number": 39116, "github_issue_id": 5397892359, "html_url": "https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/39116", "created_at": "2026-09-09T09:56:27+00:00", "author_association": "NONE", "title": "Custom `JavaCompile` tasks doesn't use the toolchain", "body_text": "### Current Behavior

A custom `tasks.register("myCompile", JavaCompile)` or` project.task("myCompile", type: JavaCompile)` task does not use the JVM required in the toolchain and instead uses the daemon JVM,
In contrast, custom tasks based on `Javadoc`, `JavaExec`, and `Test` do use the toolchain JVM.

### Expected Behavior

`JavaCompile` should use the toolchain JVM just like the other task types mentioned.

### Context (optional)

### Affected
While uncommon, sometimes projects define custom compile tasks. They assume that the toolchain JVM that is responsible for the build will be the one executing this compilation, especially when this is the case for the other tasks. However, the daemon JVM will be used silently, which can produce different binaries.

Real-world example: JavaFX defines a [custom compile task](https://github.com/openjdk/jfx/blob/1a3ebac4f909d8f01390bd6222de8a615966dfb2/build.gradle#L4383) and is hit by this.

Related are:
- #37158
- #32562

### Workaround
Manually configure the toolchain:
```groovy
tasks.withType(JavaCompile).configureEach {
    javaCompiler = javaToolchains.compilerFor {
        languageVersion = java.toolchain.languageVersion
    }
}
```

### Cause
The AI claims to have found the cause, pasting verbatim:

The `javaCompiler` convention is set in two places, and they are not
equivalent.

`platforms/jvm/language-java/src/main/java/org/gradle/api/tasks/compile/JavaCompile.java`
— applies to every `JavaCompile`, and its fallback is an *empty* toolchain
spec, which resolves to the current JVM:

```java
Provider<JavaCompiler> javaCompilerConvention = ...
    .flatMap(javaToolchainService::compilerFor)
    .orElse(javaToolchainService.compilerFor(it -> {}));   // <-- empty spec
getJavaCompiler().convention(javaCompilerConvention);
```

`platforms/jvm/plugins-java-base/src/main/java/org/gradle/api/plugins/JavaBasePlugin.java`
— the convention that consults `java.toolchain`, applied **only inside the
per-source-set configuration**:

```java
javaCompile.getJavaCompiler().convention(
    getToolchainTool(project, JavaToolchainService::compilerFor, toolchainOverrideSpec));
```

So a hand-created `JavaCompile` never sees `java.toolchain` and lands on the
empty-spec fallback.

The same file wires the other three at project level, via
`tasks.withType(...).configureEach`, which is why they behave correctly however
they were created:

```java
javaExec.getJavaLauncher().convention(
    getToolchainTool(project, JavaToolchainService::launcherFor, toolchainOverrideSpec));
javadoc.getJavadocTool().convention(
    getToolchainTool(project, JavaToolchainService::javadocToolFor, toolchainOverrideSpec));
```

Moving the `JavaCompile` wiring to `tasks.withType(JavaCompile).configureEach`
would make all four consistent.


### Self-contained Reproducer Project

Two different JDKs are required - one for the daemon and one for the build/toolchain.
The build file hardcodes Java 26, but you can change it to any version that isn't the same as the daemon's.

[javacompile-toolchain-fallback.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32001998/javacompile-toolchain-fallback.zip)

When executing `:toolchainReport` locally, I get 

```
Gradle daemon on Java 25, java.toolchain requests Java 26

  compileJava         (source set) -> Java 26
  handCreatedCompile  (registered) -> Java 25   <-- daemon JVM, java.toolchain ignored
  javadoc             (source set) -> Java 26
  handCreatedJavadoc  (registered) -> Java 26
  test                (source set) -> Java 26
  handCreatedTest     (registered) -> Java 26
  handCreatedJavaExec (registered) -> Java 26
```

As can be seen, only `handCreatedCompile` is wrong.

### Gradle version

9.7.0, 9.7.1

body_text:
### Context

Historically, CC was developed as an "add-on" to the rest of Gradle, and therefore most of its code and practically all of its tests are located in the single subproject `:configuration-cache`. For similar historical reasons, all IP code and tests also live in the same `:configuration-cache` subproject.

For the rest of Gradle's test coverage, the tests are usually located inside the platform, features of which they are testing. CC and IP are exceptions in this regard, because they are "execution modes" of Gradle, and therefore need to be tested together with practically all other Gradle's functionality.

We already have a relatively good solution in place -- `configCacheIntegTest` and `isolatedProjectsIntegTest` tasks. They are used to run practically any integration test, but with enabling CC and/or IP. We also have annotations for the tests themselves that can tell whether or not a given test should be executed or should be expected to fail when run with a CC/IP executor.

### Problems

* CC-related tests in the `:configuration-cache` subproject don't run with IP executor. In that subproject, we disable both `configCacheIntegTest` and `isolatedProjectsIntegTest` tasks, because each test is supposed to control CC/IP explicitly. But that means some CC scenarios that should be applicable to IP are not tested with it.
* Tests for certain functionality are fragmented between the owning platform and the CC subproject. Same for IP
* If a test is annotated with `NotConfigCached`, because it controls CC, it is not going to run with IP

### Goals

CC and IP are cross-cutting execution modes. All existing and new functionality should be tested against them. Therefore, there should be next to no friction in doing so within a platform, where the functionality belongs.

We need to provide
* The tools to easily express tested scenarios that also exercise CC/IP
* Guidance on how to think about testing strategies when adding new APIs, so that new features become well tested against CC/IP

We should also relocate the existing tests in the `:configuration-cache` into the platforms.

`Task.notCompatibleWithConfigurationCache(reason)` has become the accepted way to opt a task out of the configuration cache when that task cannot be made compatible. Users reach for it precisely when a task is invoked and would otherwise fail the build.

Because Isolated Projects is positioned as the step after CC — and cannot be active without it — users reasonably expect an opt-out that works for CC to keep working once IP is enabled. It does not, fully.

Consider a two-project build where the task in `:a` opts out of CC and reads `:b` in its action:

```kotlin
val root = project.rootProject
tasks.register("crossProject") {
    notCompatibleWithConfigurationCache("reads sibling project at execution time")
    doLast { println(root.project(":b").layout.buildDirectory.get()) }
}
```

With `--configuration-cache` the build succeeds: the serialization problem is reported and demoted, the entry is discarded, the task runs.

With Isolated Projects the build fails:

```
Execution failed for task ':a:crossProject'.
> Project ':a' cannot access 'Project.layout' functionality on another project ':b'
```

Both problems are reported in that run, but only one stops the build. The CC serialization problem is demoted, as the opt-out promises. The IP coupling violation is thrown.

There is an assumption underneath this that the opt-out quietly breaks. Under IP we generally take it that CC has done its work, so a task that reached execution can hold nothing capable of raising an IP problem — project references in particular don't survive serialization. A task that opts out keeps them and runs anyway. The opt-out therefore produces exactly the situation IP assumes cannot arise: an un-serialized task, holding live project state, executing inside an IP build. Whatever coupling that task performs surfaces at execution time, where IP has no story for it.

From a user's vantage this is hard to read. The same method, on the same task, with the same stated reason, holds the build up under one mode and not the other — and the failure arrives as a task error rather than as a configuration cache problem, so it does not look like the opt-out is involved at all.

body_text:
Normal builds only configure what they need. Tasks that are never realized never get a chance to raise an IP problem, so a build can pass CI with IP enabled while still holding violations that nothing has touched yet.

`./gradlew tasks --all` forces them into the open by realizing every task in every project.

This surfaced from a real case: a task that fails at creation under IP passed the build's own CI fine, but broke IntelliJ sync — the IDE creates all tasks, so it hit the violation that ordinary builds never reached.

That suggests `tasks --all` is worth recommending when enabling IP, and possibly worth running as its own CI job, as a proxy for whether someone has broken IDE sync with a change that otherwise passes.

Open question how far this goes: whether `tasks --all` is thorough enough, whether there are other laziness-hidden violations it misses, and whether this belongs in docs, in a checklist, or somewhere else.

`org.gradle.configuration-cache.inputs.unsafe.ignore.file-system-checks` is a temporary Configuration Cache opt-out introduced in Gradle 8.3.
It restores the earlier behavior where file system checks such as `File.exists()` and `File.isFile()` on the listed paths are not tracked as configuration inputs.

Once deprecated (#39163), the property and the code paths it guards should be removed, making the stricter behavior unconditional.

- [ ] Remove the property
- [ ] Document the removal in the upgrade guide
- [ ] Remove existing documentation references

`org.gradle.configuration-cache.unsafe.skip-task-logging-listeners-serialization` is a temporary Configuration Cache opt-out introduced in Gradle 9.8.
It restores the earlier behavior where task output listeners registered during configuration are dropped on a cache hit instead of being stored.

Once deprecated (#39166), the property and the code paths it guards should be removed, making the stricter behavior unconditional.

- [ ] Remove the property
- [ ] Document the removal in the upgrade guide
- [ ] Remove existing documentation references

### Expected Behavior

Without configuration-cache the same code passes without issue. We should expect converting `File` to `RegularFile` to still work regardless of which code path we use.

### Context (optional)

Dealing with converting `File` to `RegularFile` is a pain in Gradle ever since it was introduced. The method `ProjectLayout#file(File)` and `ProjectLayout#file(Provider<File>)` were introduced to help with this pain however they were forgotten in the rush to configuration cache ready. The problem seems to be related to [how everything is captured](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/blob/master/platforms/core-configuration/file-operations/src/main/java/org/gradle/api/internal/file/DefaultProjectLayout.java#L102) fooling Gradle into serializing the service and not a reference to the service.

Note the same issue is likely to be present for `ProjectLayout#dir(File)` and `ProjectLayout#dir(Provider<File>)`.

	static MyModel parseString(String s) {
		return new MyModel()
	}
}

	@Inject
	MyEnv(ObjectFactory objects, ProjectLayout layout, ProviderFactory providers) {
		// The following cause the crash under configuration-cache
		Provider<RegularFile> myFile = layout.file(providers.gradleProperty('myFile').orElse('myFile.json').map { new File(it) })
