### Expected Behavior

Without configuration-cache the same code passes without issue. We should expect converting `File` to `RegularFile` to still work regardless of which code path we use.

### Context (optional)

Dealing with converting `File` to `RegularFile` is a pain in Gradle ever since it was introduced. The method `ProjectLayout#file(File)` and `ProjectLayout#file(Provider<File>)` were introduced to help with this pain however they were forgotten in the rush to configuration cache ready. The problem seems to be related to [how everything is captured](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/blob/master/platforms/core-configuration/file-operations/src/main/java/org/gradle/api/internal/file/DefaultProjectLayout.java#L102) fooling Gradle into serializing the service and not a reference to the service.

Note the same issue is likely to be present for `ProjectLayout#dir(File)` and `ProjectLayout#dir(Provider<File>)`.

body_text:
When one plugin registers a callback and a second plugin's code performs a cross-project access inside it, the configuration cache report groups the violation under the first plugin. The plugin that must be fixed is not named anywhere in the grouping. On a build with thousands of violations, this makes "Problems grouped by location" unusable for deciding what to fix, and each entry has to be expanded by hand.

### Context

Plugins commonly apply other plugins and drive them through deferred callbacks — a convention plugin applies an ecosystem plugin, which registers an `afterEvaluate` that calls into a third plugin's extension. When a violation happens inside such a callback, the grouping is the reader's only practical index into a large report.

### Problem

The location a violation is grouped under names the plugin whose application was current when the callback was registered.

In the reproducer below the report shows:

```
Plugin 'repro.middle': Project ':' cannot access 'Project.extensions' functionality on subprojects
```

`repro.middle` performs no cross-project access. The access is in `InnerExtension`, which `repro.inner` owns and registers. `repro.inner` is not named in the grouping.

The expanded problem entry does carry the accurate frame:

```
at repro.InnerExtension.resolve(InnerExtension.java:14)
```

A reader expects the grouping to name the plugin that performs the access, or the chain of applications that leads to it, so that the grouping identifies which plugin to fix. As it stands the grouping names a plugin that has nothing to fix.

The trigger is the callback crossing a plugin boundary, not the nesting. Two variants are grouped correctly: a violation in the inner plugin's own `apply`, and a violation in an `afterEvaluate` that the inner plugin registers itself. Only a violation in a callback registered by another plugin is misgrouped.

### Reproducer

Two plugins in an included build. `repro.middle` applies `repro.inner`, then drives it from a callback it registers itself; the cross-project access is in the inner plugin's extension.

`MiddlePlugin.java`

```java
public class MiddlePlugin implements Plugin<Project> {
    public void apply(Project project) {
        project.getPluginManager().apply("repro.inner");
        project.afterEvaluate(p -> p.getExtensions().getByType(InnerExtension.class).resolve());
    }
}
```

`InnerPlugin.java`

```java
public class InnerPlugin implements Plugin<Project> {
    public void apply(Project project) {
        project.getExtensions().create("inner", InnerExtension.class, project);
    }
}
```

`InnerExtension.java` — the access that is reported.

```java
public void resolve() {
    for (Project other : project.getRootProject().getSubprojects()) {
        other.getExtensions().getExtraProperties().set("touchedBy", "inner");
    }
}
```

The root build script applies `repro.middle` only. One empty subproject is enough for `getSubprojects()` to return something. `gradle.properties` needs:

```properties
org.gradle.isolated-projects=true
org.gradle.isolated-projects.dangerously-ignore-problems=true
```

Run `./gradlew help`. The build ends in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` and prints the violation grouped under `repro.middle`.

Full reproducer: [repro-attribution.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32284191/repro-attribution.zip)

### Environment

Observable on 9.9 nightlies, and most likely on every version that reports Isolated Projects violations — the grouping has probably always worked this way, though only 9.9 was checked. Observed from CLI output and the HTML report on macOS, on a local build of master at `45f98545be7d`, which includes #38738.

Seen originally during Isolated Projects adoption on an 1101-subproject Android build, in a report with 2606 problems and 155 unique. There a convention plugin applied AGP and the access was inside Apollo's `DefaultService.dependsOn`; the report named `com.android.internal.library`, so neither Apollo nor the convention plugin was identified.

### References

- [google/ksp#2844](https://github.com/google/ksp/issues/2844) — an independent report showing the same shape: the location reads `plugin 'com.android.internal.application'` with a KSP frame beneath it.
- `DefaultUserCodeApplicationContext` — holds one application per thread, so no stack of plugin applications is retained.
- `DefaultCollectionCallbackActionDecorator` — captures the current application when a callback is registered and reinstates it when the callback runs.
- `ProblemReportingCrossProjectModelAccess.reportCrossProjectAccessProblem` — reads the current application for the `BuildLogic` trace entry.

```java
public class InnerPlugin implements Plugin<Project> {
    public void apply(Project project) {
        project.getExtensions().create("inner", InnerExtension.class, project);
    }
}
```

`InnerExtension.java` — the access that is reported.

```java
public void resolve() {
    for (Project other : project.getRootProject().getSubprojects()) {
        other.getExtensions().getExtraProperties().set("touchedBy", "inner");
    }
}
```

The root build script applies `repro.middle` only. One empty subproject is enough for `getSubprojects()` to return something. `gradle.properties` needs:

```properties
org.gradle.isolated-projects=true
org.gradle.isolated-projects.dangerously-ignore-problems=true
```

Run `./gradlew help`. The build ends in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` and prints the violation grouped under `repro.middle`.

Full reproducer: [repro-attribution.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32284191/repro-attribution.zip)

### Environment

Observable on 9.9 nightlies, and most likely on every version that reports Isolated Projects violations — the grouping has probably always worked this way, though only 9.9 was checked. Observed from CLI output and the HTML report on macOS, on a local build of master at `45f98545be7d`, which includes #38738.

Seen originally during Isolated Projects adoption on an 1101-subproject Android build, in a report with 2606 problems and 155 unique. There a convention plugin applied AGP and the access was inside Apollo's `DefaultService.dependsOn`; the report named `com.android.internal.library`, so neither Apollo nor the convention plugin was identified.

### References

- [google/ksp#2844](https://github.com/google/ksp/issues/2844) — an independent report showing the same shape: the location reads `plugin 'com.android.internal.application'` with a KSP frame beneath it.
- `DefaultUserCodeApplicationContext` — holds one application per thread, so no stack of plugin applications is retained.
- `DefaultCollectionCallbackActionDecorator` — captures the current application when a callback is registered and reinstates it when the callback runs.
- `ProblemReportingCrossProjectModelAccess.reportCrossProjectAccessProblem` — reads the current application for the `BuildLogic` trace entry.

body_text:
A managed type whose `@Nested` getter refers back to its own type is accepted when it is created, but the build fails with a `StackOverflowError` as soon as such a value is isolated or snapshotted. Value source parameters show this today. The recursion is in code shared by several parameter kinds, so the reach is wider than value sources.

### Context

Gradle already rejects `@Nested` cycles for task inputs. `AbstractTypeMetadataWalker` detects them and fails with a message that names both ends of the cycle:

```
Cycles between nested beans are not allowed. Cycle detected between: 'nested' and 'nested.nested'.
```

That guard is identity-based: it records each bean instance on the current path. It applies to the task property walk, not to the value processor described below.

### Problem

`AbstractValueProcessor` walks a managed value by unpacking its state and processing each property in turn:

```java
// AbstractValueProcessor.java:127
T state = processValue(managed.unpackState(), visitor);
```

Nothing on this path records where it has been. For a type cycle, each level supplies a nested value of the same type, so the walk descends until the stack is exhausted.

There are two outcomes, neither of which names the cycle:

- Isolation wraps the error: `Could not isolate value <...> of type Params`, caused by `java.lang.StackOverflowError (no error message)`. Close to the stack limit the cause is sometimes dropped, leaving the same message with nothing under it. Which of the two appears depends on the stack space left, so it varies between machines and between runs.
- Snapshotting does not wrap it. A bare `StackOverflowError` reaches the build.

The expected diagnosis is the one the task input path already gives — a message that names the types in the cycle — because the shape is invalid in the same way and for the same reason. A cycle cannot expand to a finite object graph.

### What the console shows

The full output of the reproducer:

```
* Where:
Build file '/…/build.gradle' line: 16

* What went wrong:
A problem occurred evaluating root project 'ux'.
> Could not isolate value Params_Decorated@40358ba2 of type Params
   > java.lang.StackOverflowError (no error message)

* Try:
> Run with --stacktrace option to get the stack trace.
```

Nothing here is actionable:

- The named type is `Params_Decorated`, a generated class. `SelfNested`, which was declared in the build script and holds the cycle, is not named, and neither is `getSelf`.
- Line 16 is where the value source is used, not where the cycle was declared.
- The deepest cause prints as `(no error message)`, because a `StackOverflowError` carries none.

Following the `--stacktrace` hint does not help either. The trace runs to about 1,200 frames, of which roughly 1,015 are 203 repetitions of the same five `AbstractValueProcessor` frames. The declared type appears only as generated frames, `SelfNested_Decorated.unpackState` and `SelfNested_Decorated.getName`, both reported as `(Unknown Source)` with no file or line. The word "cycle" appears nowhere in the output.

The identity-based guard used for task inputs is not sufficient here. A nested value is cached per property, so the same getter returns the same instance, but each level of the cycle is a different instance:

```groovy
instance.self.is(instance.self)          // true
instance.self.is(instance.self.self)     // false
```

Termination therefore needs a guard on the types along the path, or a depth limit, rather than a set of visited instances.

### Reproducer

`build.gradle`:

```groovy
import org.gradle.api.provider.*

interface SelfNested {
    @Nested SelfNested getSelf()
    Property<String> getName()
}

interface Params extends ValueSourceParameters {
    @Nested SelfNested getNested()
}

abstract class Probe implements ValueSource<String, Params> {
    @Override String obtain() { return "ok" }
}

println("probe = " + providers.of(Probe) {}.get())
```

Run `gradle help`. The build fails as above and never prints `probe = ok`.

The reproducer needs no injected services and no configuration cache. Parameters that nest themselves directly fail the same way:

```groovy
interface Params extends ValueSourceParameters {
    @Nested Params getSelf()
}
```

The repeating frames are:

```
AbstractValueProcessor.processManaged(AbstractValueProcessor.java:127)
AbstractValueProcessor.processValue(AbstractValueProcessor.java:98)
AbstractValueProcessor.processArrayElements(AbstractValueProcessor.java:183)
AbstractValueProcessor.processArray(AbstractValueProcessor.java:176)
AbstractValueProcessor.processValue(AbstractValueProcessor.java:92)
AbstractValueProcessor.processManaged(AbstractValueProcessor.java:127)
```

### Scope

Reproduced:

| Shape | Result |
|---|---|
| Value source parameters, `@Nested` cycle through a second type | `IsolationException`, caused by `StackOverflowError` |
| Value source parameters, direct self-nesting | `IsolationException`, caused by `StackOverflowError` |
| Isolation of a managed type with a mutual cycle (`A` nests `B`, `B` nests `A`) | `IsolationException`, caused by `StackOverflowError` |
| Snapshotting of the same shapes | bare `StackOverflowError`, not wrapped |
| Instantiation of such a type, without isolation | accepted, no error |
| Same shapes with the configuration cache enabled | unchanged |
| Build service parameters, obtained by `registerIfAbsent(...).get()` | no failure; not isolated on this path |

Not checked: artifact transform parameters, worker parameters, and task `@Nested` inputs whose cycle is formed by types rather than by assignment.

### Environment

Reproduced on Gradle master (9.9.0), with Java 17 and macOS 26.7, run from the CLI. The configuration cache was checked and makes no difference. Earlier versions were not examined.

{"repository": "gradle/gradle", "task_candidate_id": 6726, "repository_id": 118, "issue_number": 39202, "github_issue_id": 5487677787, "html_url": "https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/39202", "created_at": "2026-09-17T12:59:25+00:00", "author_association": "MEMBER", "title": "StackOverflowError when a managed type has a `@Nested` getter that forms a type cycle", "body_text": "A managed type whose `@Nested` getter refers back to its own type is accepted when it is created, but the build fails with a `StackOverflowError` as soon as such a value is isolated or snapshotted. Value source parameters show this today. The recursion is in code shared by several parameter kinds, so the reach is wider than value sources.

### Context

Gradle already rejects `@Nested` cycles for task inputs. `AbstractTypeMetadataWalker` detects them and fails with a message that names both ends of the cycle:

```
Cycles between nested beans are not allowed. Cycle detected between: 'nested' and 'nested.nested'.
```

That guard is identity-based: it records each bean instance on the current path. It applies to the task property walk, not to the value processor described below.

### Problem

`AbstractValueProcessor` walks a managed value by unpacking its state and processing each property in turn:

```java
// AbstractValueProcessor.java:127
T state = processValue(managed.unpackState(), visitor);
```

Nothing on this path records where it has been. For a type cycle, each level supplies a nested value of the same type, so the walk descends until the stack is exhausted.

There are two outcomes, neither of which names the cycle:

- Isolation wraps the error: `Could not isolate value <...> of type Params`, caused by `java.lang.StackOverflowError (no error message)`. Close to the stack limit the cause is sometimes dropped, leaving the same message with nothing under it. Which of the two appears depends on the stack space left, so it varies between machines and between runs.
- Snapshotting does not wrap it. A bare `StackOverflowError` reaches the build.

The expected diagnosis is the one the task input path already gives — a message that names the types in the cycle — because the shape is invalid in the same way and for the same reason. A cycle cannot expand to a finite object graph.

### What the console shows

The full output of the reproducer:

```
* Where:
Build file '/…/build.gradle' line: 16

* What went wrong:
A problem occurred evaluating root project 'ux'.
> Could not isolate value Params_Decorated@40358ba2 of type Params
   > java.lang.StackOverflowError (no error message)

* Try:
> Run with --stacktrace option to get the stack trace.
```

Nothing here is actionable:

- The named type is `Params_Decorated`, a generated class. `SelfNested`, which was declared in the build script and holds the cycle, is not named, and neither is `getSelf`.
- Line 16 is where the value source is used, not where the cycle was declared.
- The deepest cause prints as `(no error message)`, because a `StackOverflowError` carries none.

Following the `--stacktrace` hint does not help either. The trace runs to about 1,200 frames, of which roughly 1,015 are 203 repetitions of the same five `AbstractValueProcessor` frames. The declared type appears only as generated frames, `SelfNested_Decorated.unpackState` and `SelfNested_Decorated.getName`, both reported as `(Unknown Source)` with no file or line. The word "cycle" appears nowhere in the output.

The identity-based guard used for task inputs is not sufficient here. A nested value is cached per property, so the same getter returns the same instance, but each level of the cycle is a different instance:

```groovy
instance.self.is(instance.self)          // true
instance.self.is(instance.self.self)     // false
```

Termination therefore needs a guard on the types along the path, or a depth limit, rather than a set of visited instances.

### Reproducer

`build.gradle`:

```groovy
import org.gradle.api.provider.*

interface SelfNested {
    @Nested SelfNested getSelf()
    Property<String> getName()
}

interface Params extends ValueSourceParameters {
    @Nested SelfNested getNested()
}

abstract class Probe implements ValueSource<String, Params> {
    @Override String obtain() { return "ok" }
}

println("probe = " + providers.of(Probe) {}.get())
```

Run `gradle help`. The build fails as above and never prints `probe = ok`.

The reproducer needs no injected services and no configuration cache. Parameters that nest themselves directly fail the same way:

```groovy
interface Params extends ValueSourceParameters {
    @Nested Params getSelf()
}
```

The repeating frames are:

```
AbstractValueProcessor.processManaged(AbstractValueProcessor.java:127)
AbstractValueProcessor.processValue(AbstractValueProcessor.java:98)
AbstractValueProcessor.processArrayElements(AbstractValueProcessor.java:183)
AbstractValueProcessor.processArray(AbstractValueProcessor.java:176)
AbstractValueProcessor.processValue(AbstractValueProcessor.java:92)
AbstractValueProcessor.processManaged(AbstractValueProcessor.java:127)
```

### Scope

Reproduced:

| Shape | Result |
|---|---|
| Value source parameters, `@Nested` cycle through a second type | `IsolationException`, caused by `StackOverflowError` |
| Value source parameters, direct self-nesting | `IsolationException`, caused by `StackOverflowError` |
| Isolation of a managed type with a mutual cycle (`A` nests `B`, `B` nests `A`) | `IsolationException`, caused by `StackOverflowError` |
| Snapshotting of the same shapes | bare `StackOverflowError`, not wrapped |
| Instantiation of such a type, without isolation | accepted, no error |
| Same shapes with the configuration cache enabled | unchanged |
| Build service parameters, obtained by `registerIfAbsent(...).get()` | no failure; not isolated on this path |

Not checked: artifact transform parameters, worker parameters, and task `@Nested` inputs whose cycle is formed by types rather than by assignment.

### Environment

Reproduced on Gradle master (9.9.0), with Java 17 and macOS 26.7, run from the CLI. The configuration cache was checked and makes no difference. Earlier versions were not examined.

body_text:
### Current Behavior

Gradle v9.7.1 can select a non-default branch of a Git source dependency while
leaving its submodule checked out at the remote default branch revision. A
normal `assemble` succeeds and compiles the default child source even though
the selected parent commit records a different child gitlink.

### Expected Behavior

All submodules should be updated recursively to the gitlinks recorded by the
selected parent revision before the source dependency is built.

### Context (optional)

This affects source-integrity: a successful build can consume a recursive tree
different from the requested source revision. The attached report includes an
independent Git-core control.

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

`attachments.zip` contains `reproduce.patch`, which applies to a clean
Gradle v9.7.1 checkout and runs Gradle's own `GitVcsIntegrationTest`. The
reproducer and commands are documented in the attached `report.md`.

[attachments.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32363259/attachments.zip)
[report.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32363258/report.md)

### Gradle version

Gradle v9.7.1 (wrapper distribution: Gradle 9.7.0).

### Build scan URL (optional)

Not generated.

### Your Environment (optional)

Gradle source commit `92f0512e7f06d84621afba191f75e265363890cf`; Linux amd64;
OpenJDK 17.

### Expected Behavior

[Unused return value checker﻿](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/unused-return-value-checker.html) is enabled in `.kts` build scripts, or there is some way to turn it on.


### Current Behavior (optional)

There is no way to enable unused return value checker﻿ in build scripts.


### Context

The checker catches calls whose result is silently dropped, such as a `String.replace` written as a statement

Kotlin initially added the checker as experimental in 2.3, and it [will become stable in 2.5](https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/KT-12719). Gradle uses Kotlin 2.3 since 9.4.0.

The checker can be enabled in binary plugins and precompiled script plugins are covered (via KGP DSL).

Related: #24221 asks for Kotlin compiler options for build scripts in general.

Configuration Cache has a [status page](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/configuration_cache_status.html) that answers "can I use this yet, and with what?" in one screen. Isolated Projects has no equivalent.

### Problem

Its status is spread across the [feature page](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/isolated_projects.html), under `Recent changes`, `Current limitations`, and `Isolated Projects and other Gradle features` — mixed with migration material a person evaluating the feature does not need yet. There is nothing to link to when someone asks "is Isolated Projects ready for us?", and nothing to update when the answer changes.

### Proposal

Add an Isolated Projects status page, as a sibling of the Configuration Cache one.

The shape is open. The Configuration Cache page is the closest model, but the axes that matter for Isolated Projects may differ — a plugin-by-plugin table may not be the right one. Settling that is part of this work.

Related to #36940, which asked for clarity on the state of Isolated Projects overall. That one is resolved by the graduation to incubating; this is the narrower, standing reference such a question keeps needing.

body_text:
### Current Behavior

Enabling configuration cache causes each `DefaultProject` object to be retained in the heap twice. For my builds this has increased heap use to the point where they deadlock on GC thrashing and hit CI timeouts in the largest targets.

### Expected Behavior

Memory footprint should be similar to (or ideally better) than when using vintage mode.

### Context (optional)

This was previously fixed in #34775 but reverted in #34847. I independently verified the fix from #34775 does reduce memory consumption to the expected level. I do not know what the Develocity issues with "asynchronous processing" mentioned in the revert are and didn't observe any issues when testing my patched gradle build, but I also was not looking for it.

Enabling isolated projects has no effect on this behavior.

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

Should be reproducible on any project using configuration cache using any version of gradle.

### Gradle version

9.7.1

### Build scan URL (optional)

_No response_

body_text:
A settings plugin that registers an action with `Gradle.getLifecycle().beforeProject`, and reads the `Gradle` instance inside it, fails with four nested `Caused by` levels of internal Gradle class names, no source location, and a final message naming a type the author holds legitimately. The author has to infer which action is at fault and what rule it broke. Plugin authors meet this while porting `gradle.beforeProject` callbacks to `lifecycle.beforeProject`, which is the migration path for Isolated Projects.

### Context

Under Isolated Projects, each project receives its own `Gradle` wrapper, so a lifecycle action cannot carry the build-scope instance across. The check runs when the action is isolated, after settings evaluation finishes. An author porting `gradle.beforeProject` already holds a `Gradle` at the call site, and carrying it into the new action is the natural next step.

### Problem

The build fails with this chain, abbreviated at each level to the part that changes:

```
Failed to notify build listener.
> ... field `beforeProject` of `org.gradle.internal.isolate.actions.services.IsolatedProjectActions` ... 'java.util.ArrayList'
   > ... field `$action` of `...DefaultIsolatedProjectEvaluationListenerProvider$withUserCodeApplicationContext$1$1` ... 'ConventionSettingsPlugin$$Lambda$2204/0x000000b801b60c00'
      > ... field `capturedArgs` of `java.lang.invoke.SerializedLambda` ... '[Ljava.lang.Object;'
         > cannot serialize object of type 'org.gradle.invocation.DefaultGradle', a subtype of 'org.gradle.api.invocation.Gradle', as these are not supported with the configuration cache.
```

Four things make this hard to act on:

- No `* Where:` line. The failure reads "Failed to notify build listener", and nothing says where the action was registered.
- No configuration cache report. This is a hard error rather than a reported problem, so no HTML report is written and no link to one is offered.
- `--stacktrace` adds no user code frames. It repeats the same causes and names no plugin source.
- The final message states the wrong rule. It says `Gradle` is unsupported "with the configuration cache", but the author may hold a `Gradle` perfectly well, and does so on the line above. The rule that applies is narrower: the action must not carry the build-scope instance into a project.

The only trace of user code in the chain is the synthetic `ConventionSettingsPlugin$$Lambda$2204/0x000000b801b60c00`. It names the class but not which lambda, and carries no line number. A plugin that registers several actions gives its author nothing to narrow it down.

Keeping the `Gradle` in a field and registering `this::configureProject` instead adds one level reading `field 'gradle' of 'ConventionSettingsPlugin'`. That names a field the author wrote, so the more indirect version of this mistake reports better than the direct one.

A person who meets this expects the failure to name the action they registered and where they registered it, and to state the rule in terms of what they wrote: a lifecycle action must not capture the build-scope `Gradle`, and `Project.getGradle()` inside the action gives the correct per-project instance.

### Reproducer

A settings plugin `my.convention`, supplied by an included build:

```java
public class ConventionSettingsPlugin implements Plugin<Settings> {
    @Override
    public void apply(Settings settings) {
        Gradle gradle = settings.getGradle();
        gradle.getLifecycle().beforeProject(project ->
            System.out.println("configuring " + project.getName() + " in " + gradle.getRootProject().getName()));
    }
}
```

The consuming `settings.gradle` applies the plugin and includes one subproject, whose build script is empty. `gradle.properties` sets `org.gradle.unsafe.isolated-projects=true`. Run `gradle help`.

Reading a `Settings` there instead fails the same way, ending at `org.gradle.initialization.DefaultSettings`. A lambda that captures `this` but reaches no build-scope state succeeds, so the capture alone is not the problem.

Reading `project.getGradle()` inside the action succeeds, and yields the per-project `CrossProjectConfigurationReportingGradle` wrapper.

### Environment

Reproduced on Gradle 9.7.1 with Java 17 on macOS, run from the CLI. Isolated Projects enabled; not checked with the configuration cache alone. The plugin is Java; a Groovy plugin fails differently, because the closure delegates to the `Project` rather than the plugin instance. Kotlin is unverified.

Part of #38670. Stage 2 of the [Problems API - Predefined Groups](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1uyAKVISEwhy-AZppQhMST-XankI-9gtIelxhaQttqRI) spec, area 3 of 4: migrate Gradle's own producers to the predefined groups introduced in #39075.

### Scope

| Legacy group | Ids | Target |
|---|---|---|
| `dependency-version-catalog` | 19 | Dependencies > Declaration |
| `dependency-variant-resolution` | 14 | Dependencies > Graph Resolution (10), Dependencies > Artifact Resolution (4) |

Static id constants such as `VersionCatalogProblemId` become lookups at report time, since groups come from the injected `Problems` service.

### Rules shared by all stage 2 areas

- Only predefined groups; no new predefined groups are added during the migration. Where nothing fits, the mapping goes back to the spec authors.
- Problem ids are renamed from kebab-case to the spec's sentence style while each site is touched.
- Producers obtain groups from the injected `Problems` service (`problems.getGroups()`), not from a static holder; modules keep depending on `problems-api` only.
- Consumers that compare group identity switch to the predefined groups (equality is structural: name plus parent chain), never to string comparison on a joined path.
- `KnownProblemIds` and the integration tests asserting legacy fqids are updated; cross-version specs asserting legacy names are gated with `@TargetGradleVersion`.
- Develocity reads group names through the build-operation type `org.gradle.operations.problems.ProblemGroup`; the Develocity team is notified before the first area lands.
- All areas land within one release cycle, so no release ships with half of the problems under new names.

Mapping and details: [implementation roadmap](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xxC9vR1BadSbam9fJjJ243drsF8JXBn5G_j7kdOMneY), section "Stage 2".

Part of #38670. Stage 2 of the [Problems API - Predefined Groups](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1uyAKVISEwhy-AZppQhMST-XankI-9gtIelxhaQttqRI) spec, area 4 of 4: migrate Gradle's own producers to the predefined groups introduced in #39075.

### Scope

| Legacy group | Ids | Target |
|---|---|---|
| `validation:configuration-cache` | 2 message-derived families, 2 notices | Gradle > Configuration Cache, Gradle > Isolated Projects |
| `deprecation` | message-derived family | Gradle > Deprecation |
| `task-selection` | 7 | Gradle > Invocation |
| `configuration-usage` | 10 | Gradle > Build Definition (4), Gradle > Build Logic (2), Gradle > Plugin Validation (4) |
| `plugin-application`, `scripts` | 1, 1 | Gradle > Build Definition |
| `jvm-toolchain`, `daemon-toolchain:configuration-generation` | 1, 1 | Provisioning > Tools and Toolchains |
| `packaging:signing` | 1 | Packaging > Signing |
| `problems-api` | 3 | Gradle > Build Logic (spec decision pending) |

Notes for this area:

- Configuration cache and Isolated Projects problems share one group today; `ConfigurationCacheProblems.onProblem(problem, severity, forIsolatedProjects)` already has the flag that decides between the two targets.
- `Gradle > Deprecation` is reserved for Gradle and has no public getter; `DeprecationLogger` reaches it through the internal view of the Gradle root, `GradleProblemGroupInternal.getDeprecation()`. `ConsoleProblemEmitter` must suppress deprecation problems by their `DeprecationData` instead of by the legacy group, or every deprecation prints twice under `--warning-mode=all`. The logger's own console output, warning mode, summary and Build Scan event stay as they are.
- `DefaultProblemsReportCreator.kt` builds a throwaway root group for the id path element and must resolve against the predefined groups instead.
- After this area, `GradleCoreProblemGroup` and the ad hoc root groups have no producers and are deleted.
- Canonicalize groups at report time: a group created through the legacy factories whose name path matches a predefined group (for example `ProblemGroup.create("Java", "Java", groups.compilation)`) is structurally equal to the predefined one but carries no description, so the same group shows up in reports with or without a description depending on the factory used. The reporter should resolve reported groups against the predefined hierarchy by name path, the lookup `SerializedProblemGroup.readResolve` already does, so descriptions are consistent regardless of the producer's API.
- Docs: the user guide lists which predefined groups Gradle itself reports into; release notes mention the changed group names for anyone filtering reports.

### Rules shared by all stage 2 areas

- Only predefined groups; no new predefined groups are added during the migration. Where nothing fits, the mapping goes back to the spec authors.
- Problem ids are renamed from kebab-case to the spec's sentence style while each site is touched.
- Producers obtain groups from the injected `Problems` service (`problems.getGroups()`), not from a static holder; modules keep depending on `problems-api` only.
- Consumers that compare group identity switch to the predefined groups (equality is structural: name plus parent chain), never to string comparison on a joined path.
- `KnownProblemIds` and the integration tests asserting legacy fqids are updated; cross-version specs asserting legacy names are gated with `@TargetGradleVersion`.

### Scope

| Legacy group | Ids | Target |
|---|---|---|
| `validation:configuration-cache` | 2 message-derived families, 2 notices | Gradle > Configuration Cache, Gradle > Isolated Projects |
| `deprecation` | message-derived family | Gradle > Deprecation |

| `plugin-application`, `scripts` | 1, 1 | Gradle > Build Definition |

| `packaging:signing` | 1 | Packaging > Signing |
| `problems-api` | 3 | Gradle > Build Logic (spec decision pending) |

body_text:
Part of #38670. Stages 3 and 4 of the [Problems API - Predefined Groups](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1uyAKVISEwhy-AZppQhMST-XankI-9gtIelxhaQttqRI) spec, one deprecation PR. Must ship in a minor before the removals in the next major.

### Deprecations

- `getDisplayName()` on groups and ids (public API and Tooling API): keeps returning the name; the description of predefined groups replaces it where a longer text is wanted.
- The static `ProblemGroup.create` and `ProblemId.create`: creation goes through `problems.getGroups()`.
- The public `ProblemGroup.getParent()`: nothing outside Gradle reads the producer-side parent chain (Develocity and Tooling API clients have their own types); Gradle's own consumers already walk through the internal view.
- Everything the spec forbids but the old API still allows: names violating the character and length rules of the new entry points, new root groups, sub-groups under the Gradle root or under `Undefined` or under a third-level group (a fourth level), problems attached to root groups, and reserved names created through the factories (`ProblemGroup.create("Undefined", ..., parent)` bypasses the reserved-name check, `ProblemGroup.create("Deprecation", "Deprecation", groups.gradle)` is structurally equal to the reserved `Gradle > Deprecation`). Stage 1 documents that the legacy factories do not enforce the rules; the nags use the same rules as the new entry points.

### Notes

- `DeprecationLogger` cannot be called from `problems-api` (logging depends on it). Nags fire from a module that can see it, either at report time in `problems` or through a hook installed by logging at startup; plain logger warnings bypass warning mode, the summary and Build Scans and are not used.
- Tooling API: align the client-side `DefaultProblemGroup.equals` with structural equality; wire types stay unchanged.
- Docs: upgrading-guide entry per deprecation with the migration path; the reporting guide is rewritten around name plus description.

Removals and hard enforcement follow in the next major (see the companion issue on moving the remaining internals out of `problems-api`). Details: [implementation roadmap](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xxC9vR1BadSbam9fJjJ243drsF8JXBn5G_j7kdOMneY), section "Stages 3 + 4".

Part of #38670. Stage 5a of the [Problems API - Predefined Groups](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1uyAKVISEwhy-AZppQhMST-XankI-9gtIelxhaQttqRI) spec. Spans gradle/configuration-cache-report and gradle/gradle; can ship as soon as the predefined groups (#39075) are in, it needs no deprecation cycle.

### Scope

- Report repo: `JsProblemIdElement` gains an optional `description`; `displayName` becomes optional with a fallback to `name`; the "By group" tree shows descriptions; ordering is fixed root order from the spec, sub-groups alphabetical, `Undefined` last. The root order should come from the wire rather than being hard-coded in the JS, so evolving the predefined roots needs no report release.
- gradle/gradle: `DefaultProblemsReportCreator` emits the description and the ordering hint; bump the report dependency; update `ConfigurationCacheReportFixture` and `ReceivedProblem` parsing.

Details: [implementation roadmap](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xxC9vR1BadSbam9fJjJ243drsF8JXBn5G_j7kdOMneY), section "Stage 5".

### Scope

- The identity of a problem in the report JSON becomes the array of names from the root group to the problem, for example `["Compilation", "Java", "Unused import"]`; `displayName` is no longer emitted in the identity array. Old reports stay readable (`ignoreUnknownKeys`).
- The array becomes the documented identity for tooling, usable for baselining and by external tools.

Details: [implementation roadmap](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xxC9vR1BadSbam9fJjJ243drsF8JXBn5G_j7kdOMneY), section "Stage 5".

body_text:
Part of #38670. Follow-up agreed while reviewing #39075: the `problems-api` module should not gain internals, and the existing ones should leave it.

### State after #39075

`problems-api` gains exactly one internal type, `ProblemGroupInternal`, the contract between the API module and the implementations (`getParentInternal()`, `getDescription()`, and the shared statics for viewing a group as internal and for structural equality). Name validation lives in `problems-reporting` (`ProblemNames`), rendering in `problems-rendering` (`ProblemGroupRenderer`), the predefined groups in `problems-reporting`.

### What pins the rest

The public static factories `ProblemGroup.create` and `ProblemId.create` instantiate `DefaultProblemGroup` and `DefaultProblemId`, so those two classes, and through `DefaultProblemGroup` also `ProblemGroupInternal`, must stay in `problems-api` until the factories are removed as planned once https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/38670 lands.

### Plan

1. Independent of the factories, as its own PR: move `DefaultProblem`, `DefaultProblemBuilder`, `DefaultProblemProgressDetails` and `BuildOperationProblem` to `problems-reporting`. `ProblemInternal.toBuilder()` stays as the interface method. Blocker to resolve first: the `problems-rendering` tests construct problems through the builder and `problems-reporting` depends on `problems-rendering`; use a test-only `Problem` implementation or a test-scope dependency.
2. When the next major removes `ProblemGroup.create` and `ProblemId.create` (deprecated in stages 3 and 4): move `DefaultProblemGroup`, `DefaultProblemId` and `ProblemGroupInternal` to `problems-reporting`. Consumers that depend on `problems-api` only and walk the group chain (build-operations-trace, tooling-api-builders, enterprise) then either depend on `problems-reporting` or get an equivalent view; decide at that point.

### Expected Behavior

Any argument of the public API methods that the Configuration Cache serializes is annotated with a machine-readable annotation or have it encoded in its type.

### Current Behavior (optional)

Only `IsolatedAction` has explicit serialization documentation in its contract. Everything else is at best documented somewhere - in the javadoc or in the userguide.

### Context

Gradle have already introduced a type that has isolation/serialization contract baked in - [`IsolatedAction`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/javadoc/org/gradle/api/IsolatedAction.html). However, its use today is limited to only two callbacks on `GradleLifecycle`. Anything else relies on documentation, sometimes far removed from the affected code point (e.g. the CC user guide for `doFirst`/`doLast`).

This is especially important for parameters typically implemented as lambdas, as those are prone to capturing all kinds of configuration-only state. However, instances of user-implemented types fed to Gradle APIs may also be captured. Typically, these implement some Gradle-defined interface: `Task`, `ValueSourceParameters`, etc. 

Lack of visibility makes it hard for users to reason about what is captured by the configuration cache. Automated tools, like linters, have to rely on hardcoded API lists and cannot pick up newly introduced Gradle contracts automatically without releasing a new version.

body_text:
### Current Behavior

Since the Gradle API runtime jar generation was parallelized (c812d5c51b9, first in 9.5.0-M6), generating
`gradle-api-<version>.jar` into an empty Gradle user home can fail a daemon running with the default heap
(`-Xmx512m`) with `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`.

We see this in CI. Each build runs against a fresh Gradle user home, so each one
generates the jar. We captured four heap dumps (`-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`), on Gradle 9.8.0 and 9.9.0
nightlies. In all four the daemon was inside `RuntimeShadedJarCreator` when the error was thrown:

- The `shaded jar writer` thread (`MultiProducerSingleConsumerProcessor`) was deflating entries into the output jar.
- The worker threads were still relocating classes (`RuntimeShadedJarCreator.processClassFile`).
- The writer's `MpscUnboundedArrayQueue` retained 37–38 MB of fully relocated input jars waiting to be written. The
  `InputFile` being written retained another 22–40 MB.
- About 260 MB of the heap was unreachable relocation garbage (`byte[]` 129 MB, `int[]` 41 MB,
  `org.objectweb.asm.Type` 23 MB, `String` 22 MB, `SymbolTable$Entry` 13 MB). Live heap was only 145–180 MB.

The `OutOfMemoryError` itself surfaces in whatever unrelated code allocates next. In our dumps that was a plugin
loading a class.

### Expected Behavior

Generating the API jar fits in the default daemon heap, as it did before 9.5.0.

### Context (optional)

Before c812d5c51b9, entries were relocated and written one at a time on a single thread. Only about one class was
live at once, and duplicate paths were skipped before being relocated. Since then:

- Each input jar is relocated completely into an `InputFile` (`List<byte[]>`) before being submitted to the writer.
- Up to max-workers input jars are relocated at once.
- The writer writes in input order. Completed `InputFile`s wait in the unbounded queue and in the consumer's `TreeSet`
  until every earlier file has been written, so one slow early jar holds back all later ones.
- The `seenPaths` duplicate check moved to the writer, so duplicate entries are now relocated before they are dropped.
- Relocation garbage is allocated by several threads at once.

Nothing bounds how much relocated content can be held at once. The peak depends on the worker count and on the
writer's speed relative to the relocating threads. A slower writer (a slow disk, or antivirus scanning the output)
pushes it higher. We only see the failure on Windows agents.

Still present on `master` as of 2026-09-26.

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

Not yet reduced. Our failing case is a build with a Kotlin DSL script, run against an empty Gradle user home with the
default daemon heap. It fails intermittently, not every run.

### Gradle version

9.5.0 and later (observed on 9.5.0, 9.6.1, 9.7.1, 9.8.0-rc-1, 9.8.0-rc-3, and 9.8.0 / 9.9.0 nightlies)

### Gradle version that used to work

9.4.1

### Build scan URL (optional)

—

### Your Environment (optional)

{"repository": "gradle/gradle", "task_candidate_id": 6740, "repository_id": 118, "issue_number": 39320, "github_issue_id": 5595538146, "html_url": "https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/39320", "created_at": "2026-09-26T16:33:16+00:00", "author_association": "MEMBER", "title": "Gradle API jar generation can exhaust the default daemon heap since 9.5.0", "body_text": "### Current Behavior

Since the Gradle API runtime jar generation was parallelized (c812d5c51b9, first in 9.5.0-M6), generating
`gradle-api-<version>.jar` into an empty Gradle user home can fail a daemon running with the default heap
(`-Xmx512m`) with `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`.

We see this in CI. Each build runs against a fresh Gradle user home, so each one
generates the jar. We captured four heap dumps (`-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`), on Gradle 9.8.0 and 9.9.0
nightlies. In all four the daemon was inside `RuntimeShadedJarCreator` when the error was thrown:

- The `shaded jar writer` thread (`MultiProducerSingleConsumerProcessor`) was deflating entries into the output jar.
- The worker threads were still relocating classes (`RuntimeShadedJarCreator.processClassFile`).
- The writer's `MpscUnboundedArrayQueue` retained 37–38 MB of fully relocated input jars waiting to be written. The
  `InputFile` being written retained another 22–40 MB.
- About 260 MB of the heap was unreachable relocation garbage (`byte[]` 129 MB, `int[]` 41 MB,
  `org.objectweb.asm.Type` 23 MB, `String` 22 MB, `SymbolTable$Entry` 13 MB). Live heap was only 145–180 MB.

The `OutOfMemoryError` itself surfaces in whatever unrelated code allocates next. In our dumps that was a plugin
loading a class.

### Expected Behavior

Generating the API jar fits in the default daemon heap, as it did before 9.5.0.

### Context (optional)

Before c812d5c51b9, entries were relocated and written one at a time on a single thread. Only about one class was
live at once, and duplicate paths were skipped before being relocated. Since then:

- Each input jar is relocated completely into an `InputFile` (`List<byte[]>`) before being submitted to the writer.
- Up to max-workers input jars are relocated at once.
- The writer writes in input order. Completed `InputFile`s wait in the unbounded queue and in the consumer's `TreeSet`
  until every earlier file has been written, so one slow early jar holds back all later ones.
- The `seenPaths` duplicate check moved to the writer, so duplicate entries are now relocated before they are dropped.
- Relocation garbage is allocated by several threads at once.

Nothing bounds how much relocated content can be held at once. The peak depends on the worker count and on the
writer's speed relative to the relocating threads. A slower writer (a slow disk, or antivirus scanning the output)
pushes it higher. We only see the failure on Windows agents.

Still present on `master` as of 2026-09-26.

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

Not yet reduced. Our failing case is a build with a Kotlin DSL script, run against an empty Gradle user home with the
default daemon heap. It fails intermittently, not every run.

### Gradle version

9.5.0 and later (observed on 9.5.0, 9.6.1, 9.7.1, 9.8.0-rc-1, 9.8.0-rc-3, and 9.8.0 / 9.9.0 nightlies)

### Gradle version that used to work

9.4.1

### Build scan URL (optional)

—

### Your Environment (optional)

Windows 10 CI agents, JDK 21.0.12 (Liberica), default daemon heap (`-Xmx512m`). Heap dumps are available on request.

body_text:
### Current Behavior

When I _stack_ convention plugins, I get the following error for transitive plugin dependencies:

```
> Task :build-logic-local:generatePrecompiledScriptPluginAccessors FAILED

FAILURE: Build failed with an exception.

* Where:
Precompiled script plugin 'build-logic-local/src/main/kotlin/my-local-plugin.settings.gradle.kts' line: 1

* What went wrong:
An exception occurred applying plugin request [id: 'my-common-plugin']
> Failed to apply plugin 'my-common-plugin'.
   > Plugin with id 'org.gradle.toolchains.foojay-resolver-convention' not found.
```

### Expected Behavior

`generatePrecompiledScriptPluginAccessors` succeeds.

### Context (optional)

_No response_

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

I have the following setup

- `build-logic-common` contains convention plugins shared across an organization (in the real case, this gets published)
- `build-logic-local` contains convention plugins for one project, building on top of `build-logic-common`

Reproducer with everything in one Gradle project:


```sh
├── build-logic-common
│   ├── build.gradle.kts
│   │     # plugins { `kotlin-dsl` }
│   │     # repositories { gradlePluginPortal() }
│   │     # group = "org.example"
│   │     # dependencies { implementation("org.gradle.toolchains:foojay-resolver:0.2") }
│   ├── settings.gradle.kts
│   └── src/main/kotlin
│       └── my-common-plugin.settings.gradle.kts
│             # plugins { id("org.gradle.toolchains.foojay-resolver-convention") }
├── build-logic-local
│   ├── build.gradle.kts
│   │     # plugins { `kotlin-dsl` }
│   │     # repositories { gradlePluginPortal() }
│   │     # dependencies { implementation("org.example:build-logic-common") }
│   ├── settings.gradle.kts
│   │     # includeBuild("../build-logic-common")
│   └── src/main/kotlin
│       └── my-local-plugin.settings.gradle.kts
│             # plugins { id("my-common-plugin") }
└── settings.gradle.kts
      # pluginManagement { includeBuild("build-logic-local") }
      # plugins { id("my-local-plugin") }
```

Run `gradle help` to get the error.

Notes:

- `org.gradle.toolchains:foojay-resolver:0.2` is an example of a published settings plugin, failure can be reproduced with other published settings plugins
- The actual application of plugins in the build work, if you disable `generatePrecompiledScriptPluginAccessors` in `build-logic-local` (see below) – scan: https://scans.gradle.com/s/hwpsgwizlg4qk/plugins


```
// disable 'generatePrecompiledScriptPluginAccessors' in 'build-logic-local/build.gradle.kts'
tasks.named("generatePrecompiledScriptPluginAccessors") {
    val accessorsDir = layout.buildDirectory.dir("kotlin-dsl/precompiled-script-plugins-metadata/accessors").get()
    actions.clear()
    doLast { accessorsDir.asFile.mkdirs() }
}
```

### Gradle version

9.8.0 (no working version known)

body_text:
### Current Behavior

In a large multi-project build (~1270 Java projects, ~3700 `JavaCompile` tasks), a full compilation
(`gradlew testClasses --rerun-tasks --no-build-cache`) **fails with `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`
when the configuration cache is enabled**, while the very same build **succeeds without the configuration cache**
(same daemon heap, same machine, same commands).

With the configuration cache the heap-after-GC grows steadily with every executed compile task and is never
released until the build ends; without it, heap-after-GC stays bounded and drops again.

| | CC disabled | CC enabled |
|---|---|---|
| Result | BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 17m 40s | **OutOfMemoryError** after ~37 min |
| Max heap after GC (`-Xmx10g`) | 7.3 GB | 10.2 GB (limit) |
| Full GCs | 0 | 410 |
| **Live heap after ~877 executed compile tasks** (`jcmd GC.class_histogram`, i.e. after full GC) | **2.43 GB** | **5.12 GB** |

Heap-after-GC over time (MB):

- CC disabled: 1934 → 3306 → 3980 → 4024 → 5282 → 5714 → 6482 → 4608 → 4422 (end)
- CC enabled: 3357 → 5667 → 6303 → 9020 → 10172 → 10100 (Full GC) → … → OOM

Class histogram diff at the same point of the build (after ~877 compile tasks):

| Class | CC enabled | CC disabled |
|---|---|---|
| `java.util.HashMap$Node` | 1648 MB (54.0 M instances) | 21 MB (0.69 M) |
| `java.lang.Object[]` | 971 MB (6.46 M) | 120 MB (2.75 M) |
| `com.google.common.collect.ImmutableMapEntry` | 447 MB (19.5 M) | 75 MB (3.3 M) |
| `java.util.HashMap$Node[]` | 402 MB | 73 MB |
| `com.google.common.collect.ImmutableMapEntry[]` | 226 MB | 25 MB |
| `…ImmutableMapEntry$NonTerminalImmutableMapEntry` | 212 MB (9.3 M) | 31 MB (1.4 M) |
| `com.google.common.collect.RegularImmutableSet` | 90 MB (2.96 M) | 5 MB (0.18 M) |
| `org.gradle.api.internal.tasks.compile.incremental.compilerapi.deps.DependentsSet$DefaultDependentsSet` | 68 MB (**2.97 M**) | 2 MB (**89 k**) |
| `java.io.File` | 35 MB (1.17 M) | 1 MB (46 k) |

The growth is dominated by what looks like the incremental Java compilation analysis
(`DependentsSet`, class-dependency / class-hash maps) of already **executed** `JavaCompile` tasks, which appears to stay
reachable for the rest of the build when the configuration cache is enabled.

Note: when the build is up-to-date (no compilation), the configuration cache does **not** increase memory
(reusing the entry actually lowers the peak: 3.65 GB RSS vs 5.3 GB), so the problem is specific to task execution.

This looks similar in symptoms to #30654 (fixed in 9.0.0 RC1), but it still reproduces on 9.5.1 and the retained
objects are different (no included builds are involved on our side beyond the settings plugins).

### Expected Behavior

Memory retained by a `JavaCompile` task for incremental compilation should be released after the task has executed,
the same way as without the configuration cache, so that enabling the configuration cache does not change the
peak heap of a full build by ~2x.

### Context (optional)

We would like to enable the configuration cache for all local builds (configuration time drops from ~40 s to ~4 s),
but full builds run out of memory, so we have to keep it disabled.

- ~1270 Java library projects (`java-library` + `java-test-fixtures`), deep project dependency graph
- `options.incremental = true`, `-parameters`, javac runs **in-process** (no fork), toolchain Java 21 = daemon JDK
- `org.gradle.parallel=true`, `org.gradle.workers.max=12`, `org.gradle.caching=true`
- Daemon: `-Xmx10g`, G1

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

We cannot share the project. The pattern is:

1. A multi-project build with ~1000+ Java projects depending on each other (many `project(...)` dependencies, large compile classpaths).
2. `gradlew testClasses --rerun-tasks --no-build-cache -Dorg.gradle.configuration-cache=true` with `-Xmx10g`.
3. Observe heap-after-GC growing with the number of executed compile tasks until OOM.
4. Same command with `-Dorg.gradle.configuration-cache=false` completes with a bounded heap.

We can provide heap histograms / GC logs, and can try to capture a heap dump or run a diagnostic build if that helps.

### Gradle version

9.5.1

### Build scan URL (optional)

Not available (corporate network).

### Your Environment (optional)

- OS: Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200, x86_64 (i7-12800H, 20 threads, 64 GB RAM)
- JDK: 21 (daemon runs on 21.0.10; Java 21 toolchain)

Disclosure: an LLM was used to help write the bug report and generate the reproducer) 

### Current Behavior

A build tree where two included builds in different parent builds have the same name fails when the configuration cache is enabled. [In the reproducer](https://github.com/tauntz/gradle-issue-reproducer-config-cache/), the root build includes `common` and `library`, and `library` also includes its own `common`:

```
* What went wrong:
Builds are not stored in ascending base node id order, cannot find the node with id 4 targeted by other build task :common:hello.
```

The failure happens on the first run, right after "Configuration cache entry stored". It only happens when both builds with the same name have tasks in the task graph.

The cause looks like the state file name for an included build. It's built from `BuildDefinition.name` rather than the build's path ([`ConfigurationCacheRepository.includedBuildFileFor`](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/blob/v9.8.0/platforms/core-configuration/configuration-cache/src/main/kotlin/org/gradle/internal/cc/impl/ConfigurationCacheRepository.kt#L350)):

```kotlin
resolveSibling("$name.${build.name}")
```

Both builds therefore write to the same `work.bin.common`, and the second one overwrites the first. When the cache is loaded, `:common` gets `:library:common`'s task graph, and the new cross-build node id check fails.

Reproducer: https://github.com/tauntz/gradle-issue-reproducer-config-cache

Run `./gradlew hello`. CI run: https://github.com/tauntz/gradle-issue-reproducer-config-cache/actions/runs/36690661864/job/109806836429

### Expected Behavior

Each included build gets its own configuration cache state, and the build succeeds as it does with `--no-configuration-cache`. Two included builds that have the same name but different paths (`:common` and `:library:common`) are a valid setup, so the state file should be keyed by something unique, such as the build path.

### Context (optional)

In our real project, both the main build and a nested included build have their own `build-logic` convention-plugin build. After we upgraded to 9.8.0, our GitHub dependency submission job started failing.

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

https://github.com/tauntz/gradle-issue-reproducer-config-cache/

### Gradle version

9.8.0

When Gradle runs a user-provided build action that builds tooling models, it should be possible for those models to be reused between invocations.

Under Isolated Projects, it should be possible to reuse models from individual projects that were produced in previous invocations.

This is especially appliable to IDE Sync scenarios, when environment or build logic changes affect only part of the build, while the rest of the model building can be reused, providing a performance benefit.

body_text:
### Current Behavior

In CI (GitHub Actions), a `./gradlew <task-a> <task-b>` invocation intermittently hangs at the end of the configuration phase.

### Expected Behavior

The build starts executing tasks and eventually completes.

### Context (optional)

According to the build operation trace, every project had finished configuring, but the parent `Configure build` build operation never completed, and the build made no further progress until our 5-minute step timeout fired.

1. The daemon started at about 08:42:13 UTC. The last trace event is at 08:42:33 UTC (`ConfigureProjectBuildOperationType` finishing).
2. When the trace stops, only two build operations are open: `Run build` (id 1) and its child `Configure build` (id 4488). All project configuration operations (`ConfigureProject`, `NotifyProjectAfterEvaluated`) have ended.
3. The thread dump was taken at 08:46:30, about 4 minutes after the last event:
   - `Daemon worker` is parked (`WAITING (parking)`) in `DefaultProjectsPreparer.prepareProjects` -> `TaskPathProjectEvaluator.configureHierarchyInParallel` -> `scheduleProjectsJustInTime` -> `DefaultBuildOperationExecutor.executeInParallel` -> `runAllWithAccessToProjectState`.
   - The only `Execution worker` is idle in `DefaultPlanExecutor$ExecutorWorker.getNextItem` -> `DefaultResourceLockCoordinationService.withStateLock` (`Object.wait`), about 1.4s CPU in 247s.
   - The `jar transforms` threads are idle in `LinkedBlockingQueue.take`, and the Develocity worker is sleeping.
   - 0 threads are BLOCKED, and no thread is in project script evaluation or plugin code.

Attachments:
- `gradle-trace-log.txt` (build operation trace, 8 MB; ends at the hang)
- `GradleDaemon-thread-dump.txt` (daemon thread dump)


### Self-contained Reproducer Project

The hang is not easily reproducible and only occurs every couple builds.

### Gradle version

9.8.0

### Build scan URL (optional)

_No response_

### Your Environment (optional)

- OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM 25.0.4.1+10-LTS (Corretto), Linux (GitHub Actions runner)
- Develocity plugin applied (version 4.5.1)
- Large multi-project Kotlin build with many subprojects
- No configuration cache entry available for this run ("Calculating task graph as no cached configuration is available")
- `gradle.properties`:
  ```
  org.gradle.parallel=true
  org.gradle.caching=true
  org.gradle.configuration-cache=true
  org.gradle.configuration-cache.problems=warn
  org.gradle.isolated-projects=true
  org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx8g -Xms2g -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=1g
  ```

If gradle receives a 403 during one of its HEAD requests to the remote repo, [it tries to parse the response body as RFC9457](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/pull/36209), but the body (properly) doesn't exist because HEAD requests have no body. Also, the warning is giant, even when the build is not running in --stacktrace.

403 from a HEAD should either re-request the body using GET, or not try to parse the body. The parse warning should probably be smaller or entirely absent, since it's not actionable.

body_text:
### Current Behavior

A build applies the Develocity plugin explicitly, from a settings convention plugin that it adds via the `buildscript` classpath and `apply plugin:`. `develocity-gradle-plugin` is therefore only a **transitive** dependency on the settings classpath.

When that build runs with `--scan`, Gradle still auto-applies `com.gradle.develocity`, and `GradleEnterprisePluginConfig.isAutoApplied()` reports `true`. The convention plugin's own `settings.plugins.apply(DevelocityPlugin)` then has no effect, because the plugin is already applied.

Because Develocity is treated as auto-applied, no `Test` task gets the `develocity` (`DevelocityTestConfiguration`) extension. Test retry, Predictive Test Selection and Test Distribution configuration are silently lost. Code that guards on the extension (`extensions.findByType(DevelocityTestConfiguration)`) skips its configuration without any warning, and code that uses `develocity.testRetry { }` directly fails to configure.

In the reproducer:

```text
$ ./gradlew test
[repro] Test task 'develocity' extension present: true
2 tests completed, 1 failed
BUILD SUCCESSFUL            <- flaky test passed on retry

$ ./gradlew test --scan
[repro] Test task 'develocity' extension present: false
> Task :test FAILED
BUILD FAILED                <- no retry
```

The only difference between the two runs is `--scan`. Both resolve the same plugin version (4.5.0, the version Gradle 9.7.1 auto-applies), so this is not a version-mismatch problem.

### Expected Behavior

If the build explicitly applies the Develocity plugin, adding `--scan` should not change how it behaves. In particular, it should not remove the `Test` task extensions. The javadoc for `GradleEnterprisePluginConfig.isAutoApplied()` says it means the plugin was "auto-applied via `--scan` without being explicitly applied", which is not the case here.

If that can't be guaranteed, Gradle or Develocity should at least warn that Test task features are disabled because the plugin is considered auto-applied.

### Context (optional)

As far as I can tell, the auto-apply decision is made in `DefaultPluginHandler.filterAlreadyAppliedOrRequested(...)`, before the settings script body runs. It skips the auto-apply only when the plugin is:

- already applied (`isAlreadyApplied`),
- requested in a `plugins {}` block (`isAlreadyRequestedInPluginsBlock`), or
- **declared directly** as a settings `buildscript` dependency. `isAlreadyRequestedInBuildScriptBlock` checks `classpathConfiguration.getDependencies()`, the declared dependencies, not the resolved graph.

A plugin that arrives transitively and is applied later, from the script body, a settings plugin, or a `settingsEvaluated` hook, is invisible to all three checks. So Gradle auto-applies Develocity and reports it as auto-applied, and Develocity decides from that flag not to register the `Test` extensions. That use of the flag is the documented intent of #22674.

Observations from the reproducer:

- If the same convention plugin is applied through the settings `plugins {}` block (for example from an included build), the problem does **not** occur. Develocity is then already applied when the auto-apply decision is made.
- **Workaround:** also declare `com.gradle:develocity-gradle-plugin` directly on the settings `buildscript` classpath. This stops the auto-apply, and `--scan` keeps the extensions.

We noticed this because test retry was silently not happening in CI, which runs every test suite with `--scan`.

Related:

- #22272: `--scan` can apply a different version of the plugin when a custom settings plugin applies it transitively (the same setup, but the version symptom). Fixed by #25549.
- #25549: checks whether auto-applied plugins are already on the classpath. As far as I can tell the plugin is still marked auto-applied in this setup.
- #22674: added `isAutoApplied()` so the plugin can decide whether to register `Test` task extensions for TD, PTS and retry.
- #22667: the earlier spike exposing explicit vs. auto-applied.
- #22768: skips the auto-apply when the plugin marker is on the buildscript classpath, and documents that the `--scan` application happens before a `settingsEvaluated` application from an init script.
- #27365: auto-apply only if Develocity has not already been applied or requested.

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

https://github.com/DPUkyle/gradle-scan-autoapply-repro

```shell
./gradlew -p build-logic publish   # publishes the settings convention plugin to ./local-repo
./gradlew test                     # extension present, test retried, BUILD SUCCESSFUL
./gradlew test --scan              # extension missing, no retry, BUILD FAILED
```

### Gradle version

9.7.1

### Build scan URL (optional)

N/A. The bug is about how `--scan` changes the build.

### Your Environment (optional)

OpenJDK 21.0.8, Linux. Develocity Gradle plugin 4.5.0.

As far as I can tell, the auto-apply decision is made in `DefaultPluginHandler.filterAlreadyAppliedOrRequested(...)`, before the settings script body runs. It skips the auto-apply only when the plugin is:

- already applied (`isAlreadyApplied`),
- requested in a `plugins {}` block (`isAlreadyRequestedInPluginsBlock`), or
- **declared directly** as a settings `buildscript` dependency. `isAlreadyRequestedInBuildScriptBlock` checks `classpathConfiguration.getDependencies()`, the declared dependencies, not the resolved graph.

A plugin that arrives transitively and is applied later, from the script body, a settings plugin, or a `settingsEvaluated` hook, is invisible to all three checks. So Gradle auto-applies Develocity and reports it as auto-applied, and Develocity decides from that flag not to register the `Test` extensions. That use of the flag is the documented intent of #22674.

Observations from the reproducer:

- If the same convention plugin is applied through the settings `plugins {}` block (for example from an included build), the problem does **not** occur. Develocity is then already applied when the auto-apply decision is made.
- **Workaround:** also declare `com.gradle:develocity-gradle-plugin` directly on the settings `buildscript` classpath. This stops the auto-apply, and `--scan` keeps the extensions.

We noticed this because test retry was silently not happening in CI, which runs every test suite with `--scan`.

Related:

- #22272: `--scan` can apply a different version of the plugin when a custom settings plugin applies it transitively (the same setup, but the version symptom). Fixed by #25549.
- #25549: checks whether auto-applied plugins are already on the classpath. As far as I can tell the plugin is still marked auto-applied in this setup.
- #22674: added `isAutoApplied()` so the plugin can decide whether to register `Test` task extensions for TD, PTS and retry.
- #22667: the earlier spike exposing explicit vs. auto-applied.
- #22768: skips the auto-apply when the plugin marker is on the buildscript classpath, and documents that the `--scan` application happens before a `settingsEvaluated` application from an init script.
- #27365: auto-apply only if Develocity has not already been applied or requested.

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

https://github.com/DPUkyle/gradle-scan-autoapply-repro

```shell
./gradlew -p build-logic publish   # publishes the settings convention plugin to ./local-repo
./gradlew test                     # extension present, test retried, BUILD SUCCESSFUL
./gradlew test --scan              # extension missing, no retry, BUILD FAILED
```

### Gradle version

9.7.1

### Build scan URL (optional)

N/A. The bug is about how `--scan` changes the build.

### Your Environment (optional)

OpenJDK 21.0.8, Linux. Develocity Gradle plugin 4.5.0.

### Current Behavior

After upgrading https://github.com/aeron-io/aeron project to Gradle `9.8.1` (also fails in `9.8.0`) one of the tasks started to fail due to warning. 

Steps to reproduce:
* Clone https://github.com/aeron-io/aeron repo.
* Checkout https://github.com/aeron-io/aeron/commit/1bae7dd012eb98415cd86aa67d61b8fdaf339200 commit.
* Run
```bash
./gradlew copyTestLogs --rerun-tasks --console=plain --warning-mode=fail
```

This will fail with:
```
> Task :buildSrc:compileJava
> Task :buildSrc:compileGroovy NO-SOURCE
> Task :buildSrc:processResources NO-SOURCE
> Task :buildSrc:classes
> Task :buildSrc:jar

> Task :copyTestLogs
Producing a file in one build and consuming it in another build without declaring an explicit dependency has been deprecated.
This will fail with an error in Gradle 10. Gradle detected a problem with the following location: '.../projects/aeron'.
Task ':copyTestLogs' uses this output of task ':buildSrc:compileJava' without declaring an explicit or implicit dependency.
This can lead to incorrect results being produced, depending on what order the tasks are executed. 
For more information, please refer to https://docs.gradle.org/9.8.1/userguide/validation_problems.html#implicit_dependency 
in the Gradle documentation.
...
```

If I switch back to `9.7.1` the task succeeds:
```
> Task :buildSrc:compileJava
> Task :buildSrc:compileGroovy NO-SOURCE
> Task :buildSrc:processResources NO-SOURCE
> Task :buildSrc:classes
> Task :buildSrc:jar
> Task :copyTestLogs

BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 2s
3 actionable tasks: 3 executed
```

Since `buildSrc` is special it is **not** listed in the included build (i.e. `org.gradle.api.invocation.Gradle#getIncludedBuilds`) nor its tasks are available anywhere. I haven't found a way to add an explicit dependency between `copyTestLogs` task and the `:buildSrc:compileJava`.

Please advise if there is a workaround or an official way to setup those explicit task dependencies.

### Expected Behavior

The task should execute without errors.

### Context (optional)

_No response_

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

The issue happens in the https://github.com/aeron-io/aeron project. See description.

### Gradle version

9.8.1

### Gradle version that used to work

9.7.1

body_text:
### Current Behavior

On macOS, Gradle keeps idle worker daemons alive while the system is under critical memory pressure (memory compressor full, swap growing). Builds that start many process-isolated workers with distinct classpaths can make the machine close to unusable.

Gradle is supposed to stop idle worker daemons when free memory drops below 10% of physical memory (`DefaultMemoryManager` → `WorkerDaemonExpiration`). On macOS the "free" value Gradle reads does not reflect memory pressure:

- [`NativeOsMemoryInfo`](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/blob/54cb44a80e40017e238969424c263b63f65abb29/platforms/core-runtime/process-memory-services/src/main/java/org/gradle/process/internal/health/memory/NativeOsMemoryInfo.java) uses native-platform `MemoryInfo.getAvailablePhysicalMemory()`, which on macOS counts inactive pages as available.
- Under pressure macOS keeps a pool of inactive pages while it compresses and swaps everything else, so this value stays above the 10% threshold while the kernel reports critical pressure.
- The virtual memory aspect is `Unavailable` on macOS, so swap usage is not considered at all.

Observed on a 32 GB Apple Silicon laptop while running a large multi-project build (`./gradlew sanityCheck` in gradle/gradle):

| What | Value |
|---|---|
| Idle `Gradle Worker Daemon` processes | 102 (and growing) |
| Swap used | 48.7 GB of 49 GB |
| Memory compressor | 14 GB |
| What Gradle sees as free (`OsMemoryInfo`) | 4.6 GB = **14%**, so nothing gets expired |

The workers in that build come from `ValidatePlugins`, whose per-project runtime classpath makes every worker incompatible with all the others. Many workers on their own are a known limitation (https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/22076, https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/20821). This issue is about the safety net that's supposed to cap them, which doesn't work on macOS.

### Expected Behavior

When macOS is under memory pressure, Gradle should stop idle worker daemons just as it does on Linux, where the same reproducer keeps idle workers within physical RAM. Possible signals:

body_text:
### Current Behavior

Since 9.4.0, a Kotlin DSL script that belongs to a build outside the build-tree root is compiled again when the same checkout is at a different path. The usual case is an included build in a sibling directory, such as `pluginManagement { includeBuild("../plugins") }`. #37055 fixed #36964 only for scripts inside the build-tree root.

`KotlinScriptHost.buildTreeScriptPath` makes a script's path relative to the build-tree root when the script is inside it, and keeps the absolute path when it isn't ([v9.8.1](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/blob/v9.8.1/platforms/core-configuration/kotlin-dsl/src/main/kotlin/org/gradle/kotlin/dsl/support/KotlinScriptHost.kt#L61-L72)). That path is an immutable input of the script compilation work in `KotlinScriptEvaluator`. So it changes both the workspace under `caches/<version>/kotlin-dsl/scripts` and the build cache key.

### Expected Behavior

Two checkouts with the same layout at different paths reuse each other's compiled scripts, as they did in 9.3.1.

One way to get there: use `path.relativeTo(buildTreeRootDir)` for scripts outside the root as well. Here that gives `../plugins/settings.gradle.kts`, which is the same in every checkout with this layout.

### Context

Our monorepo has a Gradle build per service, and each one includes shared builds from sibling directories, such as `includeBuild("../tiamat/build-logic")`. Each change is worked on in its own git worktree. Every new worktree therefore compiles the scripts of all those included builds again, and adds new entries to the script cache.

### Self-contained Reproducer Project

The script below creates `checkout-a/app`, which includes `checkout-a/plugins`, and copies it to `checkout-b`. It runs `hello` in each with the same fresh Gradle user home, then prints the scripts each run compiled, read from the build operation trace. Run it as `./repro.sh <path to bin/gradle> <work dir>`.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Usage: repro.sh <gradle launcher> <work dir> [plugins dir relative to app, default ../plugins]
# Creates a root build `app` that includes the build `plugins`, copies it to a
# second path, runs it from each, and prints which scripts each run compiled.
set -euo pipefail

gradle="$1"
work="$2"
plugins="${3:-../plugins}"
rm -rf "$work"
mkdir -p "$work/checkout-a/app" "$work/checkout-a/app/$plugins"

cat > "$work/checkout-a/app/settings.gradle.kts" <<EOF
pluginManagement {
    includeBuild("$plugins")
}
rootProject.name = "app"
EOF
echo 'tasks.register("hello")' > "$work/checkout-a/app/build.gradle.kts"
echo 'rootProject.name = "plugins"' > "$work/checkout-a/app/$plugins/settings.gradle.kts"

cp -R "$work/checkout-a" "$work/checkout-b"

export GRADLE_USER_HOME="$work/gradle-home"

for checkout in checkout-a checkout-b; do
    "$gradle" --no-daemon -q -p "$work/$checkout/app" hello \
        -Dorg.gradle.internal.operations.trace="$work/$checkout-trace"
    echo "== $checkout compiled:"
    python3 - "$work/$checkout-trace-log.txt" <<'EOF'
import json, sys
ops = [json.loads(line) for line in open(sys.argv[1]) if line.startswith('{"displayName"')]
parent = {op["id"]: op.get("parentId") for op in ops}
names = {op["id"]: op["displayName"] for op in ops}
for op in ops:
    if op["displayName"].startswith("Compile script"):
        p = op["id"]
        while p is not None and not names.get(p, "").startswith("Apply "):
            p = parent.get(p)
        print("  ", op["displayName"], "<-", names.get(p))
EOF
    echo "   kotlin-dsl/scripts entries: $(ls "$GRADLE_USER_HOME"/caches/*/kotlin-dsl/scripts | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
done
```

Output with 9.8.1:

```
== checkout-a compiled:
   Compile script settings.gradle.kts (CLASSPATH) <- Apply settings file 'settings.gradle.kts' to settings 'app'
   Compile script settings.gradle.kts (BODY) <- Apply settings file 'settings.gradle.kts' to settings 'app'
   Compile script settings.gradle.kts (CLASSPATH) <- Apply settings file '../plugins/settings.gradle.kts' to settings 'plugins'
   Compile script build.gradle.kts (BODY) <- Apply build file 'build.gradle.kts' to root project 'app'
   kotlin-dsl/scripts entries: 5
== checkout-b compiled:
   Compile script settings.gradle.kts (CLASSPATH) <- Apply settings file '../plugins/settings.gradle.kts' to settings 'plugins'
   kotlin-dsl/scripts entries: 6
```

9.4.1 gives the same result. With 9.3.1, checkout-b compiles nothing.

A third argument of `plugins` puts the included build inside `app/` and includes it with `includeBuild("plugins")`. Then checkout-b compiles nothing on 9.8.1 either.

### Gradle version

9.8.1

### Gradle version that used to work

9.3.1

### Your Environment

macOS 26.6.2 on arm64, Amazon Corretto 25.0.4.

---

Drafted with Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), which also wrote and ran the reproducer.
