body_text: ## Bug In my testing (Graylog 7.2), keyword-based time ranges behave incorrectly when searches are executed after 8:00 PM EDT (00:00 UTC the following day) The Keyword selector _preview_ correctly interprets the expression using my configured timezone (`America/New_York`), but the actual search request uses `Etc/UTC`, causing the start date to shift forward by one day (observed in the actual JSON payloads via Chrome devtools) I read the natty related docs at [Time Frame Selector](https://go2docs.graylog.org/current/making_sense_of_your_log_data/time_frame_selector.html) and I think my syntax is correct ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Configure `root_timezone = America/New_York` in server.conf 2. Log in as the built-in admin user 3. After 8:00 PM EDT (or whatever time in your local TZ that would translate to > midnight UTC…) create a new search 4. Select Keyword as the time range and enter eg: **7am -0400 till now** 5. Observe that the **Preview** does display the correct local timestamps! 6. Execute the search (it should result in an Error) and inspect the resulting timestamps and Network request payload ## Expected Behavior At 9:21 PM EDT on October 17, 2026: ``` Start: 2026-10-17 07:00 EDT (2026-10-17 11:00 UTC) End: 2026-10-17 21:21 EDT (2026-10-18 01:21 UTC) ``` The API request should specify `"timezone": "America/New_York"` ## Actual Behavior The API request contains: ```json { "type": "keyword", "keyword": "7am -0400", "timezone": "Etc/UTC" } ``` The resulting time range is incorrect: ``` Start: 2026-10-18 11:00 UTC (incorrect: +24 hours) End: 2026-10-18 01:21 UTC (correct) ``` This causes the search to fail because the start time is later than the end time. ### additional details * server.conf contains `root_timezone = America/New_York` * REST API `/api/users/admin` confirms `"timezone": "America/New_York"` * The Keyword selector preview correctly uses `America/New_York` * despite that, the search request contains `"timezone": "Etc/UTC"` * The issue is reproducible with newly created searches * The issue only manifests after 8 PM EDT, when the UTC calendar date advances to the following day while the local date remains unchanged ## Context I have some key automations that run between e.g. 6:45am-7am and so I check for anomalies that occurred AFTER 7am thru "now"... this bug makes it impossible to save a search that focuses that time range after 8pm ## Environment * Graylog: 7.2.0+8c9a833 * Java Version: openjdk 21.0.12 2026-07-21 LTS * OpenSearch Version: 3.7.0, Build: tar/72121f014083f9ca010fd5a7da83b2ec4886027f/2026-06-03T23:30:14.822289255Z, JVM: 25.0.3 * MongoDB Version: v7.0.43 * Operating System: Debian 13 * Browser version: Chrome 156 * User: Built-in admin * Timezone: America/New_York (UTC−04:00 during daylight saving time) ## Screenshots

body_text:
## Expected Behavior

The `gl-datanode-metrics-ism` policy should roll each `.ds-gl-datanode-metrics-*` backing index up into `gl-datanode-metrics-daily` and then delete it after 14 days (`rollup` → `delete`, `min_index_age: 14d`).

## Current Behavior

The rollup action fails on every backing index, so no index ever reaches the `delete` state. Backing indices pile up at one per day. Our single-node cluster has 223 of them, going back to the first Data Node start in 04/2025, and they count towards `cluster.max_shards_per_node`.

In the OpenSearch log (`datanode-cluster-*.log`) the error appears once per backing index:

```
[ERROR][o.o.i.r.RollupMapperService] [zg-syslog-01] Failed to create target index [gl-datanode-metrics-daily] because
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: cannot create index with name [gl-datanode-metrics-daily], because it matches with
template [gl-datanode-metrics-template] that creates data streams only, use create data stream api instead
	at org.opensearch.cluster.metadata.MetadataCreateIndexService.applyCreateIndexRequestWithV2Template(MetadataCreateIndexService.java:770)
```

ISM explain for a backing index:

```json
"state": {"name": "rollup"},
"action": {"name": "rollup", "failed": true, "consumed_retries": 3},
"step": {"name": "wait_for_rollup_completion", "step_status": "failed"},
"info": {"cause": "Failed to create target index [gl-datanode-metrics-daily]",
         "message": "Rollup job [...] failed [index=.ds-gl-datanode-metrics-000222]"}
```

The cause is a name clash between two things Graylog creates itself:

- index template `gl-datanode-metrics-template`: `index_patterns: ["gl-datanode-metrics*"]`, `data_stream: {timestamp_field: timestamp}`, `priority: 99999`
- ISM rollup target in `gl-datanode-metrics-ism`: `target_index: "gl-datanode-metrics-daily"`

The rollup target matches the template pattern. Because that template creates data streams only, OpenSearch refuses to create the target as a regular index, so the rollup can never succeed.

Backing indices created before the newer metric fields existed (in our case `000001`–`000132`) also fail with `Invalid mappings for index [...] because [missing field cpu_percent, missing field mem_total, ...]`. Those indices can never be rolled up, even after the target problem is fixed, so they need to be deleted or moved straight to the `delete` state.

## Possible Solution

Either of these would work:

- rename the rollup target so it doesn't match `gl-datanode-metrics*`, e.g. `gl-datanode-rollup-daily`, or
- narrow the data stream template pattern to the exact data stream name: `index_patterns: ["gl-datanode-metrics"]`.

It would also help if indices whose rollup failed permanently (e.g. because of a mapping mismatch) still went on to `delete` after `min_index_age`, for example by using an ISM `on_failure`-style transition, so that a rollup failure can't cause unbounded shard growth.

Our workaround is a higher-priority, non-data-stream template for the exact target name:

```json
PUT _index_template/gl-datanode-metrics-daily-rollup
{"index_patterns":["gl-datanode-metrics-daily"],"priority":100000,
 "template":{"settings":{"number_of_shards":1,"number_of_replicas":0}}}
```

followed by `POST _plugins/_ism/retry/<failed backing indices>` and deleting the old-mapping backing indices.

## Steps to Reproduce (for bugs)

1. Install Graylog with Data Node and let it run for more than one day, so that `gl-datanode-metrics` rolls over at least once.
2. `GET _plugins/_ism/explain/.ds-gl-datanode-metrics-000001`: the index is stuck in `rollup` / `wait_for_rollup_completion` with status `failed`.
3. `GET gl-datanode-metrics-daily` returns `index_not_found_exception`.
4. `POST _index_template/_simulate_index/gl-datanode-metrics-daily` shows that it resolves to the data-stream template.

## Context

The policy can never delete these indices, so shard count grows by one per day indefinitely. This is related to #27040 and PR #27162, which make new backing indices managed by the policy. Once those land, the new backing indices will still get stuck at the rollup step for the reason above and will never be deleted.

## My Environment

- Graylog Version: 7.2.0 (server + Data Node, also present on 7.1.x, 7.0.x and the first 6.x Data Node install in 04/2025)
- OpenSearch Version: 2.19.6 (bundled with Data Node)
- MongoDB Version: 7.0.43
- Operating System: Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS
- Single Data Node, single Graylog server

The `gl-datanode-metrics-ism` policy should roll each `.ds-gl-datanode-metrics-*` backing index up into `gl-datanode-metrics-daily` and then delete it after 14 days (`rollup` → `delete`, `min_index_age: 14d`).

## Current Behavior

The rollup action fails on every backing index, so no index ever reaches the `delete` state. Backing indices pile up at one per day. Our single-node cluster has 223 of them, going back to the first Data Node start in 04/2025, and they count towards `cluster.max_shards_per_node`.

In the OpenSearch log (`datanode-cluster-*.log`) the error appears once per backing index:

```
[ERROR][o.o.i.r.RollupMapperService] [zg-syslog-01] Failed to create target index [gl-datanode-metrics-daily] because
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: cannot create index with name [gl-datanode-metrics-daily], because it matches with
template [gl-datanode-metrics-template] that creates data streams only, use create data stream api instead
	at org.opensearch.cluster.metadata.MetadataCreateIndexService.applyCreateIndexRequestWithV2Template(MetadataCreateIndexService.java:770)
```

ISM explain for a backing index:

```json
"state": {"name": "rollup"},
"action": {"name": "rollup", "failed": true, "consumed_retries": 3},
"step": {"name": "wait_for_rollup_completion", "step_status": "failed"},
"info": {"cause": "Failed to create target index [gl-datanode-metrics-daily]",
         "message": "Rollup job [...] failed [index=.ds-gl-datanode-metrics-000222]"}
```

The cause is a name clash between two things Graylog creates itself:

- index template `gl-datanode-metrics-template`: `index_patterns: ["gl-datanode-metrics*"]`, `data_stream: {timestamp_field: timestamp}`, `priority: 99999`
- ISM rollup target in `gl-datanode-metrics-ism`: `target_index: "gl-datanode-metrics-daily"`

The rollup target matches the template pattern. Because that template creates data streams only, OpenSearch refuses to create the target as a regular index, so the rollup can never succeed.

Backing indices created before the newer metric fields existed (in our case `000001`–`000132`) also fail with `Invalid mappings for index [...] because [missing field cpu_percent, missing field mem_total, ...]`. Those indices can never be rolled up, even after the target problem is fixed, so they need to be deleted or moved straight to the `delete` state.

## Possible Solution

Either of these would work:

- rename the rollup target so it doesn't match `gl-datanode-metrics*`, e.g. `gl-datanode-rollup-daily`, or
- narrow the data stream template pattern to the exact data stream name: `index_patterns: ["gl-datanode-metrics"]`.

It would also help if indices whose rollup failed permanently (e.g. because of a mapping mismatch) still went on to `delete` after `min_index_age`, for example by using an ISM `on_failure`-style transition, so that a rollup failure can't cause unbounded shard growth.

Our workaround is a higher-priority, non-data-stream template for the exact target name:

```json
PUT _index_template/gl-datanode-metrics-daily-rollup
{"index_patterns":["gl-datanode-metrics-daily"],"priority":100000,
 "template":{"settings":{"number_of_shards":1,"number_of_replicas":0}}}
```

followed by `POST _plugins/_ism/retry/<failed backing indices>` and deleting the old-mapping backing indices.

## Steps to Reproduce (for bugs)

1. Install Graylog with Data Node and let it run for more than one day, so that `gl-datanode-metrics` rolls over at least once.
2. `GET _plugins/_ism/explain/.ds-gl-datanode-metrics-000001`: the index is stuck in `rollup` / `wait_for_rollup_completion` with status `failed`.
3. `GET gl-datanode-metrics-daily` returns `index_not_found_exception`.
4. `POST _index_template/_simulate_index/gl-datanode-metrics-daily` shows that it resolves to the data-stream template.

## Context

The policy can never delete these indices, so shard count grows by one per day indefinitely. This is related to #27040 and PR #27162, which make new backing indices managed by the policy. Once those land, the new backing indices will still get stuck at the rollup step for the reason above and will never be deleted.

## My Environment

- Graylog Version: 7.2.0 (server + Data Node, also present on 7.1.x, 7.0.x and the first 6.x Data Node install in 04/2025)
- OpenSearch Version: 2.19.6 (bundled with Data Node)
- MongoDB Version: 7.0.43
- Operating System: Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS
- Single Data Node, single Graylog server

## Expected Behavior
Number (single value) widgets on dashboards should render the value on all supported browsers, as they did before upgrading to 7.2.0.

## Current Behavior
Since upgrading to Graylog 7.2.0, number widgets on a dashboard fail to render when the dashboard is opened in the built-in web browser of an LG TV (webOS). Instead of the value, the widget shows:

    While rendering this widget, the following error occurred:
    Error: Minified React error #185; visit https://reactjs.org/docs/error-decoder.html?invariant=185 for the full message or use the non-minified dev environment for full errors and additional helpful warnings

React error #185 means "Maximum update depth exceeded", so the widget seems to end up in an infinite re-render loop.

The same dashboard renders correctly in a desktop browser on a PC monitor. The issue persists after upgrading to 7.2.1.

## Possible Solution
Just a guess: the automatic font sizing of the number visualization may oscillate on this screen size / scaling (font size change -> container re-measure -> font size change ...), which eventually hits React's update depth limit.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Upgrade Graylog to 7.2.0 or 7.2.1.
2. Create a dashboard with a number (single value) widget.
3. Open the dashboard in the web browser of an LG TV (webOS).
4. The widget shows "Minified React error #185" instead of the value.

## Context
The dashboard is displayed on a wall-mounted TV for monitoring. Before 7.2.0, it worked without issues on the same TV. Other widget types on the same dashboard (e.g. charts, message tables) render correctly – only number widgets are affected.

## Description

When editing a user, the "Start page" picker only lists entities the user can access through the `*` permission or through explicit shares. Access granted through roles is ignored. For a user whose read access comes from a role (for example `dashboards:read` or `streams:read`), the Dashboard and Stream dropdowns stay empty, even though the user can open those entities.

Reproduced on a self-managed 7.3 snapshot; not Cloud-specific.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Create a role with `dashboards:read`, `view:read` and `streams:read`.
2. Create a user with the roles `Reader` and the new role. Do not share any dashboards or streams with them.
3. Log in as that user: dashboards and streams are listed and can be opened.
4. As an admin, edit that user, go to "Start page" and select type "Dashboard" or "Stream".
5. The entity dropdown is empty.

For comparison, a user with the built-in `Admin` role sees all dashboards and streams in the same dropdowns.

## Root cause

`StartpageFormGroup` checks whether the selected user has `*` (`hasAdminPermission`):
- With `*`, it lists all dashboards, streams and searches.
- Without `*`, it lists only entities returned by `/authz/shares/user/{userId}`. That endpoint returns grants (user, team, global and collection shares) but not permissions from roles.

The "missing permission" warning is computed from that same list.

## Related

Found while investigating Graylog2/graylog-plugin-enterprise#15531, which turned out to have a different, Okta-related cause.

body_text: ## Description The details page of a "DSV File from HTTP" data adapter shows the "Check interval" without a value, only the unit: `Check interval: seconds`. The configured value is saved and used by the adapter, it is just not displayed. ## Steps to reproduce 1. Create a "DSV File from HTTP" data adapter with any check interval, e.g. 60. 2. Open the data adapter's details page (or a lookup table using it). 3. "Check interval" shows `seconds` with no number. The Edit form shows the correct value. ## Root cause `DSVHTTPAdapterSummary.tsx` reads `config.check_interval`, but this adapter's config field is `refresh_interval` (`DSVHTTPDataAdapter.Config`, also used by `DSVHTTPAdapterFieldSet.tsx`). The field is always undefined, so only the unit is rendered.

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.17.0-dev
(behaviour described here is the same on v1.16.x and earlier)
```

### Use Cases

When reviewing a change to infrastructure, or onboarding someone onto an existing stack, the question people actually ask is architectural: *what does this system look like, and what talks to what?* Today Terraform can tell you the resources and their dependency order, but there is no first-class way to see the shape of the infrastructure being described.

Concrete situations where this comes up:

1. **Change review.** A plan touching 60 resources is reviewed as a wall of text. A reviewer wants to see that the change adds a subnet inside an existing VPC and repoints a load balancer, not to reconstruct that mentally from `+`/`~`/`-` lines.
2. **Onboarding and handover.** New joiners on an existing module set need the network/zone/subnet containment hierarchy. That information is fully present in the configuration and state, but has to be redrawn by hand into a diagram that then goes stale.
3. **Documentation that stays current.** Teams keep architecture diagrams in Confluence/`docs/` that drift from the real infrastructure within weeks, because nothing regenerates them from the source of truth.
4. **Design/compliance review.** Reviewers want to confirm that a database sits in a private subnet and is not routable from the internet — a containment and reachability question that reads naturally off a diagram.

### Attempted Solutions

`terraform graph` is the closest existing feature, and it is genuinely useful, but it answers a different question. It renders Terraform's internal dependency graph — evaluation order between nodes — in DOT or Mermaid:

```
terraform graph
terraform graph -type=plan -format=mermaid
```

That output is a dependency DAG keyed on Terraform addresses. It deliberately does not model infrastructure topology: there are no regions, VPCs, availability zones or subnets as containers, no notion that an ALB fronts an instance, and no distinction between "A must be created before B" and "A sends traffic to B". For a non-trivial configuration the resource-dependency graph is also large enough that it is hard to read as a picture of the system.

The other route is the JSON plan:

```
terraform plan -out=tfplan && terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json
```

This is a documented, stable interface and it does carry the information needed. But every consumer then has to independently rebuild the same provider-specific knowledge — which attribute on `aws_instance` points at a subnet, that `google_compute_subnetwork` lives inside a VPC network, that `ip_configuration[0].subnet_id` is the Azure equivalent — before it can draw anything.

I have built one such consumer, [`tf-arch-diagram-generator`](https://github.com/mchittineni/tf-arch-diagram-generator) (disclosure: I am the author), which takes `terraform show -json` output and renders an architecture diagram for AWS, Google Cloud and Azure, with the containment hierarchy, inferred traffic flows and per-resource plan diffs. I mention it as evidence that the transformation is tractable from data Terraform already emits, not to propose it as the implementation.

### Proposal

The concrete gap is that architecture-level visualisation has no supported place in the workflow, so each tool re-derives provider semantics from scratch and the results are inconsistent.

There are a few directions, in increasing order of scope. I would be glad to be told that only the first is in scope for Terraform Core:

**1. Point people at the right interface (smallest).** Document in the `terraform graph` reference that it renders the dependency graph rather than an architecture diagram, and that `terraform show -json` is the intended interface for external visualisation. This is cheap and would save a lot of misdirected effort — `terraform graph` is what people reach for first, and it is not what they want.

**2. Make `terraform graph` readable as a picture.** Optionally group nodes into subgraphs by module in the Mermaid output, so that the existing command produces something legible for a medium-sized configuration:

```
terraform graph -format=mermaid -group=module
```

This stays entirely within Terraform's own model — no provider-specific knowledge — and is a much smaller change than anything below.

**3. A supported way to express containment (largest).** The reason external tools need per-provider heuristics is that nothing in the schema says "this attribute references a container this resource lives inside". If providers could advertise that (for example, a schema-level hint that `subnet_id` is a containment reference), any consumer of `terraform show -json` could build the hierarchy generically, and diagram tooling could stop hardcoding resource-type tables. This is clearly the most invasive option and would need provider-protocol design, so I raise it as the underlying problem rather than as a request.

I am not asking Terraform to render images. Option 1 alone would be a real improvement, and I am happy to open a PR for it.

### References

- `terraform graph` — existing dependency-graph rendering (DOT/Mermaid)
- `terraform show -json` — the documented machine-readable plan interface
- [mchittineni/tf-arch-diagram-generator](https://github.com/mchittineni/tf-arch-diagram-generator) — prior art demonstrating the transformation from `terraform show -json` (authored by me)

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.17.0-dev
on darwin_arm64
```

### Use Cases

I run Terraform drift checks on a schedule and in CI, across a lot of workspaces. I want them to fire only when something has actually changed outside of Terraform, and to never be able to change anything themselves.

Detection isn't the missing piece, though it's fiddly. `terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode` already returns exit `2` only when there's drift (an unapplied config change doesn't trigger it), and `-json` emits `resource_drift`, but you have to know that exact flag combination and parse the JSON to see what actually changed. Two bigger things are the problem.

First, I can't tell a check to ignore drift I already know about, just for that run. There's always some noise, like a tag a scanner rewrites every hour or an attribute the provider keeps normalizing. My only knob today is `ignore_changes`, and it's the wrong tool for an alarm (more on that below). So I either get paged for noise or mute the whole resource and miss real drift on it.

Second, the check isn't guaranteed read-only. I'm running `plan`, which takes `-out` and is one step from something appliable. I'd be a lot more comfortable scheduling that across dozens of workspaces, or handing it to compliance, if it simply couldn't change anything.

### Attempted Solutions

For finding drift the refresh-only route is fine.

```
terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode          # 2 on drift, 0 otherwise
terraform plan -refresh-only -json | jq '[.. | select(.type? == "resource_drift")]'
```

It's the suppression part that breaks down. Take that scanner rewriting `tags["LastScanned"]` every hour, so every run lights up on it. Right now I have two options.

- Put `ignore_changes = [tags["LastScanned"]]` in the config. That quiets the alarm, but now `apply` won't reconcile that tag either, it needs a review, and it's global, not scoped to this one check.
- Filter the `-json` in `jq` and work out the exit code myself. That's a fragile script I have to babysit per resource type.

Neither lets me ignore that one tag for this check while still failing on any other drift.

I also looked at `terraform refresh`, but it does the opposite of what I need here. It writes the drifted values into state, which erases the very drift I'm trying to detect.

### Proposal

I'd propose a `terraform drift` command. What makes it more than a wrapper around `plan -refresh-only` is a `-ignore` flag that hides expected drift from the report, and only the report.

`terraform drift -ignore=aws_s3_bucket.demo` drops a whole resource; `-ignore='aws_instance.web:tags["LastScanned"]'` drops one attribute. The address is just the normal resource instance address you already use in plan output and `-target` (count/for_each and modules work, managed resources only), and the attribute part is the same syntax as `ignore_changes`. It only affects what's printed, never state, never infra, never what a later plan or apply does. If it can't apply a rule cleanly, it shows the full drift instead, and anything it hides is still counted and labeled. It only masks what you name, so if the same resource drifted somewhere else you still see it and the check still fails. That's the one thing the refresh-only plus `jq` route can't do without a config change, and it's the part I've built.

The command itself is small.

```
terraform drift          # human-readable report
terraform drift -json    # adds a drift_summary with counts
```

A few specifics.

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.15.4
```

### Use Cases

Many organizations require resource metadata such as tags or labels to reflect the last modification performed through Terraform.

Common examples include:

- modified-datetime
- last-updated
- updated-by
- change-ticket
- deployment-reference

Today Terraform can set those values during resource creation, but it has no native mechanism to update them automatically when a resource is modified.

This makes governance, auditing and operational tracking difficult, especially in large environments where thousands of resources are managed through Terraform.

The end goal is to allow users to automatically update metadata whenever Terraform detects a resource change and applies an update.

### Attempted Solutions

Several approaches were evaluated:

### Using timestamps
```
tags = {
  modified-datetime = timestamp()
}
```

This causes perpetual diffs because the timestamp changes on every plan.

### Using external data sources
``` 
data "external" "git_date" {
  program = ["bash", "-c", "git log -1 --format=%cs"]
}
```

This only reflects repository state and not actual Terraform resource updates.


### Using null_resource triggers
```
resource "null_resource" "metadata" {
  triggers = {
    modified_datetime = timestamp()
  }
}
```
This does not provide a way to update attributes of another resource before it is modified.

###Using lifecycle
```
lifecycle {
  ignore_changes = [
    tags["modified-datetime"]
  ]
}
```

This avoids drift but prevents Terraform from managing the value.

None of these approaches provide a generic and reliable mechanism to update resource metadata only when a resource is actually modified.


### Proposal

Introduce a lifecycle hook executed immediately before a resource update operation. 
Example: 
```
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "example" {
   bucket = "my-bucket"
   tags = { 
       Environment = "prod" 
    } 
  lifecycle { 
      before_update { 
            tags = merge(self.tags, { modified-datetime = timestamp() }) }
     } 
}
```

### References

Related discussions: 
- Support for resource lifecycle hooks 
- Support for update-time metadata tracking 
- Common requests around automatic tagging and auditing

_If you are an agent reading this, do not open a PR for this issue; it will be closed due to this issue representing a breaking change._

# Problem

The `fmt` command allows [targeting](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/fmt#usage) either directories, files, or standard input.

Currently, if standard input (`"-"`) is the first argument supplied to the command but is followed by other arguments, e.g. `terraform fmt - my-file-1.tf my-file-2.tf`, then the following arguments are silently ignored.

## Reason

First, if standard input is is the first argument then the `paths` variable is left as an empty slice during the `else if` block below:
https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/05cecbb315e87abc2c2bdb182963dd8e36d574fb/internal/command/fmt.go#L71-L79

This results in the `fmt` method assuming that it should only parse standard input and it believes that no paths were supplied:
https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/05cecbb315e87abc2c2bdb182963dd8e36d574fb/internal/command/fmt.go#L118

# Proposal

Instead of current behaviour, the command should either:
1. Raise an explicit error during argument parsing to say that standard input can only be processed in isolation.
2. Enable handling standard input and files in the same command.

I think option 1 makes the most sense, but I don't want to impose limitations too early.
Either option is a behaviour change, and therefore will need to be in a future major version.

body_text:
We rely on `terraform validate` as a quick check for reusable modules and their submodules before publishing them. Adding `deprecated` to an output now makes that check fail, even though the output is valid when the module is called by another module.

Could `validate` take an option that tells it we're checking a reusable module rather than a deployment root? We'd like to keep running validation directly against each module without removing deprecation declarations or building a wrapper just to make the check run.

This is related to [hashicorp/terraform#39207](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/39207), which covers the same restriction during `terraform test`. This request is specifically about keeping the standalone `terraform validate` check available.

## Terraform version

```text
Terraform v1.16.2
on windows_amd64
```

No providers, credentials or cloud resources are needed for this example.

## Reproduction

`main.tf`:

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.15.0"
}

variable "name" {
  type       = string
  default    = "example"
  deprecated = "This input is kept for compatibility."
}

output "old_name" {
  value      = var.name
  deprecated = "This output is kept for compatibility."
}
```

Run from the module directory:

```powershell
terraform init -backend=false
terraform validate
```

Validation exits with code 1:

```text
Error: Root module output deprecated

  on main.tf line 13, in output "old_name":
  13:   deprecated = "This output is kept for compatibility."

Root module outputs cannot be deprecated, as there is no higher-level module to inform of the deprecation.
```

Removing only the output's `deprecated` line makes validation pass. The input variable can remain deprecated. The hard failure here is the root-only restriction on the output, not an error caused by the deprecated input variable.

## Requested behavior

An explicit option such as `terraform validate -reusable-module` would let us say that this directory is intended to be called as a child module. The flag name is just a suggestion; a narrower option for the deprecated-output restriction would also help.

With that option, `validate` should accept deprecated outputs that are valid in a reusable module, retain any applicable deprecation warnings, and still fail on invalid syntax, bad references, type errors, invalid arguments and other genuine validation errors. The existing behavior should remain the default for normal root configurations, and this should not change `plan` or `apply`.

This isn't a request for a general "ignore errors" switch. We want the validation checks, without a failure that comes solely from treating a reusable module as a deployment root.

## Why this matters

The documentation describes `validate` as being "primarily useful for general verification of reusable modules": https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/validate

Validating examples is useful too, but it only checks modules that those examples actually reference. A separate check against each module directory is valuable, including for submodules that don't yet have an example. Writing wrappers also means supplying inputs and provider wiring just to run a static check.

I understand from [hashicorp/terraform#38309](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/38309) that `validate` currently expects a complete root configuration, and that changing this may involve more than one output validation rule. That issue covers the similar problem with ephemeral outputs. An explicit reusable-module option would make the intended context clear without quietly changing how existing configurations are checked.

Validation exits with code 1:

```text
Error: Root module output deprecated

  on main.tf line 13, in output "old_name":
  13:   deprecated = "This output is kept for compatibility."

Root module outputs cannot be deprecated, as there is no higher-level module to inform of the deprecation.
```

Removing only the output's `deprecated` line makes validation pass. The input variable can remain deprecated. The hard failure here is the root-only restriction on the output, not an error caused by the deprecated input variable.

## Requested behavior

An explicit option such as `terraform validate -reusable-module` would let us say that this directory is intended to be called as a child module. The flag name is just a suggestion; a narrower option for the deprecated-output restriction would also help.

With that option, `validate` should accept deprecated outputs that are valid in a reusable module, retain any applicable deprecation warnings, and still fail on invalid syntax, bad references, type errors, invalid arguments and other genuine validation errors. The existing behavior should remain the default for normal root configurations, and this should not change `plan` or `apply`.

This isn't a request for a general "ignore errors" switch. We want the validation checks, without a failure that comes solely from treating a reusable module as a deployment root.

## Why this matters

The documentation describes `validate` as being "primarily useful for general verification of reusable modules": https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/validate

Validating examples is useful too, but it only checks modules that those examples actually reference. A separate check against each module directory is valuable, including for submodules that don't yet have an example. Writing wrappers also means supplying inputs and provider wiring just to run a static check.

I understand from [hashicorp/terraform#38309](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/38309) that `validate` currently expects a complete root configuration, and that changing this may involve more than one output validation rule. body_text:
I was annoyed with how slow `terraform init` is, so I went looking for bugs in the provider installer. This is one I found, AI-assisted.

When a provider is linked from the global plugin cache and the lock file has checksums for it, the installer reads and hashes the whole cached package three times. I have a small fix to `internal/providercache/installer.go` that hashes it at most once and reuses the result. It leaves the lock file checks themselves (#32129) unchanged. For the configuration below it takes `terraform init` from 1.28s to 0.50s wall time and from 0.99s to 0.35s CPU time (median of 8 runs, Apple silicon Mac). I'd like to open a PR for it if that's welcome.

### Terraform Version

```
Terraform v1.16.3
on darwin_arm64
```

Also reproduces on `main` (78194be60).

### Terraform Configuration Files

```terraform
terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "6.44.0"
    }
  }
}
```

### Debug Output

Not attached. The trace log has no lines for the hashing itself, only a gap before `providercache.Dir.LinkFromOtherCache: linking registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws`.

### Expected Behavior

The cached package is read and hashed once.

### Actual Behavior

The same package is hashed three times during `EnsureProviderVersions`, and each pass reads the whole package (770MB for `hashicorp/aws` 6.44.0):

1. `installer.go:426`: `cached.MatchesAnyHash(preferredHashes)` checks the cache entry against the lock file.
2. `dir_modify.go:66`: `LinkFromOtherCache` checks the same hashes again before linking.
3. `installer.go:540`: `cached.Hash()` computes the hash again for the lock file update.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Save the configuration above as `main.tf`, with a plugin cache enabled: `export TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR=$HOME/.terraform.d/plugin-cache`.
2. `terraform providers lock -platform=darwin_arm64 -platform=linux_amd64`
3. `terraform init` once, to fill the plugin cache.
4. Copy `main.tf` and `.terraform.lock.hcl` into an empty directory and run `time terraform init` there.

### Additional Context

It only happens with the global plugin cache enabled and a lock file that has checksums for the provider. Without a lock file entry, the cache entry is only used with `plugin_cache_may_break_dependency_lock_file` set, and is then hashed once.

### Terraform Version

```shell
### Terraform Version

Terraform v1.16.4
```

### Use Cases

When reviewing a terraform plan, I want to know which Terraform resource an unknown argument refers to before approving the apply.

For example, a security group can be configured with vpc_id = aws_vpc.example.id. When the VPC is being created in the same plan, the security group's vpc_id is displayed as (known after apply). The AWS VPC ID cannot be known yet, but the Terraform reference aws_vpc.example.id is already known from the configuration.

### Example configuration
- main.tf
```hcl
provider "aws" {
  region                      = "ap-northeast-1"
  access_key                  = "test"
  secret_key                  = "test"
  skip_credentials_validation = true
  skip_metadata_api_check     = true
  skip_requesting_account_id  = true
  endpoints {
    ec2 = "http://kumo:4566"
  }
}
resource "aws_vpc" "example" {
  cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"
  tags = {
    Name = "plan-reference-example"
  }
}
resource "aws_security_group" "example" {
  name        = "plan-reference-example"
  description = "Demonstrates an unknown value from a resource reference"
  vpc_id      = aws_vpc.example.id

  tags = {
    Name = "plan-reference-example"
  }
}
```
- versions.tf
```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = "= 1.16.4"

  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "= 6.66.0"
    }
  }
}
```
### terraform plan output
```bash
Terraform used the selected providers to generate the following execution plan. Resource actions are indicated with the following symbols:
  + create

Terraform will perform the following actions:

  # aws_security_group.example will be created
  + resource "aws_security_group" "example" {
      + arn                    = (known after apply)
      + description            = "Demonstrates an unknown value from a resource reference"
      + egress                 = (known after apply)
      + id                     = (known after apply)
      + ingress                = (known after apply)
      + name                   = "plan-reference-example"
      + name_prefix            = (known after apply)
      + owner_id               = (known after apply)
      + region                 = "ap-northeast-1"
      + revoke_rules_on_delete = false
      + tags                   = {
          + "Name" = "plan-reference-example"
        }
      + tags_all               = {
          + "Name" = "plan-reference-example"
        }
      + vpc_id                 = (known after apply)
    }

  # aws_vpc.example will be created
  + resource "aws_vpc" "example" {
      + arn                                  = (known after apply)
      + cidr_block                           = "10.0.0.0/16"
      + default_network_acl_id               = (known after apply)
      + default_route_table_id               = (known after apply)
      + default_security_group_id            = (known after apply)
      + dhcp_options_id                      = (known after apply)
      + enable_dns_hostnames                 = (known after apply)
      + enable_dns_support                   = true
      + enable_network_address_usage_metrics = (known after apply)
      + id                                   = (known after apply)
      + instance_tenancy                     = "default"
      + ipv6_association_id                  = (known after apply)
      + ipv6_cidr_block                      = (known after apply)
      + ipv6_cidr_block_network_border_group = (known after apply)
      + main_route_table_id                  = (known after apply)
      + owner_id                             = (known after apply)
      + region                               = "ap-northeast-1"
      + tags                                 = {
          + "Name" = "plan-reference-example"
        }
      + tags_all                             = {
          + "Name" = "plan-reference-example"
        }
    }

Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
```

This VPC example is intentionally simple. In a large plan with many resources, however, seeing only (known after apply) makes it difficult to tell which resource an argument refers to. I would like the plan itself to show that reference so it can be reviewed without tracing it through the configuration.

### Attempted Solutions

I ran terraform plan with the configuration shown above. The security group's vpc_id appeared as (known after apply), without indicating that its value comes from aws_vpc.example.id.

I can find the reference by inspecting the Terraform configuration, but I could not find an existing option to display it in the human-readable plan output. I have not tried another workaround.

### Proposal

For arguments whose value is unknown because they reference another Terraform resource, show the source reference in plan output.

Current output:
```bash
+ vpc_id = (known after apply)
```
Proposed output (example):
```bash
+ vpc_id = (known after apply; from aws_vpc.example.id)
```

### Terraform Version

Terraform v1.16.3, and current `main` at `db4eef44f5bbd39a115f939304279caee7cf9b12` is also affected.

### Terraform Configuration Files

```terraform
terraform {
  backend "oss" {
    bucket = "example-new-bucket"
    prefix = "daily"
    key    = "terraform.tfstate"
    region = "cn-qingdao"
  }
}
```

Credentials are supplied through the documented environment variables.

### Expected Behavior

`terraform init` should authenticate to a newly-created Alibaba Cloud OSS bucket using Signature V4.

Alibaba Cloud stopped offering Signature V1 to new UIDs on March 1, 2025 and to newly-created buckets on September 1, 2025. Its migration guide requires OSS Go SDK v1 version 3.0.2 or later, `oss.AuthVersion(oss.AuthV4)`, and an explicit region:

https://help.aliyun.com/zh/oss/developer-reference/guidelines-for-upgrading-v1-signatures-to-v4-signatures

### Actual Behavior

Initialization fails before reading or writing state:

```text
Failed to get existing workspaces: oss: service returned error: StatusCode=403,
ErrorCode=AccessDenied, ErrorMessage="V1 signature is forbidden.",
Ec=0002-00000080
```

The same credentials, bucket, and region work with `aliyun oss ... --sign-version v4`.

The current OSS backend depends on `github.com/aliyun/aliyun-oss-go-sdk v2.2.7+incompatible`, which is below Alibaba Cloud's recommended minimum version for V4 migration. That SDK version already exposes V4 client options, but the backend constructs the client without `oss.AuthVersion(oss.AuthV4)` or `oss.Region(region)`, so it keeps the V1 default:

https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/backend/remote-state/oss/backend.go

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Use an Alibaba Cloud UID or OSS bucket for which Signature V1 is unavailable.
2. Configure the `oss` backend with the bucket and its region.
3. Run `terraform init -reconfigure`.

### Additional Context and Proposed Direction

This makes the built-in OSS backend unusable for new Alibaba Cloud users and new buckets. The Alicloud provider's OSS client has already moved to Signature V4, but provider changes do not affect Terraform's built-in state backend.

I can prepare a focused PR that upgrades the OSS SDK, configures the client with its region, and adds test coverage proving requests use the V4 authorization scheme. I would appreciate maintainer guidance on compatibility policy: should V4 become the default, with an explicit V1 escape hatch for legacy endpoints, or should V4 initially be opt-in through a backend setting?

body_text:
### TL;DR
State can silently hold two addresses bound to one remote object. When that happens, `terraform plan` shows a routine-looking `destroy` that actually targets live infrastructure, with no hint that the object is also tracked elsewhere. An earlier ID-based duplicate check was deliberately relaxed (#33390 → #33434) because raw import IDs are not a sound uniqueness key — but resource identity (v1.12+) is exactly that key, and HCP Terraform already uses it in its bulk-import workflow to detect objects managed by another workspace. I propose bringing the same detection into core, within a single state: warn at plan time when two managed instances share an identity, and at import time when the imported object is already tracked.

### Use Cases

A real incident:

1. An AWS Secrets Manager secret was bound to a root-level address, likely via an old ad-hoc `terraform import` or a local apply of uncommitted config.
2. The same secret is properly managed by a module instance (`module.app.aws_secretsmanager_secret.rds_password`). State ended up with two entries pointing to one remote object.
3. The root-level address had no configuration, so `plan` proposed a `destroy`. Applying it would have scheduled deletion of the live secret referenced by running ECS tasks.
4. Nothing in the plan output indicated the duplication. A human reviewer caught it by noticing the name collision.

Duplicate tracking commonly arises from CLI `import` to a second address, local applies of never-merged config, or module refactors that import into the new address without removing the old entry. The resulting destroy diffs are indistinguishable from legitimate ones.

The import documentation states the assumption but nothing enforces it:

> Terraform expects that each remote object it is managing will be bound to only one resource address. (...) If you import the same object multiple times, Terraform may exhibit unwanted behavior.

### Current Behavior

- `plan` performs no duplicate detection across state entries.
- CLI `terraform import` performs no check against existing state.
- Config-driven import validates only duplicate *target addresses* among `import` blocks: [`internal/configs/module.go`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/configs/module.go) emits `"Duplicate import configuration for %q"` when two blocks share a `to` address. An earlier ID-based duplicate check was deliberately relaxed in #33434 (closing #33390), on the grounds that raw ID strings are not unique: abstract resources such as `time_sleep` legitimately return identical import responses for distinct instances, and as noted there, "Terraform cannot enforce any uniqueness in resources" from the ID alone.
- HCP Terraform uses resource identities in its bulk-import workflow "to determine when resources are managed by another workspace" ([bulk import docs](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/import/bulk)). The detection capability exists; it is not applied within a single state in core.

### Proposal

Resource identity (v1.12+) resolves the objection that led to relaxing the earlier check. Unlike a raw ID string, an identity is provider-defined with a documented uniqueness contract: it "must correspond to at most one remote object per provider" ([identity docs](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/framework/resources/identity)). Core already persists it per instance: `ResourceInstanceObject.Identity` is serialized into state as `IdentityJSON` with `IdentitySchemaVersion` ([`internal/states/instance_object.go`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/states/instance_object.go)). So the data needed for comparison is already in state.

1. **Plan time (primary):** warn when two managed instances of the same resource type in the same state share an identity, naming both addresses. This catches pre-existing duplicates — like the incident above — exactly when a reviewer is looking at the dangerous destroy.
2. **Import time:** apply the same check when an `import` block or CLI `terraform import` targets an object whose identity matches an existing managed instance.

Scope the check to resource types whose provider defines an identity schema, and skip the rest. That avoids re-introducing the #33390 false positives by construction: abstract resources like `time_sleep` have no meaningful remote identity and would simply not participate. Defaulting to a warning rather than a hard error keeps intentional workflows (e.g. deliberate co-management patterns) working, while making the documented assumption visible when violated. A flag could opt into an error.

### Attempted Solutions

- Process discipline (only reviewed `import` blocks, no local applies). This does not catch duplicates already present in state.
- External audit in CI: `terraform state pull | jq`, grouping instances by `(type, id)`. This works, but every team reinvents it, and raw string IDs are exactly what #33434 established as unsound — and what resource identity was introduced to improve on.

### Terraform Version

n/a — feature request; behavior confirmed against v1.16 documentation and current `main` source.

### References

- [Import docs warning](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/import) — "bound to only one resource address"
- #33390 / #33434 — the earlier ID-based duplicate check among `import` blocks and why it was relaxed to a `to`-address check
- [`internal/configs/module.go`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/configs/module.go) — current duplicate-`to` validation; [`internal/states/instance_object.go`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/states/instance_object.go) — identity persisted in state
- [Resource identity concepts](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/framework/resources/identity) — implementable in both the [Plugin Framework](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/framework/resources/identity) and [SDKv2](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/sdkv2/resources/identity), so coverage extends to legacy-SDK providers
- [Bulk import](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/import/bulk) — HCP's cross-workspace detection via identity
- #29160 — related: auto-import of existing resources matching configuration

{"repository": "hashicorp/terraform", "task_candidate_id": 7123, "repository_id": 121, "issue_number": 39332, "github_issue_id": 5707508108, "html_url": "https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/39332", "created_at": "2026-10-05T06:33:56+00:00", "author_association": "NONE", "title": "Use resource identity to detect two state entries tracking the same remote object", "body_text": "### TL;DR
State can silently hold two addresses bound to one remote object. When that happens, `terraform plan` shows a routine-looking `destroy` that actually targets live infrastructure, with no hint that the object is also tracked elsewhere. An earlier ID-based duplicate check was deliberately relaxed (#33390 → #33434) because raw import IDs are not a sound uniqueness key — but resource identity (v1.12+) is exactly that key, and HCP Terraform already uses it in its bulk-import workflow to detect objects managed by another workspace. I propose bringing the same detection into core, within a single state: warn at plan time when two managed instances share an identity, and at import time when the imported object is already tracked.

### Use Cases

A real incident:

1. An AWS Secrets Manager secret was bound to a root-level address, likely via an old ad-hoc `terraform import` or a local apply of uncommitted config.
2. The same secret is properly managed by a module instance (`module.app.aws_secretsmanager_secret.rds_password`). State ended up with two entries pointing to one remote object.
3. The root-level address had no configuration, so `plan` proposed a `destroy`. Applying it would have scheduled deletion of the live secret referenced by running ECS tasks.
4. Nothing in the plan output indicated the duplication. A human reviewer caught it by noticing the name collision.

Duplicate tracking commonly arises from CLI `import` to a second address, local applies of never-merged config, or module refactors that import into the new address without removing the old entry. The resulting destroy diffs are indistinguishable from legitimate ones.

The import documentation states the assumption but nothing enforces it:

> Terraform expects that each remote object it is managing will be bound to only one resource address. (...) If you import the same object multiple times, Terraform may exhibit unwanted behavior.

### Current Behavior

- `plan` performs no duplicate detection across state entries.
- CLI `terraform import` performs no check against existing state.
- Config-driven import validates only duplicate *target addresses* among `import` blocks: [`internal/configs/module.go`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/configs/module.go) emits `"Duplicate import configuration for %q"` when two blocks share a `to` address. An earlier ID-based duplicate check was deliberately relaxed in #33434 (closing #33390), on the grounds that raw ID strings are not unique: abstract resources such as `time_sleep` legitimately return identical import responses for distinct instances, and as noted there, "Terraform cannot enforce any uniqueness in resources" from the ID alone.
- HCP Terraform uses resource identities in its bulk-import workflow "to determine when resources are managed by another workspace" ([bulk import docs](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/import/bulk)). The detection capability exists; it is not applied within a single state in core.

### Proposal

Resource identity (v1.12+) resolves the objection that led to relaxing the earlier check. Unlike a raw ID string, an identity is provider-defined with a documented uniqueness contract: it "must correspond to at most one remote object per provider" ([identity docs](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/framework/resources/identity)). Core already persists it per instance: `ResourceInstanceObject.Identity` is serialized into state as `IdentityJSON` with `IdentitySchemaVersion` ([`internal/states/instance_object.go`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/states/instance_object.go)). So the data needed for comparison is already in state.

1. **Plan time (primary):** warn when two managed instances of the same resource type in the same state share an identity, naming both addresses. This catches pre-existing duplicates — like the incident above — exactly when a reviewer is looking at the dangerous destroy.
2. **Import time:** apply the same check when an `import` block or CLI `terraform import` targets an object whose identity matches an existing managed instance.

Scope the check to resource types whose provider defines an identity schema, and skip the rest. That avoids re-introducing the #33390 false positives by construction: abstract resources like `time_sleep` have no meaningful remote identity and would simply not participate. Defaulting to a warning rather than a hard error keeps intentional workflows (e.g. deliberate co-management patterns) working, while making the documented assumption visible when violated. A flag could opt into an error.

### Attempted Solutions

- Process discipline (only reviewed `import` blocks, no local applies). This does not catch duplicates already present in state.
- External audit in CI: `terraform state pull | jq`, grouping instances by `(type, id)`. This works, but every team reinvents it, and raw string IDs are exactly what #33434 established as unsound — and what resource identity was introduced to improve on.

### Terraform Version

n/a — feature request; behavior confirmed against v1.16 documentation and current `main` source.

- [Import docs warning](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/import) — "bound to only one resource address"
- #33390 / #33434 — the earlier ID-based duplicate check among `import` blocks and why it was relaxed to a `to`-address check
- [`internal/configs/module.go`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/configs/module.go) — current duplicate-`to` validation; [`internal/states/instance_object.go`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/states/instance_object.go) — identity persisted in state
- [Resource identity concepts](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/framework/resources/identity) — implementable in both the [Plugin Framework](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/framework/resources/identity) and [SDKv2](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/sdkv2/resources/identity), so coverage extends to legacy-SDK providers
- [Bulk import](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/import/bulk) — HCP's cross-workspace detection via identity
- #29160 — related: auto-import of existing resources matching configuration

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.16.5
on darwin_arm64
+ provider registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/google v7.46.1
+ provider registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/google-beta v7.46.1
```

### Terraform Configuration Files

```terraform
terraform {
  backend "gcs" {
    bucket                = "xxxx-xxxx"
    prefix                  = "tests"
    storage_custom_endpoint = "https://storage.s3nsapis.fr/storage/v1/b."
  }
}
```


### Debug Output

```
Error: Failed to get existing workspaces: querying Cloud Storage failed: Get "https://storage.s3nsapis.fr/storage/v1/b/xxx-xxx/o?alt=json&delimiter=%2F&endOffset=&includeFoldersAsPrefixes=false&includeTrailingDelimiter=false&matchGlob=&pageToken=&prefix=tests%2F&prettyPrint=false&projection=full&startOffset=&versions=false": the configured universe domain ("googleapis.com") does not match the universe domain found in the credentials ("s3nsapis.fr"). If you haven't configured the universe domain explicitly, "googleapis.com" is the default
```


### Expected Behavior

TF gets the states for the bucket and initialize/plan/apply

### Actual Behavior

TF can't access the states because of a GCD universe mismatch

### Steps to Reproduce

`terraform init`

### Additional Context

The GCS backend configuration is working in terraform version <= 1.13.5.
Versions >= 1.14 do not work anymore.

If it's not possible to recover the former behavior, it would be great to be able to pass universe_domain as a parameter in gcs backend configuration the same way we can already do with provider configuration

### Terraform Versions and Benchmark Results

The aggregate `self` lookup path is present in Terraform v1.16.5 and v1.17.0-beta2: `internal/lang/eval.go` resolves `self` through `GetResource`, and `internal/terraform/evaluate.go` decodes all instances for that resource.

I ran the aggregate-resolution benchmark with 128 `for_each` instances (five runs; median shown). It calls `evaluationStateData.GetResource` directly, matching the aggregate path used by `self`. These are focused evaluator microbenchmarks, not end-to-end plan measurements. The temporary baseline-only harness was adapted from the fixture in PR #39328; it does not measure the targeted implementation.

| Terraform tag | Median ns/op | B/op | allocs/op |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| v1.16.5 | 911,679 | 991,735 | 13,117 |
| v1.17.0-beta2 | 779,313 | 890,137 | 11,708 |

Environment: Linux/amd64, Go 1.27.1, AMD Ryzen 7 255 with Radeon 780M Graphics.

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.16.6
on linux_amd64
```

**Regression.** Works on 1.16.0; broken on every release from 1.16.1 through 1.16.6 and on `main` (9ec49e06a8). Bisected to 892eccad86. Also broken on 1.15.8 and 1.15.9, before 038c6f72 fixed it in 1.16.0.

### Terraform Configuration Files

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Usage: ./repro.sh [path/to/terraform]     (defaults to `terraform` on PATH)
set -e
TF="${1:-terraform}"
cd "$(mktemp -d)"

# Step 1: r2 depends on r1, so state records the dependency r2 -> r1.
cat > main.tf <<'HCL'
resource "terraform_data" "r1" {}

resource "terraform_data" "r2" {
  depends_on = [terraform_data.r1]
}
HCL
"$TF" init  -input=false > /dev/null
"$TF" apply -auto-approve -input=false > /dev/null

# Step 2: r1 is removed from the configuration, and r2 is replaced with
# create_before_destroy newly enabled. (The dependency r2 -> r1 now exists only in state.)
cat > main.tf <<'HCL'
resource "terraform_data" "r2" {
  triggers_replace = 1
  lifecycle {
    create_before_destroy = true
  }
}
HCL
"$TF" version | head -1
"$TF" plan -input=false -no-color
```

### Debug Output

https://gist.github.com/Nilsils/3947f2861ca13468aecbeb1af3e1f69b

### Expected Behavior

Step 2 applies: create the new `r2`, destroy the old `r2` (its deposed object), then destroy `r1`, which only the old `r2` depended on.

```
Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 2 destroyed.
```

That is what 1.16.0 does, and what every version does when `create_before_destroy` was already declared on `r2` in step 1, or when `r2` is replaced without it. The step-2 configuration is a single resource with no references; nothing in it can form a cycle.

### Actual Behavior

```
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 2 to destroy.

Error: Cycle:
  terraform_data.r2
  terraform_data.r1 (destroy)
  terraform_data.r2 (destroy deposed 868d7490)
```

`terraform plan` prints the plan and then fails; `terraform apply` fails the same way. Deterministic: every run, on every affected version. Forcing the replacement with `-replace=terraform_data.r2` instead of `triggers_replace` gives the same result. State is unchanged by the failed run.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Save the script above as `repro.sh`.
2. Run it:
```
$ bash repro.sh                    # uses `terraform` from PATH
$ bash repro.sh /path/to/terraform # or name a binary
```

### Additional Context

_No response_

The configuration was not written by an LLM. It was produced by an automated metamorphic testing
pipeline (an e-graph based generator of equivalent Terraform programs), then minimised to the form
above.

Claude was used to assist with the writing of this report, with the reduction, the bisect and the
version sweep. Every claim in it was verified by running the configurations against the named
binaries.

# Context

This method below can cause flakey tests due to how it cannot guarantee that stdout and sterr content is combined in the same order that a command writes to those different streams:

https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/5b3637b786e6c68ad536288f963ec115d4c64e7e/internal/terminal/testing.go#L164-L177

## Test failures due to this helper:

* https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/pull/39398
* https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/pull/39404

# Proposal

We prevent this method being used in new tests, instead preferring explicit assertions about what's in stdout and stderr separately.
Old tests will need to be migrated to this approach.
Once the method's no longer used we would remove it from the codebase.

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.18.0-dev
on darwin_arm64
```

Built from `main` at 44fcc1316e (2026-10-16). The code path involved has not changed since 53cafc542b (2018), so released versions should behave the same way.

### Terraform Configuration Files

```terraform
resource "terraform_data" "example" {
  input = "hello"
}
```

### Debug Output

Relevant lines from `TF_LOG=trace` (timestamps stripped):

```
[TRACE] statemgr.Filesystem: preparing to manage state snapshots at ro/out.tfstate
[DEBUG] State storage *statemgr.Filesystem declined to persist a state snapshot
[TRACE] statemgr.Filesystem: reading initial snapshot from terraform.tfstate
[TRACE] statemgr.Filesystem: snapshot file has nil snapshot, but that's okay
[TRACE] statemgr.Filesystem: read nil snapshot
[TRACE] statemgr.Filesystem: preparing to manage state snapshots at ro/out.tfstate
Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
State path: ro/out.tfstate
```

### Expected Behavior

When the local state file can't be created or opened, `terraform apply` should fail with an error. Terraform's existing recovery path should then run: it reports "Failed to persist state to backend" and writes `errored.tfstate`. This is what already happens when locking is enabled, because `Lock()` calls the same `createStateFiles()` and returns its error.

### Actual Behavior

With `-lock=false`, the apply creates the resource, prints `Apply complete!` and `State path: ro/out.tfstate`, and exits 0, but **no state file is written anywhere**. The created resource is now untracked, and nothing tells the user.

The cause is in `internal/states/statemgr/filesystem.go`, in `(*Filesystem).writeState`:

```go
if s.stateFileOut == nil {
    if err := s.createStateFiles(); err != nil {
        return nil   // error is discarded
    }
}
```

With locking enabled, `Lock()` calls `createStateFiles()` first and handles the error correctly. Without a lock, `writeState` is the first caller, so the error is swallowed and the method reports success.

### Steps to Reproduce

```shell
mkdir repro && cd repro
cat > main.tf <<'EOF'
resource "terraform_data" "example" {
  input = "hello"
}
EOF
mkdir ro && chmod 0555 ro
terraform init
terraform apply -auto-approve -lock=false -state-out=ro/out.tfstate
echo "exit=$?"     # exit=0, "Apply complete!"
ls ro              # empty: no state was written
```

For comparison, the same command without `-lock=false` fails correctly with `Error acquiring the state lock ... open ro/out.tfstate: permission denied`.

### Additional Context

I tried the one-line change `return nil` → `return err` locally. The repro above then fails with `Error: Failed to persist state to backend` and writes `errored.tfstate` to the working directory, which is the intended recovery behaviour.

If the team agrees this is the right fix, I'd be happy to open a PR with it, plus a regression test in `internal/states/statemgr/filesystem_test.go`.

### References

- #34266 is a related but separate local-state durability issue (non-atomic writes). This one is about the error being discarded entirely.

### Terraform Configuration Files
```
# Provisioners run scripts or commands as part of resource creation or destruction. 
# They are useful for tasks Terraform’s declarative model can’t express, but HashiCorp calls them a last resort,
#  because Terraform can’t track what a script did. 
# They don’t appear in plan, and they only run when the resource is created or destroyed.
# az vm list-skus --location southindia --size Standard_B --resource-type virtualMachines --output table
resource "azurerm_resource_group" "rg" {
  name     = "azurerm"
  location = var.location

  provisioner "local-exec" {
    command = "echo resource group created with name ${self.name}"
  }
}

check "location" {
  assert {
    condition   = azurerm_resource_group.rg.location == "southindia"
    error_message = "location should be southindia"
  }
}

resource "azurerm_virtual_network" "vnet" {
    name = "vnet"
    location = var.location
    address_space = ["10.0.0.0/16"]
    resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name
}

resource "azurerm_subnet" "subnet" {
    name = "subnet"
    resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name
    virtual_network_name = azurerm_virtual_network.vnet.name
    address_prefixes = ["10.0.2.0/24"]
}

resource "azurerm_network_interface" "nic" {
    name = "nic"
    location = var.location
    resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name

    ip_configuration {
        name = "internal"
        private_ip_address_allocation = "Dynamic"
        subnet_id = azurerm_subnet.subnet.id
    }
}

resource "azurerm_public_ip" "pip" {
  name                = "demo-pip"
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.rg.location
  allocation_method   = "Static"
  sku                 = "Standard"
}


resource "azurerm_linux_virtual_machine" "vm" {
  name                  = "demo-vm"
  resource_group_name   = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name
  location              = azurerm_resource_group.rg.location
  size                  = "Standard_B1s"
  admin_username        = "azureuser"
  network_interface_ids = [azurerm_network_interface.nic.id]

  admin_ssh_key {
    username   = "azureuser"
    public_key = file("~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub")
  }

  os_disk {
    caching              = "ReadWrite"
    storage_account_type = "Standard_LRS"
  }

  source_image_reference {
    publisher = "Canonical"
    offer     = "0001-com-ubuntu-server-jammy"
    sku       = "22_04-lts"
    version   = "latest"
  }

  connection {
    type        = "ssh"
    user        = "azureuser"
    private_key = file("~/.ssh/id_rsa")
    host        = azurerm_public_ip.pip.ip_address
  }

  provisioner "remote-exec" {
    inline = [
      "sudo apt-get update -y",
      "sudo apt-get install -y nginx",
      "sudo systemctl enable --now nginx"
    ]
  }
}

### Terraform Version

```shell
terraform version
Terraform v1.16.6
on linux_amd64
```

### Use Cases

We currently run almost 1000 root modules in our environment. Our average plan file size is 30mb. This adds up to a lot of bandwidth used when we transfer the plans from our CI runners in our cloud environment to our source control. There is also the storage costs of plans as well as network bandwidth. 

### Attempted Solutions

Terraform does not currently support additional compression providers for plans.

### Proposal

I propose adding Zstd as an additional compression backend to Deflate. Our testing of this showed a decrease in our plan file size from 30mb to 1.7mb at no loss of compute efficiency, compression and decompression times were the same. Based on my reading of how Terraform utilizes the plan files, Deflate's incremental decompression does not seem to be used, so the fact that Zstd does not allow this isn't a blocker.

### References

I have not found any previous issues discussing this.

body_text:
### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.11.3
on windows_amd64
```

Also reproduced with a local build of `main` at cdbff3e.

### Terraform Configuration Files

```terraform
terraform {
  required_providers {
    null = {
      source  = "hashicorp/null"
      version = "3.2.1"
    }
  }
}
```

### Debug Output

Not applicable: nothing is logged, because the error from the failed delete is discarded.

### Expected Behavior

After `terraform init` installs a provider downloaded from a registry, the downloaded archive is deleted from the temporary directory.

### Actual Behavior

The archive stays behind as `%TEMP%\terraform-provider<random>`: one file for every provider package downloaded, on every init (4.7 MB for `hashicorp/null` 3.2.1, about 180 MB for `hashicorp/aws`). `terraform providers lock` leaves one per provider per requested platform. On one workstation 1,764 of these files (195 GB) built up in ten days and filled the system drive.

### Steps to Reproduce

PowerShell, in an empty directory:

1. Save the configuration above as `work\main.tf`.
2. `mkdir tmp; $env:TMP = "$PWD\tmp"; $env:TEMP = "$PWD\tmp"`
3. `terraform -chdir=work init`
4. `Get-ChildItem tmp` lists `terraform-provider<N>`.

### Additional Context

`installFromHTTPURL` in `internal/providercache/package_install.go`:

```go
f, err := os.CreateTemp("", "terraform-provider")
// ...
defer f.Close()
defer os.Remove(f.Name())
```

Deferred calls run last-in, first-out, so `os.Remove` runs while `f` is still open. On Windows that removal fails and its error is discarded. Linux and macOS allow removing a file that is still open, so the leak only shows on Windows.

The handle is only used to reserve the name (`HttpGetter.GetFile` opens the file again by path), so closing it straight away and deferring only the removal fixes it. That change, with a regression test, is on a branch: https://github.com/rmagri/terraform/commit/a74cbfb6f8802187afee2e6dc802562470fec29a. With a local build of `main` the reproduction above leaves the archive behind; with the change it leaves nothing. I'm happy to open a PR if the approach is acceptable.

Workaround until then: with a dependency lock file and `TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR` set, installs served from the cache download nothing and leave nothing behind.

### References

None found.

{"key": "hashicorp/terraform#39434", "repository": "hashicorp/terraform", "issue_number": 39434, "github_issue_id": "5980970217", "url": "https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/39434", "title": "Provider archives downloaded by terraform init are left in the temporary directory on Windows", "source_files": ["D:\OSS-Mentor\data\teacher_clickhouse\inventory_20261022T172108Z\issues_discovered.json"], "historical_labels": [], "beginner_difficulty_confirmed": false, "frozen": false, "decision": "availability_passed", "reason": "current_unassigned_no_observed_claim_or_open_pr", "open_pr_references": [], "claim_signals": [], "current_labels": ["bug", "windows", "new"], "current_signal_group": "historical_signal_only", "body": "### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.11.3
on windows_amd64
```

Also reproduced with a local build of `main` at cdbff3e.

### Terraform Configuration Files

```terraform
terraform {
  required_providers {
    null = {
      source  = "hashicorp/null"
      version = "3.2.1"
    }
  }
}
```

### Debug Output

Not applicable: nothing is logged, because the error from the failed delete is discarded.

### Expected Behavior

After `terraform init` installs a provider downloaded from a registry, the downloaded archive is deleted from the temporary directory.

### Actual Behavior

The archive stays behind as `%TEMP%\terraform-provider<random>`: one file for every provider package downloaded, on every init (4.7 MB for `hashicorp/null` 3.2.1, about 180 MB for `hashicorp/aws`). `terraform providers lock` leaves one per provider per requested platform. On one workstation 1,764 of these files (195 GB) built up in ten days and filled the system drive.

### Steps to Reproduce

PowerShell, in an empty directory:

1. Save the configuration above as `work\main.tf`.
2. `mkdir tmp; $env:TMP = "$PWD\tmp"; $env:TEMP = "$PWD\tmp"`
3. `terraform -chdir=work init`
4. `Get-ChildItem tmp` lists `terraform-provider<N>`.

### Additional Context

`installFromHTTPURL` in `internal/providercache/package_install.go`:

```go
f, err := os.CreateTemp("", "terraform-provider")
// ...
defer f.Close()
defer os.Remove(f.Name())
```

Deferred calls run last-in, first-out, so `os.Remove` runs while `f` is still open. On Windows that removal fails and its error is discarded. Linux and macOS allow removing a file that is still open, so the leak only shows on Windows.

The handle is only used to reserve the name (`HttpGetter.GetFile` opens the file again by path), so closing it straight away and deferring only the removal fixes it. That change, with a regression test, is on a branch: https://github.com/rmagri/terraform/commit/a74cbfb6f8802187afee2e6dc802562470fec29a. With a local build of `main` the reproduction above leaves the archive behind; with the change it leaves nothing. I'm happy to open a PR if the approach is acceptable.

Workaround until then: with a dependency lock file and `TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR` set, installs served from the cache download nothing and leave nothing behind.

### References

None found.

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.16.6
on darwin_arm64
```

### Use Cases

AWS WAF byte match rules can apply an `MD5` text transformation to a request component before comparing it with `SearchString`. Writing such a rule requires the comparison value to be the Base64 encoding of the raw 16-byte MD5 digest.

Terraform's `md5` function returns a hexadecimal string. `base64encode(md5(value))` encodes the ASCII hexadecimal representation, not the raw digest bytes. The existing `base64sha256` and `base64sha512` functions provide the required behavior for their respective algorithms, but there is no MD5 equivalent or general conversion function.

This differs from converting between two provider arguments. The value is derived from arbitrary input and must match a transformation performed by the remote service.

### Attempted Solutions

The closest expression using built-in functions is:

```hcl
base64encode(md5(var.value))
```

This Base64-encodes the hexadecimal digest rather than the raw digest bytes.

A shell workaround is:

```shell
printf '%s' "$INPUT" | openssl dgst -md5 -binary | openssl base64 -A
```

Using this from Terraform requires an external data source, provider-defined function, or another out-of-process step. This adds dependencies and execution overhead for a deterministic transformation.

### Proposal

Provide a built-in way to return the Base64 encoding of raw MD5 digest bytes.

One option is a `base64md5` function, consistent with `base64sha256` and `base64sha512`:

```hcl
base64md5("hello world")
```

Alternatively, a general function that directly transcodes hexadecimal data to Base64 would allow composition without introducing binary strings:

```hcl
base64_from_hex(md5("hello world"))
```

The exact API name is open for discussion. In either form, the result would be:

```text
XrY7u+Ae7tCTyyK7j1rNww==
```

### References

- #19245 requested `base64md5` and was closed in favor of provider-side conversion.
- #26163 requested hex-to-binary conversion and was closed after its original provider-specific use case was resolved.

body_text:
Hi,

I personally don't find the autocompletion editing for function signature to be helpful as a programmer - I just read the arguments from the tooltip instead. It would be convenient to have an option to disable this while still being able to autocomplete the function name itself. This could also be a separate entry in the completion menu or shortcut, since you might need the function name itself as a variable (i. e. as the target of a pointer).

For example, if I have the zig function `pub fn reallyCoolFunction (bar: [] const u8, baz: u64) void {...}` declared, the autocomplete option would just expand to `reallyCoolFunction`, instead of  `reallyCoolFunction (bar: [] const u8, baz: u64)`.

body_text:
Description

Incrementing `9__99` with `Ctrl-a` causes the editor to stop responding.

Steps to reproduce

1. Enter `9__99` in a buffer.
2. Select the entire number without the newline.
3. Press `Ctrl-a`.

Expected behavior

The command should finish without hanging.
If consecutive separators are unsupported then leaving the selection unchanged would be preferable to freezing the editor.

Actual behavior

The editor stops responding.
An integration test reproducing these key presses did not finish within 10 seconds and had to be terminated.
A control test incrementing `001000` completed successfully.

Possible cause

In `helix-core/src/increment/integer.rs` adjacent separators produce `spacing = 0`.
The subsequent loop never advances when `spacing` is zero:

```rust
while index - prefix_length > spacing {
    index -= spacing;
    // A separator is inserted on each iteration.
}
```

The index stays unchanged while the string keeps growing.

Version

Reproduced on `master` at commit `079a789e8cb08ead67f19e1971a1b7438b37354b` using the Helix integration test harness on macOS.
